sanskrit:
धृतराष्ट्र उवाच ।
धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः ।
मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत सञ्जय ॥१॥
translation: Dhritarashtra said: What did the sons of Pandu and my own sons do, O Sanjaya, when they assembled, eager to fight, on the sacred field of Kurukshetra?
explanation: The Gita opens with a blind king's anxious question. Dhritarashtra's own words betray him — he separates "my sons" from "Pandu's sons," revealing the attachment and partiality that will drive the entire tragedy. The battlefield is called dharma-kshetra, the field of righteousness, hinting that this is more than a war — it is a test of conscience.

sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच ।
दृष्ट्वा तु पाण्डवानीकं व्यूढं दुर्योधनस्तदा ।
आचार्यमुपसङ्गम्य राजा वचनमब्रवीत् ॥२॥
translation: Sanjaya said: Having observed the Pandava army arrayed for battle, King Duryodhana approached his teacher Drona and spoke these words.
explanation: The narrative shifts to Duryodhana, whose first act is a calculated one — seeking out his teacher Drona not for guidance, but to boast and stir anxiety about the opposing army. A subtle character study: insecurity dressed as bravado.

sanskrit:
पश्यैतां पाण्डुपुत्राणामाचार्य महतीं चमूम् ।
व्यूढां द्रुपदपुत्रेण तव शिष्येण धीमता ॥३॥
translation: Behold, O teacher, this great army of the sons of Pandu, arrayed by your own gifted disciple, the son of Drupada.
explanation: Duryodhana needles Drona with an uncomfortable irony — the army opposing them was organized by Dhrishtadyumna, Drona's own former student. Old loyalties and present enmities tangle from the very first verses.

sanskrit:
अत्र शूरा महेष्वासा भीमार्जुनसमा युधि ।
युयुधानो विराटश्च द्रुपदश्च महारथः ॥४॥
translation: Here are heroes, great archers, equal in battle to Bhima and Arjuna — Yuyudhana, Virata, and the great chariot-warrior Drupada.
explanation: Duryodhana begins listing the Pandava side's warriors — a roll call meant to sound impressive, but really betraying his own nervousness at the scale of the opposition.

sanskrit:
धृष्टकेतुश्चेकितानः काशिराजश्च वीर्यवान् ।
पुरुजित्कुन्तिभोजश्च शैब्यश्च नरपुङ्गवः ॥५॥
translation: Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the valiant king of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Shaibya, the best of men.
explanation: The list of Pandava commanders continues — each name would have carried weight and reputation for the original audience, signaling the seriousness of the force assembled against the Kauravas.

sanskrit:
युधामन्युश्च विक्रान्त उत्तमौजाश्च वीर्यवान् ।
सौभद्रो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्व एव महारथाः ॥६॥
translation: The valiant Yudhamanyu, the mighty Uttamaujas, the son of Subhadra, and the sons of Draupadi — all of them great chariot-warriors.
explanation: The roll call closes with Abhimanyu (Subhadra's son) and Draupadi's five sons — the younger generation of the Pandava side, whose presence raises the stakes of the coming war for the entire family line.

sanskrit:
अस्माकं तु विशिष्टा ये तान्निबोध द्विजोत्तम ।
नायका मम सैन्यस्य संज्ञार्थं तान्ब्रवीमि ते ॥७॥
translation: Now hear, O best of the twice-born, of the distinguished ones on our side — the commanders of my army. I name them for your information.
explanation: Having built up the enemy's strength, Duryodhana pivots to reassure Drona (and himself) by naming his own side's leaders — a commander managing morale before battle.

sanskrit:
भवान्भीष्मश्च कर्णश्च कृपश्च समितिञ्जयः ।
अश्वत्थामा विकर्णश्च सौमदत्तिस्तथैव च ॥८॥
translation: Yourself, Bhishma, Karna, the ever-victorious Kripa, Ashvatthama, Vikarna, and the son of Somadatta.
explanation: Duryodhana names his own generals — starting with Drona himself and the towering figure of Bhishma, the two elder statesmen whose loyalty, despite personal reservations about the war, remains with the Kaurava side.

sanskrit:
अन्ये च बहवः शूरा मदर्थे त्यक्तजीविताः ।
नानाशस्त्रप्रहरणाः सर्वे युद्धविशारदाः ॥९॥
translation: And many other heroes, skilled in various weapons, all experts in warfare, who have given up their lives for my sake.
explanation: Duryodhana closes his roster with a broader claim — that countless warriors are ready to die for him personally. Telling that he frames their loyalty as owed to him, not to any cause of justice.

sanskrit:
अपर्याप्तं तदस्माकं बलं भीष्माभिरक्षितम् ।
पर्याप्तं त्विदमेतेषां बलं भीमाभिरक्षितम् ॥१०॥
translation: Our army, protected by Bhishma, is insufficient, while their army, protected by Bhima, is sufficient.
explanation: This much-debated verse has puzzled commentators for centuries — Duryodhana seems to admit his own side's limits despite Bhishma's leadership, revealing a private anxiety beneath his public bravado.

sanskrit:
अयनेषु च सर्वेषु यथाभागमवस्थिताः ।
भीष्ममेवाभिरक्षन्तु भवन्तः सर्व एव हि ॥११॥
translation: Therefore, all of you, stationed in your respective positions at the entrances of the army divisions, should support Bhishma alone.
explanation: Duryodhana issues his first tactical order — protect Bhishma at all costs. The old grandsire is treated as the linchpin of the entire Kaurava strategy.

sanskrit:
तस्य सञ्जनयन्हर्षं कुरुवृद्धः पितामहः ।
सिंहनादं विनद्योच्चैः शङ्खं दध्मौ प्रतापवान् ॥१२॥
translation: Then Bhishma, the powerful grandsire of the Kurus, the eldest of the dynasty, roared like a lion and blew his conch shell loudly, cheering Duryodhana.
explanation: The first sound of the war — Bhishma's conch, meant to fill Duryodhana with confidence. A moment of theatre before the real fighting starts.

sanskrit:
ततः शङ्खाश्च भेर्यश्च पणवानकगोमुखाः ।
सहसैवाभ्यहन्यन्त स शब्दस्तुमुलोऽभवत् ॥१३॥
translation: Then conches, kettledrums, tabors, drums, and horns were suddenly sounded together, and the sound became tumultuous.
explanation: A cascade of instruments erupts across the battlefield — the Gita opens not in silence but in a wall of sound, setting an almost cinematic tone before a single arrow is fired.

sanskrit:
ततः श्वेतैर्हयैर्युक्ते महति स्यन्दने स्थितौ ।
माधवः पाण्डवश्चैव दिव्यौ शङ्खौ प्रदध्मतुः ॥१४॥
translation: Then, seated in a great chariot yoked with white horses, Krishna and Arjuna blew their divine conches.
explanation: The scene shifts to the other side. Krishna and Arjuna, sharing one magnificent chariot, answer the Kaurava fanfare — the divine paired with the human, a partnership at the heart of the entire Gita.

sanskrit:
पाञ्चजन्यं हृषीकेशो देवदत्तं धनञ्जयः ।
पौण्ड्रं दध्मौ महाशङ्खं भीमकर्मा वृकोदरः ॥१५॥
translation: Krishna blew his conch Panchajanya, Arjuna blew Devadatta, and Bhima, of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Paundra.
explanation: Each hero's conch is named individually — a detail that gives even the instruments of war a kind of personality and mythic weight in this tradition.

sanskrit:
अनन्तविजयं राजा कुन्तीपुत्रो युधिष्ठिरः ।
नकुलः सहदेवश्च सुघोषमणिपुष्पकौ ॥१६॥
translation: King Yudhishthira, son of Kunti, blew his conch Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughosha and Manipushpaka.
explanation: The five Pandava brothers each sound their own conch in turn — a roll call of unity, each brother individually named and honored before the battle begins.

sanskrit:
काश्यश्च परमेष्वासः शिखण्डी च महारथः ।
धृष्टद्युम्नो विराटश्च सात्यकिश्चापराजितः ॥१७॥
translation: The great archer, the king of Kashi, the mighty warrior Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and the unconquered Satyaki.
explanation: More key figures on the Pandava side sound their conches — including Shikhandi and Dhrishtadyumna, both of whom will play pivotal roles later in the war's most fateful moments.

sanskrit:
द्रुपदो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्वशः पृथिवीपते ।
सौभद्रश्च महाबाहुः शङ्खान्दध्मुः पृथक्पृथक् ॥१८॥
translation: Drupada, the sons of Draupadi, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadra all blew their conches, each one separately, O ruler of the earth.
explanation: The list of conches closes — Sanjaya narrates all this to the blind king Dhritarashtra, a reminder throughout Chapter 1 that this whole scene is being relayed secondhand to a father anxious about his sons' fate.

sanskrit:
स घोषो धार्तराष्ट्राणां हृदयानि व्यदारयत् ।
नभश्च पृथिवीं चैव तुमुलोऽभ्यनुनादयन् ॥१९॥
translation: That tumultuous sound, echoing through the sky and the earth, shattered the hearts of Dhritarashtra's sons.
explanation: The combined blast of the Pandava conches has a visceral effect on the Kaurava side — a foreshadowing, perhaps, of the fear and doom that awaits them despite their earlier bravado.

sanskrit:
अथ व्यवस्थितान्दृष्ट्वा धार्तराष्ट्रान्कपिध्वजः ।
प्रवृत्ते शस्त्रसम्पाते धनुरुद्यम्य पाण्डवः ।
हृषीकेशं तदा वाक्यमिदमाह महीपते ॥२०॥
translation: Then, seeing Dhritarashtra's sons arrayed for battle, as the weapons were about to clash, Arjuna, whose banner bore Hanuman, took up his bow and spoke these words to Krishna, O king.
explanation: Arjuna, marked by the emblem of Hanuman on his flag, raises his bow — the moment right before speech, right before the crisis that will unfold across the rest of the chapter.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच ।
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये रथं स्थापय मेऽच्युत ।
यावदेतान्निरीक्षेऽहं योद्धुकामानवस्थितान् ॥२१॥
translation: Arjuna said: O Krishna, place my chariot between the two armies, so that I may see those assembled here, eager for battle.
explanation: Arjuna's very first request to Krishna is simple but momentous — he wants to see, clearly and directly, exactly who stands opposed to him. The entire Gita will unfold from this single moment of looking.

sanskrit: कैर्मया सह योद्धव्यमस्मिन् रणसमुद्यमे ॥२२॥
translation: ...with whom I must fight in this great combat.
explanation: The continuation of Arjuna's request — he wants to know, before the battle begins, precisely whose lives are about to be weighed against his own decision to fight.

sanskrit:
योत्स्यमानानवेक्षेऽहं य एतेऽत्र समागताः ।
धार्तराष्ट्रस्य दुर्बुद्धेर्युद्धे प्रियचिकीर्षवः ॥२३॥
translation: Let me see those who have gathered here to fight, intending to please the evil-minded son of Dhritarashtra in this war.
explanation: Arjuna already names Duryodhana as 'evil-minded' — his moral judgment of the cause is formed before he even looks upon the army. What follows will complicate that judgment considerably.

sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच ।
एवमुक्तो हृषीकेशो गुडाकेशेन भारत ।
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये स्थापयित्वा रथोत्तमम् ॥२४॥
translation: Sanjaya said: Thus addressed by Arjuna, Krishna drove that magnificent chariot between the two armies, O descendant of Bharata.
explanation: Krishna simply complies, without objection or comment — the first of many moments in the Gita where he lets Arjuna arrive at his own crisis before intervening with teaching.

sanskrit:
भीष्मद्रोणप्रमुखतः सर्वेषां च महीक्षिताम् ।
उवाच पार्थ पश्यैतान्समवेतान्कुरूनिति ॥२५॥
translation: In front of Bhishma, Drona, and all the rulers of the earth, Krishna said: O Partha, behold these assembled Kurus.
explanation: Krishna's words are almost clinically simple — "behold these Kurus" — a plain instruction that will trigger an overwhelming emotional collapse in Arjuna over the following verses.

sanskrit:
तत्रापश्यत्स्थितान्पार्थः पितॄनथ पितामहान् ।
आचार्यान्मातुलान्भ्रातॄन्पुत्रान्पौत्रान्सखींस्तथा ।
श्वशुरान्सुहृदश्चैव सेनयोरुभयोरपि ॥२६॥
translation: There Arjuna saw, standing in both armies, fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends, fathers-in-law, and well-wishers.
explanation: The scene pulls back to reveal the full horror of Arjuna's situation — this isn't a war against strangers, but against nearly every close relation in his life, on both sides of the field.

sanskrit:
तान्समीक्ष्य स कौन्तेयः सर्वान्बन्धूनवस्थितान् ।
कृपया परयाविष्टो विषीदन्निदमब्रवीत् ॥२७॥
translation: Seeing all these kinsmen arrayed before him, Arjuna, the son of Kunti, overwhelmed with deep compassion, spoke these sorrowful words.
explanation: The word used here — kripa, compassion — is significant. Arjuna's crisis isn't cowardice; it springs from an excess of love and pity for people he's about to be asked to kill.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच ।
दृष्ट्वेमं स्वजनं कृष्ण युयुत्सुं समुपस्थितम् ।
सीदन्ति मम गात्राणि मुखं च परिशुष्यति ॥२८॥
translation: Arjuna said: O Krishna, seeing my own kinsmen standing here, eager to fight, my limbs give way and my mouth goes dry.
explanation: Arjuna's grief is described in strikingly physical terms — this isn't abstract philosophizing but a full bodily collapse, the kind any of us might recognize from real moments of dread and heartbreak.

sanskrit:
वेपथुश्च शरीरे मे रोमहर्षश्च जायते ।
गाण्डीवं स्रंसते हस्तात्त्वक्चैव परिदह्यते ॥२९॥
translation: My body trembles, my hair stands on end, my bow Gandiva slips from my hand, and my skin burns.
explanation: The physical symptoms escalate — trembling, goosebumps, a burning sensation. Arjuna, one of history's greatest warriors, is described experiencing what today we'd easily recognize as an acute panic response.

sanskrit:
न च शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं भ्रमतीव च मे मनः ।
निमित्तानि च पश्यामि विपरीतानि केशव ॥३०॥
translation: I am unable to stand steady, my mind seems to be reeling, and I see only adverse omens, O Keshava.
explanation: Arjuna's disorientation deepens into something like vertigo — a mind spinning, unable to find solid ground, seeing doom in every direction.

sanskrit:
न च श्रेयोऽनुपश्यामि हत्वा स्वजनमाहवे ।
न काङ्क्षे विजयं कृष्ण न च राज्यं सुखानि च ॥३१॥
translation: I see no good in killing my own kinsmen in this battle. I do not desire victory, Krishna, nor kingdom, nor pleasures.
explanation: Arjuna's conclusion crystallizes: whatever the political stakes, no personal gain — victory, kingdom, or comfort — seems worth this cost to him.

sanskrit:
किं नो राज्येन गोविन्द किं भोगैर्जीवितेन वा ।
येषामर्थे काङ्क्षितं नो राज्यं भोगाः सुखानि च ॥३२॥
translation: Of what use to us are kingdom, enjoyment, or even life itself, Govinda, when it is for the sake of others that we would desire these things?
explanation: Arjuna begins to spell out the paradox at the heart of his despair: kingdom and pleasure only matter because of the people he'd share them with.

sanskrit:
त इमेऽवस्थिता युद्धे प्राणांस्त्यक्त्वा धनानि च ।
आचार्याः पितरः पुत्रास्तथैव च पितामहाः ॥३३॥
translation: Those very people — teachers, fathers, sons, and grandfathers — stand here in battle, ready to give up their lives and wealth.
explanation: The list of relations Arjuna would have to fight grows even more specific and painful — not abstract 'enemies,' but teachers, fathers, sons.

sanskrit:
मातुलाः श्वशुराः पौत्राः श्यालाः सम्बन्धिनस्तथा ।
एतान्न हन्तुमिच्छामि घ्नतोऽपि मधुसूदन ॥३४॥
translation: Uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other kin — I have no wish to kill them, even if they kill me, O Madhusudana.
explanation: Arjuna reaches the full weight of his paradox: he would rather die at their hands than take theirs, even in self-defense.

sanskrit:
अपि त्रैलोक्यराज्यस्य हेतोः किं नु महीकृते ।
निहत्य धार्तराष्ट्रान्नः का प्रीतिः स्याज्जनार्दन ॥३५॥
translation: What satisfaction could we have, Janardana, in killing the sons of Dhritarashtra, even for the sake of dominion over the three worlds, let alone this earth?
explanation: Arjuna raises the emotional stakes to their maximum — even the grandest possible prize, rulership of the entire universe, wouldn't justify this act to him.

sanskrit:
पापमेवाश्रयेदस्मान्हत्वैतानाततायिनः ।
तस्मान्नार्हा वयं हन्तुं धार्तराष्ट्रान्सबान्धवान् ।
स्वजनं हि कथं हत्वा सुखिनः स्याम माधव ॥३६॥
translation: Only sin would come to us by killing these aggressors. Therefore we should not kill the sons of Dhritarashtra and our kinsmen. How could we be happy, Madhava, by killing our own family?
explanation: Arjuna anticipates and rejects the argument that self-defense might justify the killing — even calling the enemy 'aggressors,' he concludes no resulting happiness could outweigh the sin of killing one's own family.

sanskrit:
यद्यप्येते न पश्यन्ति लोभोपहतचेतसः ।
कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं मित्रद्रोहे च पातकम् ॥३७॥
translation: Even if they, their minds overpowered by greed, see no wrong in destroying the family or in treachery toward friends...
explanation: Arjuna begins to draw a moral distinction between himself and his opponents — conceding that greed has blinded the other side to the consequences of what's about to happen.

sanskrit:
कथं न ज्ञेयमस्माभिः पापादस्मान्निवर्तितुम् ।
कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं प्रपश्यद्भिर्जनार्दन ॥३८॥
translation: ...why should we, who clearly see this wrong, not turn away from such sin, O Janardana?
explanation: The conclusion of Arjuna's argument: clear-sightedness itself, he insists, creates a responsibility to refuse wrongdoing — even if the other side cannot see it.

sanskrit:
कुलक्षये प्रणश्यन्ति कुलधर्माः सनातनाः ।
धर्मे नष्टे कुलं कृत्स्नमधर्मोऽभिभवत्युत ॥३९॥
translation: When a family is destroyed, its ancient traditions perish; and when tradition is lost, unrighteousness overtakes the entire family.
explanation: Arjuna's argument widens from personal grief to a broader social concern — the collapse of a family doesn't just mean individual deaths, but the unraveling of an entire moral and cultural fabric.

sanskrit:
अधर्माभिभवात्कृष्ण प्रदुष्यन्ति कुलस्त्रियः ।
स्त्रीषु दुष्टासु वार्ष्णेय जायते वर्णसङ्करः ॥४०॥
translation: When unrighteousness prevails, Krishna, the women of the family are affected; and from that, social confusion arises.
explanation: This verse reflects the social assumptions of its ancient context rather than a timeless ethical claim. Arjuna's broader point is his fear that war's destruction ripples outward into the collapse of an entire social order, not just onto the battlefield.

sanskrit:
सङ्करो नरकायैव कुलघ्नानां कुलस्य च ।
पतन्ति पितरो ह्येषां लुप्तपिण्डोदकक्रियाः ॥४१॥
translation: Such confusion leads to ruin for the destroyers of the family and for the family itself; the ancestors fall, deprived of ritual offerings.
explanation: Arjuna invokes the ancient belief that ancestral spirits depend on ritual offerings from living descendants — a family's collapse, in this view, harms not just the living but generations already passed.

sanskrit:
दोषैरेतैः कुलघ्नानां वर्णसङ्करकारकैः ।
उत्साद्यन्ते जातिधर्माः कुलधर्माश्च शाश्वताः ॥४२॥
translation: By these faults of the destroyers of the family, the eternal traditions of community and family are destroyed.
explanation: Arjuna continues building his case for why the war would be catastrophic beyond the immediate deaths — an entire inherited social and moral order, in his view, hangs in the balance.

sanskrit:
उत्सन्नकुलधर्माणां मनुष्याणां जनार्दन ।
नरके नियतं वासो भवतीत्यनुशुश्रुम ॥४३॥
translation: We have heard, O Janardana, that people whose family traditions are destroyed are destined to dwell in suffering.
explanation: Arjuna appeals to received wisdom and tradition itself as evidence for his position — this isn't just his own opinion, he says, but something 'we have heard,' grounding his argument in cultural authority.

sanskrit:
अहो बत महत्पापं कर्तुं व्यवसिता वयम् ।
यद्राज्यसुखलोभेन हन्तुं स्वजनमुद्यताः ॥४४॥
translation: Alas, what a great sin we are resolved to commit, that out of greed for royal pleasure we are prepared to kill our own kinsmen!
explanation: Arjuna's despair peaks in open self-reproach — notice he includes himself in the collective guilt ('we are resolved'), even though it is the Kauravas, not the Pandavas, who initiated hostilities.

sanskrit:
यदि मामप्रतीकारमशस्त्रं शस्त्रपाणयः ।
धार्तराष्ट्रा रणे हन्युस्तन्मे क्षेमतरं भवेत् ॥४५॥
translation: If the armed sons of Dhritarashtra should kill me, unarmed and unresisting, in battle, that would be better for me.
explanation: Arjuna reaches the furthest point of his despair — he would rather die passively than commit the act of killing his relatives, revealing just how completely his resolve to fight has collapsed.

sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच ।
एवमुक्त्वार्जुनः सङ्ख्ये रथोपस्थ उपाविशत् ।
विसृज्य सशरं चापं शोकसंविग्नमानसः ॥४६॥
translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna cast aside his bow and arrows and sat down on his chariot, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
explanation: Chapter 1 ends not with resolution but total collapse — Arjuna literally lays down his weapons and sits in despair. This is the emotional low point the entire rest of the Gita will respond to, starting in Chapter 2.

sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच
तं तथा कृपयाऽविष्टमश्रुपूर्णाकुलेक्षणम्।
विषीदन्तमिदं वाक्यमुवाच मधुसूदनः ॥१॥
translation: Sanjaya said: To him, overcome by pity, his troubled eyes brimming with tears, sunk in despair, Madhusudana spoke these words.
explanation: Sanjaya frames the scene precisely — Arjuna is not merely sad but physically undone, eyes clouded over. Krishna's reply comes to a man in that exact state, which shapes everything about how the teaching begins.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
कुतस्त्वा कश्मलमिदं विषमे समुपस्थितम्।
अनार्यजुष्टमस्वर्ग्यमकीर्तिकरमर्जुन ॥२॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: Where has this faintheartedness come from at such a moment, Arjuna? It is unworthy of a noble man, it closes the gate to heaven, and it brings disgrace.
explanation: Krishna's opening move is not comfort but challenge. He names the collapse kashmala — a stain, a clouding — and questions its timing. The teaching begins by refusing to accept despair as wisdom.

sanskrit:
क्लैब्यं मा स्म गमः पार्थ नैतत्त्वय्युपपद्यते।
क्षुद्रं हृदयदौर्बल्यं त्यक्त्वोत्तिष्ठ परन्तप ॥३॥
translation: Do not yield to this unmanly weakness, Partha — it does not suit you. Shake off this petty faintness of heart and rise, scorcher of foes.
explanation: The tone is deliberately bracing, almost a slap. Krishna appeals to Arjuna's own self-image as parantapa, scorcher of foes, using the name itself to remind him who he has been.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
कथं भीष्ममहं संख्ये द्रोणं च मधुसूदन।
इषुभिः प्रतियोत्स्यामि पूजार्हावरिसूदन ॥४॥
translation: Arjuna said: How can I fight Bhishma and Drona with arrows in battle, Madhusudana, when both of them deserve my worship, destroyer of enemies?
explanation: Arjuna answers challenge with a real difficulty. These are not enemies but the men who raised and trained him. To fire arrows at them inverts a lifetime of reverence — his objection is moral, not cowardly.

sanskrit:
गुरूनहत्वा हि महानुभावान्
श्रेयो भोक्तुं भैक्ष्यमपीह लोके।
हत्वार्थकामांस्तु गुरूनिहैव
भुञ्जीय भोगान् रुधिरप्रदिग्धान् ॥५॥
translation: Better to live on alms in this world than to kill these great-souled teachers. If I killed them, even though they seek worldly gain, every pleasure I tasted here would be smeared with their blood.
explanation: Arjuna imagines the victory concretely and finds it unbearable — food, wealth, kingship all stained. The image of blood-smeared enjoyments is his own, and shows a conscience working in vivid pictures.

sanskrit:
न चैतद्विद्मः कतरन्नो गरीयो
यद्वा जयेम यदि वा नो जयेयुः।
यानेव हत्वा न जिजीविषाम
स्तेऽवस्थिताः प्रमुखे धार्तराष्ट्राः ॥६॥
translation: We do not even know which is better — that we should conquer them, or that they should conquer us. The very sons of Dhritarashtra, after killing whom we would not wish to live, stand arrayed before us.
explanation: This is Arjuna's deepest confusion: both outcomes look like loss. Winning means living among the dead he loved; losing means the same grief with defeat added. He cannot locate a good result anywhere.

sanskrit:
कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभावः
पृच्छामि त्वां धर्मसंमूढचेताः।
यच्छ्रेयः स्यान्निश्िचतं ब्रूहि तन्मे
शिष्यस्तेऽहं शाधि मां त्वां प्रपन्नम् ॥७॥
translation: My nature is overcome by the flaw of pity, my mind bewildered about duty — I ask you: tell me decisively what is best. I am your student; instruct me, for I take refuge in you.
explanation: The turning point of the Gita. Arjuna stops arguing and formally becomes a student. Everything Krishna says afterward is answering a question that was genuinely asked, not advice pressed on someone unwilling.

sanskrit:
न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्या
द्यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम्।
अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धम्
राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम् ॥८॥
translation: For I see nothing that could drive away this grief which withers my senses — not unrivalled prosperity on earth, nor even lordship over the gods.
explanation: Arjuna measures his sorrow against the largest prizes he can imagine and finds them too small. It is a precise admission: this is not a problem that wealth or power can touch.

sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच
एवमुक्त्वा हृषीकेशं गुडाकेशः परन्तप।
न योत्स्य इति गोविन्दमुक्त्वा तूष्णीं बभूव ह ॥९॥
translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hrishikesha, Gudakesha, the scorcher of foes, said to Govinda, I shall not fight — and fell silent.
explanation: Three grand names for Krishna and one for Arjuna in a single line, then a flat refusal and silence. Sanjaya lets the weight of the titles collide with the smallness of four words.

sanskrit:
तमुवाच हृषीकेशः प्रहसन्निव भारत।
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये विषीदन्तमिदं वचः ॥१०॥
translation: O Bharata, in the midst of the two armies, Hrishikesha, as if smiling, spoke these words to the despairing one.
explanation: The near-smile is one of the Gita's most quoted details. Not mockery — the ease of someone who sees the whole situation while Arjuna sees only its weight. Note the setting: this happens between armies.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
अशोच्यानन्वशोचस्त्वं प्रज्ञावादांश्च भाषसे।
गतासूनगतासूंश्च नानुशोचन्ति पण्डिताः ॥११॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: You grieve for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom. The wise mourn neither the living nor the dead.
explanation: Krishna's first substantive line targets the gap between Arjuna's eloquence and his understanding. He has been reasoning well from a false premise — that death is what he assumes it to be.

sanskrit:
न त्वेवाहं जातु नासं न त्वं नेमे जनाधिपाः।
न चैव न भविष्यामः सर्वे वयमतः परम् ॥१२॥
translation: There was never a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these kings; nor will any of us cease to be hereafter.
explanation: The argument opens at the widest possible scale, and Krishna includes himself and the assembled kings in it. Continuity is not a privilege of the divine — it is the ordinary condition of everyone on the field.

sanskrit:
देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा।
तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति ॥१३॥
translation: Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so it passes into another body. The steady are not deluded by this.
explanation: The analogy is deliberately homely. Arjuna already accepts that he survived the death of his own childhood; Krishna simply extends a change he has lived through into one he fears.

sanskrit:
मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः।
आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत ॥१४॥
translation: Contacts with matter, Kaunteya, produce cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last — endure them, Bharata.
explanation: A practical instruction sits inside the metaphysics. Krishna does not promise the discomfort will stop; he asks for titiksha, endurance, on the grounds that sensations are traffic, not residents.

sanskrit:
यं हि न व्यथयन्त्येते पुरुषं पुरुषर्षभ।
समदुःखसुखं धीरं सोऽमृतत्वाय कल्पते ॥१५॥
translation: The person whom these do not disturb, who is steady and alike in pain and pleasure — that one is fit for immortality, best of men.
explanation: Immortality here is described as a fitness, something a person becomes suited for by temperament. Evenness is not indifference but a stability that suffering and delight cannot knock over.

sanskrit:
नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सतः।
उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽन्तस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभिः ॥१६॥
translation: Of the unreal there is no being; of the real there is no ceasing to be. The truth of both has been seen by those who perceive reality.
explanation: A compressed, almost mathematical verse. Krishna is drawing a line between what changes and what does not, and crediting the distinction to direct seers rather than to clever argument.

sanskrit:
अविनाशि तु तद्विद्धि येन सर्वमिदं ततम्।
विनाशमव्ययस्यास्य न कश्चित् कर्तुमर्हति ॥१७॥
translation: Know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded. No one is able to bring about the destruction of the imperishable.
explanation: The self is defined by its reach rather than its location — that which pervades everything. And its safety is absolute: destroying it is not difficult, it is not the kind of thing that can be done.

sanskrit:
अन्तवन्त इमे देहा नित्यस्योक्ताः शरीरिणः।
अनाशिनोऽप्रमेयस्य तस्माद्युध्यस्व भारत ॥१८॥
translation: These bodies of the eternal embodied one — indestructible and immeasurable — are said to have an end. Therefore fight, Bharata.
explanation: Krishna finally connects philosophy to the order. Bodies end regardless; that fact does not license cruelty, it removes Arjuna's belief that he is the one deciding whether these men are mortal.

sanskrit:
य एनं वेत्ति हन्तारं यश्चैनं मन्यते हतम्।
उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायं हन्ति न हन्यते ॥१९॥
translation: Whoever thinks this one a slayer and whoever thinks it slain — neither of them understands. It does not slay, nor is it slain.
explanation: Both the killer's pride and the mourner's horror rest on the same mistake. Krishna dismantles them together, which matters because Arjuna is currently the mourner and dreads becoming the killer.

sanskrit:
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचि
न्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः।
अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो
न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥२०॥
translation: It is never born and never dies; having come to be, it never ceases to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient — it is not killed when the body is killed.
explanation: A chain of negations rather than a description. Krishna defines the self by everything that cannot happen to it, leaving Arjuna with something that resists being pictured — which may be the point.

sanskrit:
वेदाविनाशिनं नित्यं य एनमजमव्ययम्।
कथं स पुरुषः पार्थ कं घातयति हन्ति कम् ॥२१॥
translation: Partha, one who knows this as indestructible, eternal, unborn, and unchanging — how can such a person kill anyone, or cause anyone to be killed?
explanation: The question is left open rather than answered. Krishna is not granting permission to kill; he is saying the person who genuinely sees this will no longer recognize the act as Arjuna now does.

sanskrit:
वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय
नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि।
तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णा
न्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही ॥२२॥
translation: As a person discards worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.
explanation: The Gita's most famous image, and its power lies in how casual it makes the transition sound. Clothes are intimate but not identical to us — the comparison quietly relocates where Arjuna thinks he lives.

sanskrit:
नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावकः।
न चैनं क्लेदयन्त्यापो न शोषयति मारुतः ॥२३॥
translation: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, and wind does not wither it.
explanation: Four elements, four failures. Krishna runs through the battlefield's own instruments of destruction and finds each one irrelevant — which lands differently when spoken between two armed armies.

sanskrit:
अच्छेद्योऽयमदाह्योऽयमक्लेद्योऽशोष्य एव च।
नित्यः सर्वगतः स्थाणुरचलोऽयं सनातनः ॥२४॥
translation: It cannot be cut, cannot be burned, cannot be wetted or dried. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, unmoving, everlasting.
explanation: The same four denials restated as permanent qualities, then extended. The repetition is deliberate — Krishna is drilling the point into a mind that has just been shaking too hard to hold it.

sanskrit:
अव्यक्तोऽयमचिन्त्योऽयमविकार्योऽयमुच्यते।
तस्मादेवं विदित्वैनं नानुशोचितुमर्हसि ॥२५॥
translation: It is called unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchanging. Therefore, knowing it to be such, you should not grieve.
explanation: Unthinkable is a striking admission to place inside a teaching. Krishna concedes the self cannot be captured by thought, yet insists that knowing even this much is enough to dissolve the grief.

sanskrit:
अथ चैनं नित्यजातं नित्यं वा मन्यसे मृतम्।
तथापि त्वं महाबाहो नैवं शोचितुमर्हसि ॥२६॥
translation: And even if you think of it as constantly born and constantly dying, even then, mighty-armed one, you should not grieve.
explanation: A generous move — Krishna offers a fallback argument for anyone unconvinced by the first. If Arjuna rejects the eternal self entirely, the same conclusion still holds, for entirely different reasons.

sanskrit:
जातस्य हि ध्रुवो मृत्युर्ध्रुवं जन्म मृतस्य च।
तस्मादपरिहार्येऽर्थे न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि ॥२७॥
translation: For death is certain for whatever is born, and birth is certain for whatever dies. Therefore you should not grieve over what cannot be avoided.
explanation: The fallback in full: on purely natural grounds, grief protests something as fixed as gravity. Krishna narrows sorrow to its useful range — the things that could have been otherwise.

sanskrit:
अव्यक्तादीनि भूतानि व्यक्तमध्यानि भारत।
अव्यक्तनिधनान्येव तत्र का परिदेवना ॥२८॥
translation: Beings are unmanifest in their beginnings, manifest in the middle state, and unmanifest again at their end, Bharata. What is there to lament in this?
explanation: A life is presented as a brief visible stretch between two invisibilities. Krishna is not minimizing the middle; he is asking why its entirely predictable ending should arrive as an outrage.

sanskrit:
आश्चर्यवत्पश्यति कश्चिदेन
माश्चर्यवद्वदति तथैव चान्यः।
आश्चर्यवच्चैनमन्यः श्रृणोति
श्रुत्वाप्येनं वेद न चैव कश्चित् ॥२९॥
translation: One sees this as a wonder, another speaks of it as a wonder, another hears of it as a wonder — and even having heard, no one truly knows it.
explanation: An unusual pause. After many confident verses, Krishna admits the self mostly escapes those who study it. The honesty guards his teaching against being mistaken for something already mastered.

sanskrit:
देही नित्यमवध्योऽयं देहे सर्वस्य भारत।
तस्मात्सर्वाणि भूतानि न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि ॥३०॥
translation: The embodied self within everyone's body is eternally beyond killing, Bharata. Therefore you should not grieve for any being.
explanation: The argument closes by widening from Arjuna's relatives to every being on the field, including strangers and enemies. A consolation that applied only to loved ones would not have been consolation at all.

sanskrit:
स्वधर्ममपि चावेक्ष्य न विकम्पितुमर्हसि।
धर्म्याद्धि युद्धाछ्रेयोऽन्यत्क्षत्रियस्य न विद्यते ॥३१॥
translation: Considering your own duty as well, you should not waver. For a kshatriya there exists nothing better than a righteous war.
explanation: Krishna switches register from metaphysics to social duty, meeting Arjuna where he actually lives. Note dharmya — the war is defensible because it is righteous, not because fighting is a warrior's habit.

sanskrit:
यदृच्छया चोपपन्नं स्वर्गद्वारमपावृतम्।
सुखिनः क्षत्रियाः पार्थ लभन्ते युद्धमीदृशम् ॥३२॥
translation: Happy are the kshatriyas, Partha, who are offered such a battle — an open door to heaven, arrived at unsought.
explanation: Unsought carries the weight here. Arjuna did not engineer this war; it arrived at him. Krishna reframes what feels like a trap as an opportunity that came without being manufactured.

sanskrit:
अथ चैत्त्वमिमं धर्म्यं संग्रामं न करिष्यसि।
ततः स्वधर्मं कीर्तिं च हित्वा पापमवाप्स्यसि ॥३३॥
translation: But if you will not fight this righteous battle, then, having abandoned your own duty and your honour, you will incur wrong.
explanation: The counter-case. Krishna insists that withdrawal is not neutral — refusing carries its own moral cost. Arjuna has been treating retreat as the safely blameless option, and it is not.

sanskrit:
अकीर्तिं चापि भूतानि कथयिष्यन्ति तेऽव्ययाम्।
संभावितस्य चाकीर्तिर्मरणादतिरिच्यते ॥३४॥
translation: People will speak of your lasting disgrace, and for one who has been honoured, dishonour is worse than death.
explanation: A hard, worldly argument aimed at Arjuna's standing rather than his soul. Krishna uses every register available — the higher teaching has not landed yet, so he tries reputation instead.

sanskrit:
भयाद्रणादुपरतं मंस्यन्ते त्वां महारथाः।
येषां च त्वं बहुमतो भूत्वा यास्यसि लाघवम् ॥३५॥
translation: The great chariot-warriors will think you withdrew from the battle out of fear, and you, who were highly regarded by them, will be held lightly.
explanation: Krishna names the specific audience — the very warriors Arjuna respects. Not abstract public opinion but the judgement of peers, which is what actually stings a soldier.

sanskrit:
अवाच्यवादांश्च बहून् वदिष्यन्ति तवाहिताः।
निन्दन्तस्तव सामर्थ्यं ततो दुःखतरं नु किम् ॥३६॥
translation: Your enemies will speak many unspeakable words, ridiculing your capability. What could be more painful than that?
explanation: The argument reaches its sharpest and most human point. Krishna is deliberately working the wound of pride — an approach he will abandon entirely once Arjuna is ready for something better.

sanskrit:
हतो वा प्राप्स्यसि स्वर्गं जित्वा वा भोक्ष्यसे महीम्।
तस्मादुत्तिष्ठ कौन्तेय युद्धाय कृतनिश्चयः ॥३७॥
translation: Killed, you will attain heaven; victorious, you will enjoy the earth. Therefore rise, Kaunteya, resolved to fight.
explanation: The worldly case concludes with a neat symmetry, and it directly answers Arjuna's earlier complaint that neither winning nor losing offered him anything worth having.

sanskrit:
सुखदुःखे समे कृत्वा लाभालाभौ जयाजयौ।
ततो युद्धाय युज्यस्व नैवं पापमवाप्स्यसि ॥३८॥
translation: Treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike, engage yourself in battle. In this way you will incur no wrong.
explanation: The pivot of the chapter. Krishna stops arguing about outcomes and changes the subject to attitude — the same act, done in evenness, no longer binds. Karma yoga effectively begins here.

sanskrit:
एषा तेऽभिहिता सांख्ये बुद्धिर्योगे त्विमां श्रृणु।
बुद्ध्यायुक्तो यया पार्थ कर्मबन्धं प्रहास्यसि ॥३९॥
translation: What I have told you is the understanding of Sankhya; now hear the understanding of Yoga. Equipped with this insight, Partha, you will cast off the bondage of action.
explanation: Krishna labels his own teaching in two halves, analysis and then practice. The promise is specific: not escape from action, but freedom from the way action normally binds the one who acts.

sanskrit:
नेहाभिक्रमनाशोऽस्ति प्रत्यवायो न विद्यते।
स्वल्पमप्यस्य धर्मस्य त्रायते महतो भयात् ॥४०॥
translation: In this, no effort is lost and no harm is done. Even a little of this practice protects one from great fear.
explanation: An unusually reassuring verse. Unlike ritual, which fails if performed wrongly, this path keeps whatever progress is made. Nothing invested is wasted, however incomplete the attempt turns out to be.

sanskrit:
व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिरेकेह कुरुनन्दन।
बहुशाखा ह्यनन्ताश्च बुद्धयोऽव्यवसायिनाम् ॥४१॥
translation: Here the resolute understanding is single, Kurunandana. The thoughts of the irresolute are many-branched and endless.
explanation: A precise psychological observation. Indecision does not produce one alternative but an unlimited spread of them, and the spread itself is the affliction — Arjuna's whole morning has been exactly this.

sanskrit:
यामिमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्यविपश्चितः।
वेदवादरताः पार्थ नान्यदस्तीति वादिनः ॥४२॥
translation: Undiscerning people utter this flowery speech, delighting in the letter of the Vedas, Partha, and declaring that there is nothing else.
explanation: Krishna criticizes not scripture but a way of reading it — treating ritual promises as the whole point. Flowery suggests speech that is ornamented and pleasant and leads nowhere in particular.

sanskrit:
कामात्मानः स्वर्गपरा जन्मकर्मफलप्रदाम्।
क्रियाविशेषबहुलां भोगैश्वर्यगतिं प्रति ॥४३॥
translation: Full of desires, intent on heaven, they urge many specific rites for the sake of pleasure and power, yielding rebirth as the fruit of action.
explanation: The critique sharpens: this is religion pursued as a transaction for better enjoyments. Krishna's objection is that it works — it delivers exactly the recurring births its practitioners bargained for.

sanskrit:
भोगैश्वर्यप्रसक्तानां तयापहृतचेतसाम्।
व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिः समाधौ न विधीयते ॥४४॥
translation: For those attached to pleasure and power, whose minds are carried away by such talk, the resolute understanding settled in concentration does not arise.
explanation: Attachment is described as a theft of attention rather than as a sin. A mind already spent on outcomes has nothing left over for the steadiness Krishna is describing.

sanskrit:
त्रैगुण्यविषया वेदा निस्त्रैगुण्यो भवार्जुन।
निर्द्वन्द्वो नित्यसत्त्वस्थो निर्योगक्षेम आत्मवान् ॥४५॥
translation: The Vedas deal with the three gunas; be free of them, Arjuna. Free of dualities, ever established in purity, indifferent to acquiring and keeping, be established in the self.
explanation: A radical instruction — go beyond even the scriptural framework. Yoga-kshema, acquiring and keeping, is the ordinary human project, and Krishna asks Arjuna to set down the whole enterprise.

sanskrit:
यावानर्थ उदपाने सर्वतः संप्लुतोदके।
तावान्सर्वेषु वेदेषु ब्राह्मणस्य विजानतः ॥४६॥
translation: As much use as there is in a well when water is flooding everywhere, so much use is there in all the Vedas for the knowing brahmana.
explanation: A carefully limited image. The well is not condemned — it simply becomes redundant once the flood arrives. Scripture is a means, and the point is arriving at what it points toward.

sanskrit:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ॥४७॥
translation: Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruits of action be your motive, nor be attached to inaction.
explanation: The most quoted verse in the Gita, and the closing line is what saves it from becoming an excuse. Detachment from results is not permission to stop — that door is shut in the same breath.

sanskrit:
योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनञ्जय।
सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते ॥४८॥
translation: Established in yoga, perform your actions abandoning attachment, Dhananjaya, remaining the same in success and failure. Evenness of mind is called yoga.
explanation: Krishna offers his own definition, and it is startlingly plain — yoga is samatva, evenness. Not posture, not withdrawal, but a level attitude carried into the middle of activity.

sanskrit:
दूरेण ह्यवरं कर्म बुद्धियोगाद्धनञ्जय।
बुद्धौ शरणमन्विच्छ कृपणाः फलहेतवः ॥४९॥
translation: Action is far inferior to the yoga of understanding, Dhananjaya. Seek refuge in that understanding. Wretched are those motivated by results.
explanation: Wretched sounds harsh, but kripana means pitiable rather than wicked. Krishna sees the results-driven life as a hard bargain that someone has struck against themselves without noticing.

sanskrit:
बुद्धियुक्तो जहातीह उभे सुकृतदुष्कृते।
तस्माद्योगाय युज्यस्व योगः कर्मसु कौशलम् ॥५०॥
translation: Endowed with this understanding, one sheds both good and bad deeds here. Therefore devote yourself to yoga — yoga is skill in action.
explanation: Shedding good deeds too is the surprising half; merit binds as surely as fault. And the famous definition arrives almost offhandedly: kaushalam, skill, in what one is already doing.

sanskrit:
कर्मजं बुद्धियुक्ता हि फलं त्यक्त्वा मनीषिणः।
जन्मबन्धविनिर्मुक्ताः पदं गच्छन्त्यनामयम् ॥५१॥
translation: The wise, endowed with this understanding, abandoning the fruits born of action and freed from the bondage of birth, reach the state beyond all ills.
explanation: Krishna states the destination in negative terms — a place beyond ills rather than a described paradise. Consistent with a teaching that keeps refusing to make its goal one more prize to chase.

sanskrit:
यदा ते मोहकलिलं बुद्धिर्व्यतितरिष्यति।
तदा गन्तासि निर्वेदं श्रोतव्यस्य श्रुतस्य च ॥५२॥
translation: When your understanding crosses beyond the thicket of delusion, then you will grow indifferent to all that has been heard and all that is yet to be heard.
explanation: Thicket catches the experience exactly — delusion as dense undergrowth rather than as darkness. Beyond it, the endless appetite for more teaching quiets, because the need it fed is gone.

sanskrit:
श्रुतिविप्रतिपन्ना ते यदा स्थास्यति निश्चला।
समाधावचला बुद्धिस्तदा योगमवाप्स्यसि ॥५३॥
translation: When your understanding, bewildered by scriptural teachings, stands unmoving and steady in absorption, then you will attain yoga.
explanation: Krishna acknowledges that scripture itself can bewilder, with conflicting instructions pulling in different directions. The resolution is not another text but a steadiness that no longer needs to be told.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
स्थितप्रज्ञस्य का भाषा समाधिस्थस्य केशव।
स्थितधीः किं प्रभाषेत किमासीत व्रजेत किम् ॥५४॥
translation: Arjuna said: What describes a person of steady wisdom, established in absorption, Keshava? How does the steady-minded one speak, sit, and move?
explanation: Arjuna's question is wonderfully concrete. He does not ask what such a person knows but how they walk and talk — he wants to be able to recognize one, not define one.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
प्रजहाति यदा कामान् सर्वान् पार्थ मनोगतान्।
आत्मन्येवात्मना तुष्टः स्थितप्रज्ञस्तदोच्यते ॥५५॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: When a person abandons all the desires that enter the mind, Partha, and is content within the self by the self, that one is called steady in wisdom.
explanation: Krishna answers the outer question with an inner criterion, then spends the rest of the chapter on the behaviour Arjuna actually asked about. This contentment has no external supplier.

sanskrit:
दुःखेष्वनुद्विग्नमनाः सुखेषु विगतस्पृहः।
वीतरागभयक्रोधः स्थितधीर्मुनिरुच्यते ॥५६॥
translation: Whose mind is untroubled in sorrow and free of longing in pleasure, who is rid of passion, fear, and anger — that one is called a sage of steady mind.
explanation: Note the pairing: untroubled in sorrow and unhungry in pleasure. Krishna keeps insisting that the seductive half of experience is every bit as destabilizing as the painful half.

sanskrit:
यः सर्वत्रानभिस्नेहस्तत्तत्प्राप्य शुभाशुभम्।
नाभिनन्दति न द्वेष्टि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥५७॥
translation: One who is unattached everywhere, who neither delights in the pleasant nor recoils from the unpleasant when it comes — that one's wisdom is firmly set.
explanation: The phrase when it comes matters. This is not a person who has arranged an untroubled life; good and bad still arrive, and are met without the usual grab or flinch.

sanskrit:
यदा संहरते चायं कूर्मोऽङ्गानीव सर्वशः।
इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥५८॥
translation: And when, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, one withdraws the senses entirely from their objects, that one's wisdom is firmly set.
explanation: A homely, exact image. The tortoise does not lose its limbs or stop using them — it retains the ability to pull them in at will, which is the whole point of the comparison.

sanskrit:
विषया विनिवर्तन्ते निराहारस्य देहिनः।
रसवर्जं रसोऽप्यस्य परं दृष्ट्वा निवर्तते ॥५९॥
translation: Objects fall away for the embodied one who abstains, but the taste for them remains. Even that taste falls away when the Supreme is seen.
explanation: An honest account of why willpower alone stalls. Fasting removes the food, not the appetite; Krishna says only something more compelling can retire a craving for good.

sanskrit:
यततो ह्यपि कौन्तेय पुरुषस्य विपश्चितः।
इन्द्रियाणि प्रमाथीनि हरन्ति प्रसभं मनः ॥६०॥
translation: For the turbulent senses, Kaunteya, forcibly carry away the mind even of a discerning person who is striving.
explanation: Krishna warns the sincere, not the careless. The person in this verse is both wise and trying hard, and is still overpowered — a candid admission placed just before he offers the remedy.

sanskrit:
तानि सर्वाणि संयम्य युक्त आसीत मत्परः।
वशे हि यस्येन्द्रियाणि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥६१॥
translation: Restraining them all, one should sit absorbed, intent on me. For one whose senses are mastered, wisdom is firmly set.
explanation: Here is the piece missing from the previous verse: mat-parah, intent on me. Krishna's answer to force failing is not more force but a redirection of attention toward something worth it.

sanskrit:
ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते।
सङ्गात् संजायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥६२॥
translation: Dwelling on the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment to them; from attachment desire is born, and from desire, anger.
explanation: The famous causal chain begins with something almost innocent — merely dwelling on a thing. Krishna traces catastrophe back to the small, unremarkable act of letting the mind linger.

sanskrit:
क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः संमोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः।
स्मृतिभ्रंशाद् बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति ॥६३॥
translation: From anger comes delusion, from delusion loss of memory, from loss of memory the destruction of understanding — and when understanding is destroyed, one perishes.
explanation: The chain completes in five quick steps. Loss of memory is the crucial link: in anger a person forgets what they know and value, so everything they might have used to stop is gone.

sanskrit:
रागद्वेषवियुक्तैस्तु विषयानिन्द्रियैश्चरन्।
आत्मवश्यैर्विधेयात्मा प्रसादमधिगच्छति ॥६४॥
translation: But one who moves among objects with the senses under control, free of attraction and aversion and self-possessed, attains serenity.
explanation: Krishna reverses the descent without asking for withdrawal. The senses still move among their objects; what changes is that they are being steered rather than dragged.

sanskrit:
प्रसादे सर्वदुःखानां हानिरस्योपजायते।
प्रसन्नचेतसो ह्याशु बुद्धिः पर्यवतिष्ठते ॥६५॥
translation: In serenity all sorrows are destroyed, for the understanding of one whose mind is serene soon becomes steady.
explanation: The order is worth noticing — serenity comes first and steadies the intellect, not the other way around. Clarity is presented as a consequence of peace, not as its prerequisite.

sanskrit:
नास्ति बुद्धिरयुक्तस्य न चायुक्तस्य भावना।
न चाभावयतः शान्तिरशान्तस्य कुतः सुखम् ॥६६॥
translation: There is no understanding for the undisciplined, and no contemplation for the undisciplined. For one without contemplation there is no peace, and where is happiness without peace?
explanation: A cascade of dependencies stated in the negative, ending in a rhetorical question. Krishna shows Arjuna that the happiness he wants sits at the far end of a chain he has not begun.

sanskrit:
इन्द्रियाणां हि चरतां यन्मनोऽनुविधीयते।
तदस्य हरति प्रज्ञां वायुर्नावमिवाम्भसि ॥६७॥
translation: For the mind that follows the wandering senses carries away one's wisdom, as the wind carries away a ship upon the water.
explanation: A single sense given free rein is enough — like a wind that needs no permission to move an entire ship. The image gives the mind's drift a physical inevitability.

sanskrit:
तस्माद्यस्य महाबाहो निगृहीतानि सर्वशः।
इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥६८॥
translation: Therefore, mighty-armed one, whose senses are entirely restrained from their objects — that one's wisdom is firmly set.
explanation: The refrain returns for the third time, closing the argument where it began. Krishna's repetitions in this chapter work like a drumbeat, fixing the criterion in Arjuna's memory.

sanskrit:
या निशा सर्वभूतानां तस्यां जागर्ति संयमी।
यस्यां जाग्रति भूतानि सा निशा पश्यतो मुनेः ॥६९॥
translation: What is night for all beings is waking for the disciplined one; what is waking for all beings is night for the sage who sees.
explanation: A striking inversion. The sage is not more awake than others in the same direction, but awake to a different order of things, and asleep to what everyone else stays up for.

sanskrit:
आपूर्यमाणमचलप्रतिष्ठं
समुद्रमापः प्रविशन्ति यद्वत्।
तद्वत्कामा यं प्रविशन्ति सर्वे
स शान्तिमाप्नोति न कामकामी ॥७०॥
translation: As waters enter the ocean, which is filled yet remains unmoved, so the one whom all desires enter attains peace — not the one who longs after desires.
explanation: The ocean does not refuse the rivers; it is simply too vast to be raised by them. Krishna's peace is capacious rather than defended — desires arrive and are absorbed without disturbance.

sanskrit:
विहाय कामान्यः सर्वान्पुमांश्चरति निःस्पृहः।
निर्ममो निरहंकारः स शांतिमधिगच्छति ॥७१॥
translation: The person who abandons all desires and moves about free of longing, without possessiveness and without ego, attains peace.
explanation: Three renunciations in one line, and the last is hardest — nirahankara, without the sense of being the one who acts and owns. Peace is described as what remains once that drops away.

sanskrit:
एषा ब्राह्मी स्थितिः पार्थ नैनां प्राप्य विमुह्यति।
स्थित्वाऽस्यामन्तकालेऽपि ब्रह्मनिर्वाणमृच्छति ॥७२॥
translation: This is the state of Brahman, Partha. Having attained it, one is not deluded. Established in it even at the last hour, one reaches the peace of Brahman.
explanation: The chapter ends generously — even at the last hour. Krishna leaves the door open to those who arrive late, a quiet reassurance after seventy verses of demanding description.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
ज्यायसी चेत्कर्मणस्ते मता बुद्धिर्जनार्दन।
तत्किं कर्मणि घोरे मां नियोजयसि केशव ॥१॥
translation: Arjuna said: If you consider understanding better than action, Janardana, then why do you urge me to this terrible deed, Keshava?
explanation: Arjuna catches what sounds like a contradiction and says so. Chapter 2 praised buddhi-yoga above mere action, yet ended by ordering him into battle. His objection is sharp and entirely fair.

sanskrit:
व्यामिश्रेणेव वाक्येन बुद्धिं मोहयसीव मे।
तदेकं वद निश्िचत्य येन श्रेयोऽहमाप्नुयाम् ॥२॥
translation: With these seemingly mixed words you are confusing my understanding. Tell me decisively the one path by which I may reach what is best.
explanation: Arjuna asks for a single answer, not a survey. His complaint that the words are mixed drives the rest of the Gita — much of what follows is Krishna showing the two paths are one.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
लोकेऽस्मिन्द्विविधा निष्ठा पुरा प्रोक्ता मयानघ।
ज्ञानयोगेन सांख्यानां कर्मयोगेन योगिनाम् ॥३॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: In this world there is a twofold path, as I said before, sinless one — the yoga of knowledge for the contemplative, and the yoga of action for the active.
explanation: Krishna does not deny the two paths; he distributes them by temperament. Different people are suited to different approaches, which is exactly why his teaching sounded double to Arjuna.

sanskrit:
न कर्मणामनारम्भान्नैष्कर्म्यं पुरुषोऽश्नुते।
न च संन्यसनादेव सिद्धिं समधिगच्छति ॥४॥
translation: Not by abstaining from actions does a person attain freedom from action, nor by renunciation alone does one reach perfection.
explanation: The first correction: quitting is not the same as transcending. Krishna separates the outward act of dropping work from the inward freedom Arjuna imagines it would automatically bring.

sanskrit:
न हि कश्िचत्क्षणमपि जातु तिष्ठत्यकर्मकृत्।
कार्यते ह्यवशः कर्म सर्वः प्रकृतिजैर्गुणैः ॥५॥
translation: For no one can remain even a moment without performing action. Everyone is made to act, helplessly, by the qualities born of nature.
explanation: A blunt fact of biology and psychology. Even sitting still is doing something. Since action turns out to be unavoidable, the question shifts from whether to act to how.

sanskrit:
कर्मेन्द्रियाणि संयम्य य आस्ते मनसा स्मरन्।
इन्द्रियार्थान्विमूढात्मा मिथ्याचारः स उच्यते ॥६॥
translation: One who sits restraining the organs of action while dwelling in the mind on the objects of sense is called a hypocrite, a deluded soul.
explanation: Krishna's harshest word so far, aimed at performed renunciation. The body is still, the mind is at the feast — an outward austerity quietly concealing an inward indulgence.

sanskrit:
यस्त्विन्द्रियाणि मनसा नियम्यारभतेऽर्जुन।
कर्मेन्द्रियैः कर्मयोगमसक्तः स विशिष्यते ॥७॥
translation: But one who restrains the senses with the mind, Arjuna, and undertakes karma yoga with the organs of action, unattached — that one excels.
explanation: The alternative, stated as a straight comparison. Same senses, same work, but the order is reversed: mind governing the senses instead of trailing along behind them.

sanskrit:
नियतं कुरु कर्म त्वं कर्म ज्यायो ह्यकर्मणः।
शरीरयात्रापि च ते न प्रसिद्ध्येदकर्मणः ॥८॥
translation: Perform your prescribed duty, for action is better than inaction. Even the maintenance of your body could not be accomplished without action.
explanation: Krishna grounds the argument in something undeniable — a body has to be fed and kept. Even the would-be renunciate is sustained by work, whether or not he does it himself.

sanskrit:
यज्ञार्थात्कर्मणोऽन्यत्र लोकोऽयं कर्मबन्धनः।
तदर्थं कर्म कौन्तेय मुक्तसंगः समाचर ॥९॥
translation: This world is bound by action other than that performed for the sake of sacrifice. Perform action for that purpose, Kaunteya, free from attachment.
explanation: The key distinction of the chapter is yajna. Action offered rather than owned does not bind. Krishna is not asking for less activity, only for a different relationship to it.

sanskrit:
सहयज्ञाः प्रजाः सृष्ट्वा पुरोवाच प्रजापतिः।
अनेन प्रसविष्यध्वमेष वोऽस्त्विष्टकामधुक् ॥१०॥
translation: Having created humankind together with sacrifice, the Lord of creatures said long ago: By this you shall increase; let this be the cow that yields your desires.
explanation: A creation story used as an argument. Reciprocity is presented as built into things from the beginning, not as a rule imposed later upon reluctant people.

sanskrit:
देवान्भावयतानेन ते देवा भावयन्तु वः।
परस्परं भावयन्तः श्रेयः परमवाप्स्यथ ॥११॥
translation: By this may you nourish the gods, and may the gods nourish you. Nourishing one another, you will attain the highest good.
explanation: The image is mutual feeding, a two-way exchange rather than tribute paid upward. Krishna's cosmos runs on circulation, and refusing to circulate is what jams it.

sanskrit:
इष्टान्भोगान्हि वो देवा दास्यन्ते यज्ञभाविताः।
तैर्दत्तानप्रदायैभ्यो यो भुङ्क्ते स्तेन एव सः ॥१२॥
translation: Nourished by sacrifice, the gods will give you the enjoyments you desire. One who enjoys what they have given without offering in return is simply a thief.
explanation: A startling word to choose — thief, not sinner or fool. Krishna frames pure consumption as taking from a system that one has declined to replenish.

sanskrit:
यज्ञशिष्टाशिनः सन्तो मुच्यन्ते सर्वकिल्बिषैः।
भुञ्जते ते त्वघं पापा ये पचन्त्यात्मकारणात् ॥१३॥
translation: The good, who eat what remains after sacrifice, are freed from all faults. But the wicked, who cook only for themselves, eat their own wrong.
explanation: The distinction is not what is eaten but what came first. Food received as a remainder nourishes; the very same food taken as entitlement becomes consuming one's own harm.

sanskrit:
अन्नाद्भवन्ति भूतानि पर्जन्यादन्नसम्भवः।
यज्ञाद्भवति पर्जन्यो यज्ञः कर्मसमुद्भवः ॥१४॥
translation: Beings come into being from food, food is produced from rain, rain arises from sacrifice, and sacrifice is born of action.
explanation: Krishna traces a physical chain from the plate backward to the deed. Each link is ordinary and observable until the last, which quietly folds human action into the weather.

sanskrit:
कर्म ब्रह्मोद्भवं विद्धि ब्रह्माक्षरसमुद्भवम्।
तस्मात्सर्वगतं ब्रह्म नित्यं यज्ञे प्रतिष्ठितम् ॥१५॥
translation: Know that action arises from Brahman, and Brahman springs from the imperishable. Therefore the all-pervading Brahman is ever established in sacrifice.
explanation: The chain completes by curving back on itself. Action came from the absolute and returns there through offering, which is why Krishna keeps refusing to treat work as merely mundane.

sanskrit:
एवं प्रवर्तितं चक्रं नानुवर्तयतीह यः।
अघायुरिन्द्रियारामो मोघं पार्थ स जीवति ॥१६॥
translation: One who does not follow the wheel thus set in motion here, living in sin, delighting in the senses — that one lives in vain, Partha.
explanation: The wheel is Krishna's summary image for the whole exchange. Opting out is not neutral, and the verse's verdict — lives in vain — is unusually severe for the Gita.

sanskrit:
यस्त्वात्मरतिरेव स्यादात्मतृप्तश्च मानवः।
आत्मन्येव च सन्तुष्टस्तस्य कार्यं न विद्यते ॥१७॥
translation: But the person who delights in the self alone, who is satisfied with the self and content within the self — for that one there is nothing to be done.
explanation: A genuine exemption, and Krishna states it plainly. Someone whose fulfilment has no external source has no work left that is driven by need. Arjuna is not that person yet.

sanskrit:
नैव तस्य कृतेनार्थो नाकृतेनेह कश्चन।
न चास्य सर्वभूतेषु कश्िचदर्थव्यपाश्रयः ॥१८॥
translation: Such a one has no purpose at all in what is done or not done here, nor any dependence upon any being for any purpose whatever.
explanation: The exemption spelled out. Note the second half — not merely freedom from tasks but freedom from needing anything from anyone, which is what makes the first half possible.

sanskrit:
तस्मादसक्तः सततं कार्यं कर्म समाचर।
असक्तो ह्याचरन्कर्म परमाप्नोति पूरुषः ॥१९॥
translation: Therefore, always perform without attachment the work that must be done. For the person who acts without attachment attains the Supreme.
explanation: Therefore is doing heavy lifting: since Arjuna is not the self-satisfied sage, his route runs through the work rather than around it. The condition is non-attachment, not inactivity.

sanskrit:
कर्मणैव हि संसिद्धिमास्थिता जनकादयः।
लोकसंग्रहमेवापि संपश्यन्कर्तुमर्हसि ॥२०॥
translation: Indeed, it was by action alone that Janaka and others attained perfection. You should act with a view to the welfare of the world as well.
explanation: Krishna cites a precedent Arjuna knows — Janaka, a king who ruled and was still free. And a second motive arrives here: loka-sangraha, the holding together of the world.

sanskrit:
यद्यदाचरति श्रेष्ठस्तत्तदेवेतरो जनः।
स यत्प्रमाणं कुरुते लोकस्तदनुवर्तते ॥२१॥
translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that one sets, the world follows after it.
explanation: A plain observation about influence. Arjuna's choice is not private; as an exemplar he will be teaching by example whichever way he happens to decide.

sanskrit:
न मे पार्थास्ति कर्तव्यं त्रिषु लोकेषु किञ्चन।
नानवाप्तमवाप्तव्यं वर्त एव च कर्मणि ॥२२॥
translation: There is nothing in the three worlds that I need to do, Partha, nothing unattained that I need to attain — and yet I engage in action.
explanation: Krishna offers himself as the case study. He meets the exemption of verse seventeen completely and works anyway, which reframes action as something other than a response to lack.

sanskrit:
यदि ह्यहं न वर्तेयं जातु कर्मण्यतन्द्रितः।
मम वर्त्मानुवर्तन्ते मनुष्याः पार्थ सर्वशः ॥२३॥
translation: For if I did not engage tirelessly in action, people would follow my path in every way, Partha.
explanation: The reasoning behind the divine example. Krishna acts because withdrawal, from someone in his position, would itself be an instruction — and would be followed.

sanskrit:
उत्सीदेयुरिमे लोका न कुर्यां कर्म चेदहम्।
सङ्करस्य च कर्ता स्यामुपहन्यामिमाः प्रजाः ॥२४॥
translation: These worlds would fall to ruin if I did not perform action. I would be the cause of chaos and would destroy these creatures.
explanation: An unusually stark statement of consequence. Krishna is describing responsibility that scales with capacity, which is precisely the argument being made to Arjuna about his own.

sanskrit:
सक्ताः कर्मण्यविद्वांसो यथा कुर्वन्ति भारत।
कुर्याद्विद्वांस्तथासक्तश्िचकीर्षुर्लोकसंग्रहम् ॥२५॥
translation: As the ignorant act with attachment to their work, Bharata, so should the wise act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world.
explanation: The two look identical from outside — same diligence, same care. Krishna is not asking for visibly different behaviour, only for a different engine running beneath it.

sanskrit:
न बुद्धिभेदं जनयेदज्ञानां कर्मसङ्गिनाम्।
जोषयेत्सर्वकर्माणि विद्वान् युक्तः समाचरन् ॥२६॥
translation: The wise should not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant who are attached to action, but, acting in a disciplined way, should encourage them in all their work.
explanation: A caution against destabilizing people with truths they cannot yet use. Krishna asks the wise to support others' work rather than dismantle the motives currently holding it up.

sanskrit:
प्रकृतेः क्रियमाणानि गुणैः कर्माणि सर्वशः।
अहङ्कारविमूढात्मा कर्ताऽहमिति मन्यते ॥२७॥
translation: Actions are performed in every case by the qualities of nature. One whose self is deluded by ego thinks: I am the doer.
explanation: The chapter's sharpest metaphysical turn. Krishna does not deny that things get done; he relocates the doing, leaving ego as a claim laid over a process already underway.

sanskrit:
तत्त्ववित्तु महाबाहो गुणकर्मविभागयोः।
गुणा गुणेषु वर्तन्त इति मत्वा न सज्जते ॥२८॥
translation: But one who knows the truth about the divisions of quality and action, mighty-armed one, understands that qualities act upon qualities, and is not attached.
explanation: Freedom comes from an accurate account rather than an effort of will. Seeing the machinery as machinery, one stops being personally implicated in every turn of it.

sanskrit:
प्रकृतेर्गुणसम्मूढाः सज्जन्ते गुणकर्मसु।
तानकृत्स्नविदो मन्दान्कृत्स्नविन्न विचालयेत् ॥२९॥
translation: Those deluded by the qualities of nature become attached to their functions. The one who knows the whole should not unsettle those dull ones who know only in part.
explanation: The caution of verse twenty-six returns, now with its reason attached. Partial knowledge is fragile, and Krishna asks that it not be knocked over by someone who can see further.

sanskrit:
मयि सर्वाणि कर्माणि संन्यस्याध्यात्मचेतसा।
निराशीर्निर्ममो भूत्वा युध्यस्व विगतज्वरः ॥३०॥
translation: Renouncing all actions in me, with your mind on the self, free of longing and possessiveness, fight — your fever gone.
explanation: A whole practice compressed into one line, and the last word is remarkable: vigata-jvara, fever gone. Krishna wants the action performed without the heat Arjuna has been running.

sanskrit:
ये मे मतमिदं नित्यमनुतिष्ठन्ति मानवाः।
श्रद्धावन्तोऽनसूयन्तो मुच्यन्ते तेऽपि कर्मभिः ॥३१॥
translation: Those who constantly follow this teaching of mine with faith and without cavilling are also freed from actions.
explanation: A concession for those who cannot yet see it for themselves. Practising in trust is offered as a genuine route, not as a lesser consolation prize.

sanskrit:
ये त्वेतदभ्यसूयन्तो नानुतिष्ठन्ति मे मतम्।
सर्वज्ञानविमूढांस्तान्विद्धि नष्टानचेतसः ॥३२॥
translation: But those who carp at my teaching and do not follow it — know them to be deluded about all knowledge, mindless and lost.
explanation: The counterpart, and its target is specific: not doubt but abhyasuya, faultfinding. Krishna distinguishes honest questioning, which Arjuna is doing, from the sneer that cannot learn.

sanskrit:
सदृशं चेष्टते स्वस्याः प्रकृतेर्ज्ञानवानपि।
प्रकृतिं यान्ति भूतानि निग्रहः किं करिष्यति ॥३३॥
translation: Even a person of knowledge acts according to their own nature. Beings follow their nature — what will restraint accomplish?
explanation: A candid limit on the power of resolve, and it comes from Krishna rather than a skeptic. Nature is not overruled by suppression, which is why the next verse looks elsewhere.

sanskrit:
इन्द्रियस्येन्द्रियस्यार्थे रागद्वेषौ व्यवस्थितौ।
तयोर्न वशमागच्छेत्तौ ह्यस्य परिपन्थिनौ ॥३४॥
translation: Attraction and aversion are seated in the senses toward their objects. One should not fall under the sway of these two, for they are one's adversaries.
explanation: The workable point of intervention. Krishna does not ask Arjuna to stop having preferences, only to refuse them command — the enemy is the sway, not the sensation.

sanskrit:
श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात्।
स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः ॥३५॥
translation: Better one's own duty imperfectly done than another's duty done well. Better death in one's own duty; another's duty brings danger.
explanation: One of the Gita's most demanding verses. Krishna would rather Arjuna fail at his own life than succeed at a borrowed one — a standard that cuts against every instinct to imitate.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
अथ केन प्रयुक्तोऽयं पापं चरति पूरुषः।
अनिच्छन्नपि वार्ष्णेय बलादिव नियोजितः ॥३६॥
translation: Arjuna said: Then what impels a person to commit wrong even against their own will, Varshneya, as if driven by force?
explanation: Arjuna asks the question the whole chapter has been circling, and he asks it from experience. He knows the feeling of being pushed into what he did not choose.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
काम एष क्रोध एष रजोगुणसमुद्भवः।
महाशनो महापाप्मा विद्ध्येनमिह वैरिणम् ॥३७॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: It is desire, it is anger, born of the quality of passion — all-devouring and greatly harmful. Know this to be the enemy here.
explanation: Krishna names one culprit wearing two faces: desire, and the anger it becomes when blocked. All-devouring is the crucial charge — it has no point at which it is satisfied.

sanskrit:
धूमेनाव्रियते वह्निर्यथाऽऽदर्शो मलेन च।
यथोल्बेनावृतो गर्भस्तथा तेनेदमावृतम् ॥३८॥
translation: As fire is covered by smoke, as a mirror by dust, and as an embryo by the womb, so is this covered by that.
explanation: Three images of increasing intimacy — smoke drifts off, dust wipes away, but the womb cannot simply be removed. Krishna is grading how deeply desire can be embedded.

sanskrit:
आवृतं ज्ञानमेतेन ज्ञानिनो नित्यवैरिणा।
कामरूपेण कौन्तेय दुष्पूरेणानलेन च ॥३९॥
translation: Knowledge is covered by this constant enemy of the wise, Kaunteya — by this insatiable fire in the form of desire.
explanation: Note the phrase constant enemy of the wise. Krishna is clear that knowing better does not retire the problem, and the fire is called insatiable rather than merely strong.

sanskrit:
इन्द्रियाणि मनो बुद्धिरस्याधिष्ठानमुच्यते।
एतैर्विमोहयत्येष ज्ञानमावृत्य देहिनम् ॥४०॥
translation: The senses, the mind, and the understanding are said to be its seat. Through these it deludes the embodied one by covering knowledge.
explanation: Krishna maps the enemy's territory before attacking it. Desire is not located in objects out there but occupies three positions inside, each one further in than the last.

sanskrit:
तस्मात्त्वमिन्द्रियाण्यादौ नियम्य भरतर्षभ।
पाप्मानं प्रजहि ह्येनं ज्ञानविज्ञाननाशनम् ॥४१॥
translation: Therefore, best of the Bharatas, first restrain the senses and strike down this destroyer of knowledge and discrimination.
explanation: The order of operations matters — senses first, the outermost position. Krishna gives Arjuna somewhere to begin rather than asking him to defeat desire everywhere at once.

sanskrit:
इन्द्रियाणि पराण्याहुरिन्द्रियेभ्यः परं मनः।
मनसस्तु परा बुद्धिर्यो बुद्धेः परतस्तु सः ॥४२॥
translation: The senses are said to be higher than the body; higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the understanding; and higher than the understanding is that.
explanation: A ladder built in a single verse, each rung named by what it governs. Krishna leaves the top rung unnamed — simply that — the self standing above the whole apparatus.

sanskrit:
एवं बुद्धेः परं बुद्ध्वा संस्तभ्यात्मानमात्मना।
जहि शत्रुं महाबाहो कामरूपं दुरासदम् ॥४३॥
translation: Thus knowing that which is higher than the understanding, steadying the self by the self, slay this enemy in the form of desire, mighty-armed one — so hard to overcome.
explanation: The chapter ends with the battlefield metaphor turned inward. Krishna concedes the enemy is durasada, hard to reach, even while ordering the attack — no false promise of ease.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
इमं विवस्वते योगं प्रोक्तवानहमव्ययम्।
विवस्वान् मनवे प्राह मनुरिक्ष्वाकवेऽब्रवीत् ॥१॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvan; Vivasvan told it to Manu, and Manu declared it to Ikshvaku.
explanation: Krishna answers Arjuna's doubt by giving the teaching a lineage. This is not new advice invented for a crisis but something very old being restored on a battlefield.

sanskrit:
एवं परम्पराप्राप्तमिमं राजर्षयो विदुः।
स कालेनेह महता योगो नष्टः परन्तप ॥२॥
translation: Thus received in succession, the royal sages knew it. But over a long stretch of time, that yoga was lost here, scorcher of foes.
explanation: Note who kept it — rajarshis, kings who were also sages. The teaching was carried by people who governed and fought, which is precisely Arjuna's own situation.

sanskrit:
स एवायं मया तेऽद्य योगः प्रोक्तः पुरातनः।
भक्तोऽसि मे सखा चेति रहस्यं ह्येतदुत्तमम् ॥३॥
translation: That same ancient yoga is declared by me to you today, for you are my devotee and my friend — and this is the supreme secret.
explanation: Friend does the work in this verse. Krishna explains his willingness to speak not by Arjuna's qualifications but by their relationship, which is the chapter's quiet foundation.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
अपरं भवतो जन्म परं जन्म विवस्वतः।
कथमेतद्विजानीयां त्वमादौ प्रोक्तवानिति ॥४॥
translation: Arjuna said: Your birth was later; the birth of Vivasvan was earlier. How am I to understand that you taught this in the beginning?
explanation: A fair and literal-minded objection. Arjuna is still seeing his charioteer as a contemporary, and the arithmetic does not work — a question that draws out everything following.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
बहूनि मे व्यतीतानि जन्मानि तव चार्जुन।
तान्यहं वेद सर्वाणि न त्वं वेत्थ परन्तप ॥५॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: Many births of mine have passed, and yours as well, Arjuna. I know them all, but you do not know them, scorcher of foes.
explanation: The answer is not that Arjuna is wrong about birth but that he is wrong about counting. The difference between the two of them is memory, not nature — a strikingly level claim.

sanskrit:
अजोऽपि सन्नव्ययात्मा भूतानामीश्वरोऽपि सन्।
प्रकृतिं स्वामधिष्ठाय संभवाम्यात्ममायया ॥६॥
translation: Though I am unborn and of imperishable nature, and though I am the Lord of beings, yet governing my own nature I come into being by my own power.
explanation: Krishna distinguishes his appearing from ordinary birth. Beings are pushed into bodies by nature; he presides over his own and enters deliberately, which is the whole difference.

sanskrit:
यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत।
अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदाऽऽत्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥७॥
translation: Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, Bharata, and a rise of unrighteousness, then I send forth myself.
explanation: One of the most quoted promises in Indian thought. The trigger is not wickedness in general but glani, a wearing-thin of dharma — a slow failure rather than a sudden crime.

sanskrit:
परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम्।
धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय संभवामि युगे युगे ॥८॥
translation: For the protection of the good, the destruction of wrongdoers, and the firm establishment of righteousness, I come into being age after age.
explanation: Three purposes, and the third outranks the others. Rescue and destruction both serve the restoration of dharma; the aim is a working order, not a settled score.

sanskrit:
जन्म कर्म च मे दिव्यमेवं यो वेत्ति तत्त्वतः।
त्यक्त्वा देहं पुनर्जन्म नैति मामेति सोऽर्जुन ॥९॥
translation: One who truly knows my divine birth and action in this way is not born again on leaving the body, but comes to me, Arjuna.
explanation: Knowing here means grasping what the preceding verses described. Krishna offers understanding of his own nature as itself a liberating act, not merely as information held.

sanskrit:
वीतरागभयक्रोधा मन्मया मामुपाश्रिताः।
बहवो ज्ञानतपसा पूता मद्भावमागताः ॥१०॥
translation: Freed from passion, fear, and anger, absorbed in me and taking refuge in me, purified by the austerity of knowledge, many have attained my being.
explanation: Many have attained matters here. Krishna cites precedent rather than promise, and calls knowledge a tapas — an austerity, something undergone rather than simply acquired.

sanskrit:
ये यथा मां प्रपद्यन्ते तांस्तथैव भजाम्यहम्।
मम वर्त्मानुवर्तन्ते मनुष्याः पार्थ सर्वशः ॥११॥
translation: In whatever way people approach me, in that same way I favour them. Human beings follow my path in every respect, Partha.
explanation: A remarkably open verse. The response meets the approach on its own terms, which makes room for every temperament without ranking anyone at the door.

sanskrit:
काङ्क्षन्तः कर्मणां सिद्धिं यजन्त इह देवताः।
क्षिप्रं हि मानुषे लोके सिद्धिर्भवति कर्मजा ॥१२॥
translation: Desiring the fruition of their actions, people here worship the gods; for in the human world success born of action comes quickly.
explanation: Krishna explains the appeal of transactional worship without contempt. It is popular because it works, and works fast — an honest account of what it gives, and what it does not.

sanskrit:
चातुर्वर्ण्यं मया सृष्टं गुणकर्मविभागशः।
तस्य कर्तारमपि मां विद्ध्यकर्तारमव्ययम् ॥१३॥
translation: The fourfold order was created by me according to distinctions of quality and function. Though I am its author, know me to be the unchanging non-doer.
explanation: Krishna grounds social division in guna and karma — temperament and work — rather than in birth. Then he immediately steps back from authorship in the same breath.

sanskrit:
न मां कर्माणि लिम्पन्ति न मे कर्मफले स्पृहा।
इति मां योऽभिजानाति कर्मभिर्न स बध्यते ॥१४॥
translation: Actions do not stain me, nor do I long for the fruits of action. One who knows me in this way is not bound by actions.
explanation: The verse turns doctrine into method. Krishna's freedom is not a divine exemption to admire but a model to copy — he acts without appetite for results, and so can Arjuna.

sanskrit:
एवं ज्ञात्वा कृतं कर्म पूर्वैरपि मुमुक्षुभिः।
कुरु कर्मैव तस्मात्त्वं पूर्वैः पूर्वतरं कृतम् ॥१५॥
translation: Knowing this, the ancient seekers of liberation also performed action. Therefore do the very work that was done by those of old in earlier times.
explanation: Krishna returns to lineage, this time as reassurance. The people who most wanted release still worked, so Arjuna's longing to withdraw has no precedent among them.

sanskrit:
किं कर्म किमकर्मेति कवयोऽप्यत्र मोहिताः।
तत्ते कर्म प्रवक्ष्यामि यज्ज्ञात्वा मोक्ष्यसेऽशुभात् ॥१६॥
translation: What is action and what is inaction? Even the wise are confused about this. I shall explain action to you, knowing which you will be freed from evil.
explanation: A rare admission that even sages stumble here, offered just before the chapter's most demanding passage. Krishna is preparing Arjuna to find what follows difficult.

sanskrit:
कर्मणो ह्यपि बोद्धव्यं बोद्धव्यं च विकर्मणः।
अकर्मणश्च बोद्धव्यं गहना कर्मणो गतिः ॥१७॥
translation: One must understand the nature of action, the nature of wrong action, and also the nature of inaction. The way of action is deep and hard to see.
explanation: Three categories rather than two, and Krishna calls the terrain gahana — deep, tangled, overgrown. The honesty about its difficulty is itself part of the teaching.

sanskrit:
कर्मण्यकर्म यः पश्येदकर्मणि च कर्म यः।
स बुद्धिमान् मनुष्येषु स युक्तः कृत्स्नकर्मकृत् ॥१८॥
translation: One who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among people — disciplined, and performing every action.
explanation: The chapter's central paradox and its resolution in one line. The ending saves it: this person is doing everything, not sitting still while claiming inner detachment.

sanskrit:
यस्य सर्वे समारम्भाः कामसङ्कल्पवर्जिताः।
ज्ञानाग्निदग्धकर्माणं तमाहुः पण्डितं बुधाः ॥१९॥
translation: The wise call that one learned whose every undertaking is free of desire and design, whose actions are burnt up in the fire of knowledge.
explanation: The criterion is stated as an absence — no desire propelling the start of things. Knowledge is pictured as a fire consuming the residue that action would otherwise leave.

sanskrit:
त्यक्त्वा कर्मफलासङ्गं नित्यतृप्तो निराश्रयः।
कर्मण्यभिप्रवृत्तोऽपि नैव किञ्चित्करोति सः ॥२०॥
