translation: Having given up attachment to the fruits of action, ever content and dependent on nothing, such a one does nothing at all even while fully engaged in action.
explanation: A precise description of the paradox from the inside. Nothing about the activity changes; what disappears is the dependence that made it feel like it belonged to someone.

sanskrit:
निराशीर्यतचित्तात्मा त्यक्तसर्वपरिग्रहः।
शारीरं केवलं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम् ॥२१॥
translation: With no expectations, mind and self restrained, having relinquished all possessions, performing action with the body alone, one incurs no fault.
explanation: With the body alone is the striking phrase. The work proceeds, but no inner grasping accompanies it, and that is what keeps the act from leaving a mark behind.

sanskrit:
यदृच्छालाभसन्तुष्टो द्वन्द्वातीतो विमत्सरः।
समः सिद्धावसिद्धौ च कृत्वापि न निबध्यते ॥२२॥
translation: Content with whatever comes unsought, beyond dualities, free of envy, the same in success and failure — such a one, though acting, is not bound.
explanation: Contentment with the unsought returns from Chapter 2, but envy is new. Krishna notices that measuring oneself against others is a separate chain from wanting outcomes.

sanskrit:
गतसङ्गस्य मुक्तस्य ज्ञानावस्थितचेतसः।
यज्ञायाचरतः कर्म समग्रं प्रविलीयते ॥२३॥
translation: For one free of attachment and liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge, who acts as sacrifice — the whole of that action dissolves away.
explanation: The verb matters: it dissolves, rather than being forgiven or repaid. Action offered as sacrifice never accumulates into anything that must later be settled, which is why Krishna keeps insisting the work was never the problem.

sanskrit:
ब्रह्मार्पणं ब्रह्महविर्ब्रह्माग्नौ ब्रह्मणा हुतम्।
ब्रह्मैव तेन गन्तव्यं ब्रह्मकर्मसमाधिना ॥२४॥
translation: The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman. Brahman is reached by one absorbed in Brahman as action.
explanation: A famous verse in which every element of the ritual collapses into a single reality. The chant-like repetition enacts what it describes — no separate parts left anywhere.

sanskrit:
दैवमेवापरे यज्ञं योगिनः पर्युपासते।
ब्रह्माग्नावपरे यज्ञं यज्ञेनैवोपजुह्वति ॥२५॥
translation: Some yogins offer sacrifice to the gods, while others offer sacrifice itself as an oblation in the fire of Brahman.
explanation: Krishna begins a survey of practices by pairing the most conventional with the most abstract. Both are named as sacrifice, and neither is dismissed in favour of the other.

sanskrit:
श्रोत्रादीनीन्द्रियाण्यन्ये संयमाग्निषु जुह्वति।
शब्दादीन्विषयानन्य इन्द्रियाग्निषु जुह्वति ॥२६॥
translation: Others offer hearing and the other senses into the fires of restraint; still others offer sound and the other objects into the fires of the senses.
explanation: A striking symmetry — one group feeds the senses to discipline, another feeds experience to the senses. Krishna is showing that engagement can be an offering too.

sanskrit:
सर्वाणीन्द्रियकर्माणि प्राणकर्माणि चापरे।
आत्मसंयमयोगाग्नौ जुह्वति ज्ञानदीपिते ॥२७॥
translation: Others offer all the functions of the senses and the functions of the breath into the fire of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge.
explanation: The offering moves inward again, now consuming even the involuntary. Note that the fire must be lit by knowledge — restraint on its own has nothing to burn with.

sanskrit:
द्रव्ययज्ञास्तपोयज्ञा योगयज्ञास्तथापरे।
स्वाध्यायज्ञानयज्ञाश्च यतयः संशितव्रताः ॥२८॥
translation: Others offer their wealth, their austerity, or their practice as sacrifice, while ascetics of firm vows offer study and knowledge.
explanation: The catalogue keeps widening to include whatever people actually have — money, effort, study. The list is generous, and deliberately avoids naming a single required form.

sanskrit:
अपाने जुह्वति प्राण प्राणेऽपानं तथाऽपरे।
प्राणापानगती रुद्ध्वा प्राणायामपरायणाः ॥२९॥
translation: Others, devoted to breath control, offer the outgoing breath into the incoming, and the incoming into the outgoing, restraining the flow of both.
explanation: Even breathing is enlisted. Krishna presents pranayama as a sacrifice like any other, quietly placing the most technical practice on a level with the simplest ones.

sanskrit:
अपरे नियताहाराः प्राणान्प्राणेषु जुह्वति।
सर्वेऽप्येते यज्ञविदो यज्ञक्षपितकल्मषाः ॥३०॥
translation: Others, restricting their food, offer their life-breaths into the life-breaths. All these know sacrifice, and their impurities are consumed by sacrifice.
explanation: The survey closes by gathering every practitioner into one sentence. Whatever the method, Krishna credits them all with knowing what sacrifice is — the intent, not the technique.

sanskrit:
यज्ञशिष्टामृतभुजो यान्ति ब्रह्म सनातनम्।
नायं लोकोऽस्त्ययज्ञस्य कुतो़ऽन्यः कुरुसत्तम ॥३१॥
translation: Those who eat the nectar of what remains from sacrifice go to the eternal Brahman. This world is not for one who does not sacrifice — how then the next, best of the Kurus?
explanation: The remainder returns from Chapter 3, now called nectar. And the warning sharpens: the non-offerer does not even manage this world well, let alone anything beyond it.

sanskrit:
एवं बहुविधा यज्ञा वितता ब्रह्मणो मुखे।
कर्मजान्विद्धि तान्सर्वानेवं ज्ञात्वा विमोक्ष्यसे ॥३२॥
translation: Many kinds of sacrifice are thus spread out before Brahman. Know them all to be born of action; knowing this, you will be liberated.
explanation: Krishna reveals the point of the whole catalogue. Every practice he listed is a form of doing, which means the path Arjuna wanted to escape runs straight through all of them.

sanskrit:
श्रेयान्द्रव्यमयाद्यज्ञाज्ज्ञानयज्ञः परन्तप।
सर्वं कर्माखिलं पार्थ ज्ञाने परिसमाप्यते ॥३३॥
translation: The sacrifice of knowledge is better than any material sacrifice, scorcher of foes. All action in its entirety culminates in knowledge, Partha.
explanation: After treating the practices as equals, Krishna finally ranks them. Material offerings are real but instrumental; knowledge is where the whole enterprise was heading anyway.

sanskrit:
तद्विद्धि प्रणिपातेन परिप्रश्नेन सेवया।
उपदेक्ष्यन्ति ते ज्ञानं ज्ञानिनस्तत्त्वदर्शिनः ॥३४॥
translation: Learn this by prostration, by inquiry, and by service. Those who know, who have seen the truth, will teach you knowledge.
explanation: Three conditions, and the middle one licenses questioning. Krishna asks for humility and service, yet insists that asking is part of learning rather than a failure of it.

sanskrit:
यज्ज्ञात्वा न पुनर्मोहमेवं यास्यसि पाण्डव।
येन भूतान्यशेषेण द्रक्ष्यस्यात्मन्यथो मयि ॥३५॥
translation: Knowing this, you will not fall into such delusion again, Pandava. By it you will see all beings without exception in yourself, and then in me.
explanation: The promised result is perceptual, not doctrinal. Arjuna will see the people on this field differently, which is the only thing that could actually resolve his morning.

sanskrit:
अपि चेदसि पापेभ्यः सर्वेभ्यः पापकृत्तमः।
सर्वं ज्ञानप्लवेनैव वृजिनं सन्तरिष्यसि ॥३६॥
translation: Even if you were the most sinful of all sinners, you would cross over all wickedness by the raft of knowledge alone.
explanation: Krishna states the extreme case deliberately. The raft image keeps the claim modest — knowledge does not drain the water, it carries someone across it.

sanskrit:
यथैधांसि समिद्धोऽग्निर्भस्मसात्कुरुतेऽर्जुन।
ज्ञानाग्निः सर्वकर्माणि भस्मसात्कुरुते तथा ॥३७॥
translation: As a kindled fire reduces firewood to ashes, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.
explanation: The fire image returns, now with the fuel specified. Actions are firewood — substantial, stacked up, and entirely consumable once something hot enough reaches them.

sanskrit:
न हि ज्ञानेन सदृशं पवित्रमिह विद्यते।
तत्स्वयं योगसंसिद्धः कालेनात्मनि विन्दति ॥३८॥
translation: Indeed, there is nothing here as purifying as knowledge. In time, one perfected in yoga finds it within oneself.
explanation: Two claims worth holding together: knowledge is supreme, and it arrives from within, in time. Krishna adds patience to a chapter otherwise full of urgent instruction.

sanskrit:
श्रद्धावाँल्लभते ज्ञानं तत्परः संयतेन्द्रियः।
ज्ञानं लब्ध्वा परां शान्तिमचिरेणाधिगच्छति ॥३९॥
translation: The one who has faith obtains knowledge — intent upon it, with the senses restrained. Having obtained knowledge, one quickly attains supreme peace.
explanation: Faith first, then knowledge, then peace. Krishna orders them carefully: shraddha is not the reward for understanding but the condition that makes understanding possible, which reverses the sequence most people would assume.

sanskrit:
अज्ञश्चाश्रद्दधानश्च संशयात्मा विनश्यति।
नायं लोकोऽस्ति न परो न सुखं संशयात्मनः ॥४०॥
translation: The ignorant, the faithless, and the doubting one perish. For the doubting one there is neither this world nor the next, nor any happiness.
explanation: The harshest line of the chapter, and its target is samshaya — not honest inquiry but the settled inability to commit. Perpetual doubt is described as costing everything.

sanskrit:
योगसंन्यस्तकर्माणं ज्ञानसंछिन्नसंशयम्।
आत्मवन्तं न कर्माणि निबध्नन्ति धनञ्जय ॥४१॥
translation: Actions do not bind the one who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubts are severed by knowledge, and who is possessed of the self, Dhananjaya.
explanation: Krishna gathers the chapter's threads — yoga, knowledge, self-possession — into a single sentence. Renouncing action through yoga, not instead of it, is the whole distinction.

sanskrit:
तस्मादज्ञानसंभूतं हृत्स्थं ज्ञानासिनाऽऽत्मनः।
छित्त्वैनं संशयं योगमातिष्ठोत्तिष्ठ भारत ॥४२॥
translation: Therefore, cutting with the sword of knowledge this doubt in your heart born of ignorance, take refuge in yoga. Arise, Bharata.
explanation: The chapter ends with a weapon in Arjuna's hands, though not the one he expected. And with arise — the same word from Chapter 2, now standing on an argument.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
संन्यासं कर्मणां कृष्ण पुनर्योगं च शंससि।
यच्छ्रेय एतयोरेकं तन्मे ब्रूहि सुनिश्िचतम् ॥१॥
translation: Arjuna said: You praise the renunciation of actions, Krishna, and again you praise yoga. Tell me decisively which one of these two is better.
explanation: Arjuna's third request for a single answer. He is not being slow — Krishna genuinely keeps commending both, and Arjuna wants to know what to actually do this morning.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
संन्यासः कर्मयोगश्च निःश्रेयसकरावुभौ।
तयोस्तु कर्मसंन्यासात्कर्मयोगो विशिष्यते ॥२॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: Both renunciation and the yoga of action lead to the highest good. But of the two, the yoga of action surpasses the renunciation of action.
explanation: Krishna finally ranks them, and picks the harder-sounding option. Both work, but the one that keeps a person in the world is the one he recommends to Arjuna.

sanskrit:
ज्ञेयः स नित्यसंन्यासी यो न द्वेष्टि न काङ्क्षति।
निर्द्वन्द्वो हि महाबाहो सुखं बन्धात्प्रमुच्यते ॥३॥
translation: Know that one to be a perpetual renouncer who neither hates nor desires. Free from dualities, mighty-armed one, such a person is easily released from bondage.
explanation: Renunciation is redefined as an inner condition rather than an outward arrangement. By this measure someone in armour can be a renunciate, and someone in a forest may not be.

sanskrit:
सांख्ययोगौ पृथग्बालाः प्रवदन्ति न पण्डिताः।
एकमप्यास्थितः सम्यगुभयोर्विन्दते फलम् ॥४॥
translation: Children speak of Sankhya and Yoga as distinct, but not the learned. One who is properly established in either obtains the fruit of both.
explanation: A sharp word — children — for a distinction Arjuna has pressed for two chapters. Krishna calls the split a beginner's misreading rather than a real fork in the road.

sanskrit:
यत्सांख्यैः प्राप्यते स्थानं तद्योगैरपि गम्यते।
एकं सांख्यं च योगं च यः पश्यति स पश्यति ॥५॥
translation: The state reached by the followers of Sankhya is also attained by the followers of Yoga. One who sees Sankhya and Yoga as one truly sees.
explanation: The claim is about destination, not method. Krishna does not flatten the two practices; he insists they arrive at the same place, so choosing between them is not urgent.

sanskrit:
संन्यासस्तु महाबाहो दुःखमाप्तुमयोगतः।
योगयुक्तो मुनिर्ब्रह्म नचिरेणाधिगच्छति ॥६॥
translation: But renunciation is hard to attain without yoga, mighty-armed one. The sage disciplined in yoga reaches Brahman before long.
explanation: The practical reason behind his ranking. Renunciation attempted without the groundwork of disciplined action is described as simply painful — Krishna is heading off a shortcut.

sanskrit:
योगयुक्तो विशुद्धात्मा विजितात्मा जितेन्द्रियः।
सर्वभूतात्मभूतात्मा कुर्वन्नपि न लिप्यते ॥७॥
translation: One disciplined in yoga, pure in self, master of self and senses, whose self has become the self of all beings, is not tainted even while acting.
explanation: The phrase in the middle is the remarkable one — becoming the self of all beings. Krishna makes universality, not withdrawal, the thing that keeps action from staining.

sanskrit:
नैव किंचित्करोमीति युक्तो मन्येत तत्त्ववित्।
पश्यन् श्रृणवन्स्पृशञ्जिघ्रन्नश्नन्गच्छन्स्वपन् श्वसन् ॥८॥
translation: The one who knows the truth, disciplined, thinks: I do nothing at all — while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, and breathing.
explanation: A deliberately mundane list. Krishna picks the least glamorous human activities to make his point, since these are precisely the ones nobody could claim to have renounced.

sanskrit:
प्रलपन्विसृजन्गृह्णन्नुन्मिषन्निमिषन्नपि।
इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेषु वर्तन्त इति धारयन् ॥९॥
translation: ...and while speaking, releasing, grasping, and opening and closing the eyes — holding firmly that it is the senses that move among the objects of sense.
explanation: The list continues down to blinking. The insight is not that nothing happens but that the happening belongs to the machinery, with no one standing behind it claiming credit.

sanskrit:
ब्रह्मण्याधाय कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा करोति यः।
लिप्यते न स पापेन पद्मपत्रमिवाम्भसा ॥१०॥
translation: One who acts, offering all actions to Brahman and abandoning attachment, is not touched by wrong — as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.
explanation: The lotus leaf is the Gita's finest image for engaged detachment. The leaf sits in the water, not above it; contact happens constantly and nothing soaks in.

sanskrit:
कायेन मनसा बुद्ध्या केवलैरिन्द्रियैरपि।
योगिनः कर्म कुर्वन्ति सङ्गं त्यक्त्वाऽऽत्मशुद्धये ॥११॥
translation: Yogins perform action with the body, the mind, the understanding, or even with the senses alone, abandoning attachment, for the purification of the self.
explanation: Note the purpose given: atma-shuddhi, self-purification. The work is not being done for the world's sake here, but because doing it cleanly changes the one who does it.

sanskrit:
युक्तः कर्मफलं त्यक्त्वा शान्तिमाप्नोति नैष्ठिकीम्।
अयुक्तः कामकारेण फले सक्तो निबध्यते ॥१२॥
translation: The disciplined one, abandoning the fruit of action, attains lasting peace. The undisciplined one, attached to fruit through the working of desire, is bound.
explanation: The same action, two outcomes, and the variable is not effort but appetite. Krishna keeps returning to this because Arjuna keeps hearing it as a call to do less.

sanskrit:
सर्वकर्माणि मनसा संन्यस्यास्ते सुखं वशी।
नवद्वारे पुरे देही नैव कुर्वन्न कारयन् ॥१३॥
translation: Mentally renouncing all actions, the embodied one dwells at ease and in control in the city of nine gates — neither acting nor causing action.
explanation: The body as a nine-gated city is a wonderfully architectural image. The self is resident rather than labourer, and the gates are the openings through which everything passes.

sanskrit:
न कर्तृत्वं न कर्माणि लोकस्य सृजति प्रभुः।
न कर्मफलसंयोगं स्वभावस्तु प्रवर्तते ॥१४॥
translation: The Lord creates neither the agency nor the actions of the world, nor the union of actions with their fruits. It is nature that proceeds of itself.
explanation: Krishna declines responsibility for the human predicament in unusually flat terms. The machinery of deeds and consequences runs on its own; svabhava is what moves.

sanskrit:
नादत्ते कस्यचित्पापं न चैव सुकृतं विभुः।
अज्ञानेनावृतं ज्ञानं तेन मुह्यन्ति जन्तवः ॥१५॥
translation: The all-pervading one takes on neither the wrong nor the good deeds of anyone. Knowledge is covered over by ignorance, and by that creatures are deluded.
explanation: A refusal of the bookkeeping model of divinity. And the diagnosis that follows is not that people are wicked but that something true in them has been covered over.

sanskrit:
ज्ञानेन तु तदज्ञानं येषां नाशितमात्मनः।
तेषामादित्यवज्ज्ञानं प्रकाशयति तत्परम् ॥१६॥
translation: But for those whose ignorance is destroyed by knowledge of the self, that knowledge, like the sun, illumines the Supreme.
explanation: The sun does not create what it reveals. Krishna's image implies the Supreme was there the whole time, and knowledge changes only whether it can be seen.

sanskrit:
तद्बुद्धयस्तदात्मानस्तन्निष्ठास्तत्परायणाः।
गच्छन्त्यपुनरावृत्तिं ज्ञाननिर्धूतकल्मषाः ॥१७॥
translation: With understanding fixed on that, self absorbed in that, established in that, devoted to that, they go where there is no returning, their faults shaken off by knowledge.
explanation: Four phrases saying nearly the same thing in a row. The insistent repetition of tat, that, does the work — a mind gone entirely in one direction.

sanskrit:
विद्याविनयसंपन्ने ब्राह्मणे गवि हस्तिनि।
शुनि चैव श्वपाके च पण्डिताः समदर्शिनः ॥१८॥
translation: The wise see the same in a brahmana endowed with learning and humility, in a cow, in an elephant, and in a dog or an outcaste.
explanation: One of the boldest verses in the Gita, and the list is deliberately provocative. Krishna runs from the most honoured to the most despised and refuses to let the seeing change.

sanskrit:
इहैव तैर्जितः सर्गो येषां साम्ये स्थितं मनः।
निर्दोषं हि समं ब्रह्म तस्माद्ब्रह्मणि ते स्थिताः ॥१९॥
translation: Even here, rebirth is conquered by those whose mind is established in evenness. Brahman is flawless and the same, and so they are established in Brahman.
explanation: The logic is elegant: since the absolute is uniform, a mind that has become uniform is already in it. Sameness of vision is the state itself, not a virtue rewarded later.

sanskrit:
न प्रहृष्येत्प्रियं प्राप्य नोद्विजेत्प्राप्य चाप्रियम्।
स्थिरबुद्धिरसम्मूढो ब्रह्मविद्ब्रह्मणि स्थितः ॥२०॥
translation: One should neither rejoice on obtaining the pleasant nor be disturbed on obtaining the unpleasant. Steady in understanding and undeluded, the knower of Brahman is established in Brahman.
explanation: Note what is not asked for — the pleasant and unpleasant still keep arriving. Krishna targets the reaction, not the circumstances, which is the only part actually available.

sanskrit:
बाह्यस्पर्शेष्वसक्तात्मा विन्दत्यात्मनि यत्सुखम्।
स ब्रह्मयोगयुक्तात्मा सुखमक्षयमश्नुते ॥२१॥
translation: With the self unattached to outward contacts, one finds the happiness that is in the self. With the self joined to the yoga of Brahman, one enjoys imperishable happiness.
explanation: Krishna is careful to promise happiness, not its absence. The argument is about sourcing — an inner supply that cannot run out, rather than an outer one that must.

sanskrit:
ये हि संस्पर्शजा भोगा दुःखयोनय एव ते।
आद्यन्तवन्तः कौन्तेय न तेषु रमते बुधः ॥२२॥
translation: The enjoyments born of contact are only wombs of sorrow, Kaunteya. They have a beginning and an end, and the wise do not take delight in them.
explanation: Wombs of sorrow is a striking phrase — these pleasures do not merely fade, they give birth to the grief that follows. The fault named is precisely their having ends.

sanskrit:
शक्नोतीहैव यः सोढुं प्राक्शरीरविमोक्षणात्।
कामक्रोधोद्भवं वेगं स युक्तः स सुखी नरः ॥२३॥
translation: One who can withstand here, before release from the body, the force born of desire and anger — that person is disciplined, and that person is happy.
explanation: The word vega, surge or force, is exact. Krishna is describing something with momentum that arrives whether invited or not, and endurance as the thing worth building.

sanskrit:
योऽन्तःसुखोऽन्तरारामस्तथान्तर्ज्योतिरेव यः।
स योगी ब्रह्मनिर्वाणं ब्रह्मभूतोऽधिगच्छति ॥२४॥
translation: One who finds happiness within, delight within, and light within — that yogin, having become Brahman, attains the peace of Brahman.
explanation: Three interior sources named in a row, ending with light. Krishna describes self-sufficiency not as isolation but as illumination that needs nothing outside itself to shine.

sanskrit:
लभन्ते ब्रह्मनिर्वाणमृषयः क्षीणकल्मषाः।
छिन्नद्वैधा यतात्मानः सर्वभूतहिते रताः ॥२५॥
translation: The seers whose faults are worn away, whose doubts are cut, who are self-controlled and delight in the welfare of all beings, attain the peace of Brahman.
explanation: The last item is easy to miss and hardest to fake. Krishna slips active care for every being into a list of contemplative attainments, refusing to let peace be private.

sanskrit:
कामक्रोधवियुक्तानां यतीनां यतचेतसाम्।
अभितो ब्रह्मनिर्वाणं वर्तते विदितात्मनाम् ॥२६॥
translation: For those free of desire and anger, restrained in thought, who have known the self, the peace of Brahman exists all around them.
explanation: Abhitah, all around, is the word that matters. This peace is not waiting at the end of a road but already surrounding those who have become able to perceive it.

sanskrit:
स्पर्शान्कृत्वा बहिर्बाह्यांश्चक्षुश्चैवान्तरे भ्रुवोः।
प्राणापानौ समौ कृत्वा नासाभ्यन्तरचारिणौ ॥२७॥
translation: Shutting out external contacts, fixing the gaze between the brows, making even the inward and outward breaths that move through the nostrils...
explanation: The chapter turns suddenly practical, giving posture and breath. Krishna has argued philosophically for twenty-six verses and now hands over something to actually do, as though the argument were only ever clearing ground for this.

sanskrit:
यतेन्द्रियमनोबुद्धिर्मुनिर्मोक्षपरायणः।
विगतेच्छाभयक्रोधो यः सदा मुक्त एव सः ॥२८॥
translation: ...the sage whose senses, mind, and understanding are controlled, intent on liberation, free of desire, fear, and anger, is forever free.
explanation: The sentence completes with inner conditions after outer technique. Note the order — Krishna gives the posture first and the freedom last, as its result rather than its price.

sanskrit:
भोक्तारं यज्ञतपसां सर्वलोकमहेश्वरम्।
सुहृदं सर्वभूतानां ज्ञात्वा मां शान्तिमृच्छति ॥२९॥
translation: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great Lord of all the worlds, and the friend of every being, one attains peace.
explanation: The chapter ends on suhrit, well-wisher. After all the metaphysics, Krishna's final word about himself is the most personal one — not ruler but friend, of everyone.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
अनाश्रितः कर्मफलं कार्यं कर्म करोति यः।
स संन्यासी च योगी च न निरग्निर्न चाक्रियः ॥१॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: One who performs the work that must be done without depending on its fruit is a renunciate and a yogin — not one who lights no fire and performs no rites.
explanation: Krishna opens by stripping renunciation of its outward markers. The absence of ritual fires proves nothing; what counts is whether the work was done leaning on its results.

sanskrit:
यं संन्यासमिति प्राहुर्योगं तं विद्धि पाण्डव।
न ह्यसंन्यस्तसङ्कल्पो योगी भवति कश्चन ॥२॥
translation: Know that what they call renunciation is yoga, Pandava. For no one becomes a yogin without having renounced self-will.
explanation: The two words Arjuna keeps opposing are declared identical. And the thing to be renounced is named precisely: sankalpa, the wilful intention that plans outcomes in advance.

sanskrit:
आरुरुक्षोर्मुनेर्योगं कर्म कारणमुच्यते।
योगारूढस्य तस्यैव शमः कारणमुच्यते ॥३॥
translation: For the sage who wishes to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means. For one who has ascended to yoga, stillness is said to be the means.
explanation: A genuinely useful distinction. The same practice is not right at every stage — work builds the climb, quiet consolidates the summit, and confusing the two wastes years.

sanskrit:
यदा हि नेन्द्रियार्थेषु न कर्मस्वनुषज्जते।
सर्वसङ्कल्पसंन्यासी योगारूढस्तदोच्यते ॥४॥
translation: When one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, and has renounced all self-will, then one is said to have ascended to yoga.
explanation: Krishna defines the summit so the previous verse can be used. It is not a feeling or a milestone but a specific loosening that a person can honestly check for.

sanskrit:
उद्धरेदात्मनाऽऽत्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत्।
आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः ॥५॥
translation: Let a person lift himself by himself and not degrade himself. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is its enemy.
explanation: The most self-reliant verse in the Gita, spoken by a god to a devotee. Krishna makes plain that nobody else can perform the lifting, not even the one giving the advice.

sanskrit:
बन्धुरात्माऽऽत्मनस्तस्य येनात्मैवात्मना जितः।
अनात्मनस्तु शत्रुत्वे वर्तेतात्मैव शत्रुवत् ॥६॥
translation: The self is the friend of one who has conquered the self by the self. But for one who has not, the self remains hostile, behaving like an enemy.
explanation: The same faculty stands on both sides of the fight. Krishna refuses to blame outside forces for Arjuna's paralysis — the obstruction and the way through are one apparatus.

sanskrit:
जितात्मनः प्रशान्तस्य परमात्मा समाहितः।
शीतोष्णसुखदुःखेषु तथा मानापमानयोः ॥७॥
translation: For one who has conquered the self and is at peace, the supreme self is composed — in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, in honour and dishonour alike.
explanation: Three pairs of opposites, and the last is social rather than physical. Krishna knows reputation is what a warrior finds hardest to become genuinely indifferent to.

sanskrit:
ज्ञानविज्ञानतृप्तात्मा कूटस्थो विजितेन्द्रियः।
युक्त इत्युच्यते योगी समलोष्टाश्मकाञ्चनः ॥८॥
translation: The yogin whose self is satisfied with knowledge and realization, who is unshaken and has conquered the senses, is called disciplined — the same toward a clod, a stone, and gold.
explanation: The three objects make the point concretely. Gold is not condemned; it is simply put in a row with dirt, and the yogin is described as failing to distinguish between them.

sanskrit:
सुहृन्मित्रार्युदासीनमध्यस्थद्वेष्यबन्धुषु।
साधुष्वपि च पापेषु समबुद्धिर्विशिष्यते ॥९॥
translation: One who is equal-minded toward well-wishers, friends, enemies, the indifferent, the neutral, the hateful, and relatives — and toward the good and the sinful alike — excels.
explanation: A seven-part list of social positions, and Arjuna's entire crisis is that these categories are tangled on this field. Krishna answers by dissolving the categories themselves.

sanskrit:
योगी युञ्जीत सततमात्मानं रहसि स्थितः।
एकाकी यतचित्तात्मा निराशीरपरिग्रहः ॥१०॥
translation: Let the yogin constantly discipline himself, remaining in solitude, alone, with mind and self restrained, free of expectation and free of possessions.
explanation: The formal instruction begins with circumstances rather than technique. Krishna sets the conditions — solitude, few belongings, no expectations — before naming any posture, on the assumption that a life arranged badly will defeat any method.

sanskrit:
शुचौ देशे प्रतिष्ठाप्य स्थिरमासनमात्मनः।
नात्युच्छ्रितं नातिनीचं चैलाजिनकुशोत्तरम् ॥११॥
translation: In a clean place, having established a firm seat for oneself, neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass...
explanation: A startling turn to the concrete. After chapters of metaphysics Krishna specifies furniture, and the recurring note is moderation, extending even to the height of a seat.

sanskrit:
तत्रैकाग्रं मनः कृत्वा यतचित्तेन्द्रियक्रियः।
उपविश्यासने युञ्ज्याद्योगमात्मविशुद्धये ॥१२॥
translation: ...there, seated upon that seat, making the mind one-pointed, with the activity of thought and senses controlled, one should practise yoga for self-purification.
explanation: The instruction completes with a purpose rather than a promise. Practice aims at cleaning something, a humbler goal than the visions Arjuna will later be given.

sanskrit:
समं कायशिरोग्रीवं धारयन्नचलं स्थिरः।
संप्रेक्ष्य नासिकाग्रं स्वं दिशश्चानवलोकयन् ॥१३॥
translation: Holding the body, head, and neck erect, still and steady, gazing at the tip of one's own nose and not looking about in any direction...
explanation: The physical detail is exact enough to follow. Not looking about is the quiet instruction — a body that keeps turning to check its surroundings cannot settle.

sanskrit:
प्रशान्तात्मा विगतभीर्ब्रह्मचारिव्रते स्थितः।
मनः संयम्य मच्चित्तो युक्त आसीत मत्परः ॥१४॥
translation: ...with a serene self, free of fear, firm in the vow of continence, restraining the mind, absorbed in me — let one sit, intent on me.
explanation: The posture sequence ends where Krishna always ends: mat-parah, intent on me. Technique is never the whole instruction, and here the object of attention is supplied.

sanskrit:
युञ्जन्नेवं सदाऽऽत्मानं योगी नियतमानसः।
शान्तिं निर्वाणपरमां मत्संस्थामधिगच्छति ॥१५॥
translation: Constantly disciplining himself in this way, the yogin of restrained mind attains the peace that culminates in liberation and abides in me.
explanation: The result promised for the practice just described. Krishna characterizes it as peace rather than power, consistent with everything he has said about chasing outcomes.

sanskrit:
नात्यश्नतस्तु योगोऽस्ति न चैकान्तमनश्नतः।
न चातिस्वप्नशीलस्य जाग्रतो नैव चार्जुन ॥१६॥
translation: Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all, nor for one given to too much sleep, nor for one who stays awake, Arjuna.
explanation: A firm rejection of extremism, and it lands as a relief. The heroic austerities Arjuna might imagine are ruled out as obstacles rather than offered as shortcuts.

sanskrit:
युक्ताहारविहारस्य युक्तचेष्टस्य कर्मसु।
युक्तस्वप्नावबोधस्य योगो भवति दुःखहा ॥१७॥
translation: For one who is moderate in food and recreation, moderate in effort at his actions, moderate in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.
explanation: Yukta, well-yoked, repeats four times — the word that means disciplined also means fitting. Krishna's discipline is a matter of proportion rather than severity, and the promised result is not power but the end of sorrow.

sanskrit:
यदा विनियतं चित्तमात्मन्येवावतिष्ठते।
निःस्पृहः सर्वकामेभ्यो युक्त इत्युच्यते तदा ॥१८॥
translation: When the well-controlled mind rests in the self alone, free of longing for all desires, then one is said to be disciplined.
explanation: The criterion is rest, not effort. Krishna describes arrival as a mind that has stopped going out, which is a different thing from a mind being forcibly held in place.

sanskrit:
यथा दीपो निवातस्थो नेङ्गते सोपमा स्मृता।
योगिनो यतचित्तस्य युञ्जतो योगमात्मनः ॥१९॥
translation: As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker — that is the simile remembered for the yogin of restrained mind, practising the yoga of the self.
explanation: The Gita's most beautiful image of concentration. A flame is not made steady by gripping it; it is steady when nothing disturbs it, which relocates the entire problem.

sanskrit:
यत्रोपरमते चित्तं निरुद्धं योगसेवया।
यत्र चैवात्मनाऽऽत्मानं पश्यन्नात्मनि तुष्यति ॥२०॥
translation: Where thought comes to rest, checked by the practice of yoga, and where, seeing the self by the self, one is content within the self...
explanation: Krishna begins a long sentence describing the state from inside. Note the recursive phrasing — the self is subject, instrument, and object, with nothing external involved.

sanskrit:
सुखमात्यन्तिकं यत्तद्बुद्धिग्राह्यमतीन्द्रियम्।
वेत्ति यत्र न चैवायं स्थितश्चलति तत्त्वतः ॥२१॥
translation: ...where one knows that absolute happiness which is grasped by the understanding and lies beyond the senses, and, established there, does not stray from the truth...
explanation: Happiness beyond the senses is Krishna's most precise claim about what practice yields. Not intense pleasure but a different category, reached by a different faculty.

sanskrit:
यं लब्ध्वा चापरं लाभं मन्यते नाधिकं ततः।
यस्मिन्स्थितो न दुःखेन गुरुणापि विचाल्यते ॥२२॥
translation: ...which, having gained, one thinks no other gain greater, and established in which one is not shaken even by heavy sorrow...
explanation: The test is comparative and severe. Not merely feeling good, but finding nothing else worth wanting, and holding steady under weight that would ordinarily break someone.

sanskrit:
तं विद्याद् दुःखसंयोगवियोगं योगसंज्ञितम्।
स निश्चयेन योक्तव्यो योगोऽनिर्विण्णचेतसा ॥२३॥
translation: Know that state, free from any union with sorrow, to be what is called yoga. It should be practised with resolve and with an undespairing mind.
explanation: The definition finally lands, and Krishna attaches a warning. An undespairing mind admits this will take long enough that discouragement is a real and expected risk.

sanskrit:
सङ्कल्पप्रभवान्कामांस्त्यक्त्वा सर्वानशेषतः।
मनसैवेन्द्रियग्रामं विनियम्य समन्ततः ॥२४॥
translation: Abandoning without exception all desires born of self-will, and restraining the whole array of the senses on every side with the mind...
explanation: The word used for the senses is grama, a village or gathering — a whole community of appetites, each pulling its own way, to be governed rather than fought one by one.

sanskrit:
शनैः शनैरुपरमेद् बुद्ध्या धृतिगृहीतया।
आत्मसंस्थं मनः कृत्वा न किञ्चिदपि चिन्तयेत् ॥२५॥
translation: ...little by little let one come to rest, with the understanding held firm. Fixing the mind upon the self, let one think of nothing at all.
explanation: Little by little is the mercy in this passage. Krishna, having described an extraordinary state, prescribes gradualness — the mind is talked down, not seized.

sanskrit:
यतो यतो निश्चरति मनश्चञ्चलमस्थिरम्।
ततस्ततो नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥२६॥
translation: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, from there let it be restrained and brought back under the control of the self.
explanation: The most practically useful verse in the chapter. Krishna assumes the wandering will happen repeatedly and offers no scolding — only the instruction to bring it back again.

sanskrit:
प्रशान्तमनसं ह्येनं योगिनं सुखमुत्तमम्।
उपैति शान्तरजसं ब्रह्मभूतमकल्मषम् ॥२७॥
translation: Supreme happiness comes to this yogin whose mind is at peace, whose passion is quieted, who has become Brahman and is free of fault.
explanation: Note the order once again: peace arrives first and happiness follows. Krishna consistently treats delight as a by-product of stillness rather than as a target to pursue.

sanskrit:
युञ्जन्नेवं सदाऽऽत्मानं योगी विगतकल्मषः।
सुखेन ब्रह्मसंस्पर्शमत्यन्तं सुखमश्नुते ॥२८॥
translation: Thus constantly disciplining himself, the yogin freed from fault easily attains the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman.
explanation: Easily appears at last — but only after constant practice. Krishna is honest that the ease arrives at the end of the road rather than anywhere near its beginning.

sanskrit:
सर्वभूतस्थमात्मानं सर्वभूतानि चात्मनि।
ईक्षते योगयुक्तात्मा सर्वत्र समदर्शनः ॥२९॥
translation: One whose self is disciplined by yoga sees the self present in all beings and all beings in the self, seeing the same everywhere.
explanation: The two directions matter equally: the self in all beings, and all beings in the self. Neither dissolves the other, and the result is described as a way of seeing.

sanskrit:
यो मां पश्यति सर्वत्र सर्वं च मयि पश्यति।
तस्याहं न प्रणश्यामि स च मे न प्रणश्यति ॥३०॥
translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me — for that one I am not lost, and that one is not lost to me.
explanation: A tender verse in the middle of technical instruction. The promise is mutual and stated as an absence of loss, which is a very different thing from a reward offered.

sanskrit:
सर्वभूतस्थितं यो मां भजत्येकत्वमास्थितः।
सर्वथा वर्तमानोऽपि स योगी मयि वर्तते ॥३१॥
translation: The yogin who, established in oneness, worships me dwelling in all beings, abides in me, in whatever way he may be living.
explanation: The last clause is extraordinarily generous. Whatever the outward circumstances of such a person's life, the abiding holds — which quietly answers Arjuna's fear about his own.

sanskrit:
आत्मौपम्येन सर्वत्र समं पश्यति योऽर्जुन।
सुखं वा यदि वा दुःखं सः योगी परमो मतः ॥३२॥
translation: One who sees the same everywhere by comparison with oneself, Arjuna, whether in pleasure or in pain, is regarded as the highest yogin.
explanation: Krishna's ethical summit is reached with the simplest instrument — atma-aupamya, comparison with oneself. Treat another's pain as you know your own to be, and you have arrived.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
योऽयं योगस्त्वया प्रोक्तः साम्येन मधुसूदन।
एतस्याहं न पश्यामि चञ्चलत्वात् स्थितिं स्थिराम् ॥३३॥
translation: Arjuna said: This yoga of evenness that you have described, Madhusudana — I do not see how it can stand firm, because of restlessness.
explanation: Arjuna interrupts with an honest report of failure. He is not disputing the teaching; he is saying his own mind will not hold still long enough for him to attempt it.

sanskrit:
चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम्।
तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥३४॥
translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna — turbulent, powerful, and unyielding. I think restraining it is as hard as restraining the wind.
explanation: Four adjectives and one perfect image. The wind comparison concedes that the mind is not merely difficult but arguably the wrong kind of thing to try gripping at all.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
असंशयं महाबाहो मनो दुर्निग्रहं चलं।
अभ्यासेन तु कौन्तेय वैराग्येण च गृह्यते ॥३५॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: Without doubt, mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and hard to restrain. But by practice and by dispassion, Kaunteya, it is held.
explanation: Krishna concedes the difficulty entirely before answering — no correction, no reassurance. Then two words: abhyasa and vairagya, repetition and cooling. That is the whole method.

sanskrit:
असंयतात्मना योगो दुष्प्राप इति मे मतिः।
वश्यात्मना तु यतता शक्योऽवाप्तुमुपायतः ॥३६॥
translation: Yoga is hard to attain by one whose self is unrestrained — this is my view. But it can be obtained by proper means by one who strives with a controlled self.
explanation: A carefully balanced answer. Krishna neither pretends it is easy nor lets Arjuna off; the difficulty is real, and it yields to means, applied by someone actually trying.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
अयतिः श्रद्धयोपेतो योगाच्चलितमानसः।
अप्राप्य योगसंसिद्धिं कां गतिं कृष्ण गच्छति ॥३७॥
translation: Arjuna said: One who has faith but does not strive, whose mind falls away from yoga and fails to reach perfection in it — what course does that one take, Krishna?
explanation: A question about failure, and it is really about himself. Arjuna wants to know the cost of trying and not finishing, which is the fear that keeps people from starting.

sanskrit:
कच्चिन्नोभयविभ्रष्टश्छिन्नाभ्रमिव नश्यति।
अप्रतिष्ठो महाबाहो विमूढो ब्रह्मणः पथि ॥३८॥
translation: Fallen from both, without support, deluded on the path of Brahman — does that one not perish like a scattered cloud, mighty-armed one?
explanation: The scattered cloud is Arjuna's own image and a fine one: something that had gathered and then simply disperses, leaving nothing behind where it used to be.

sanskrit:
एतन्मे संशयं कृष्ण छेत्तुमर्हस्यशेषतः।
त्वदन्यः संशयस्यास्य छेत्ता न ह्युपपद्यते ॥३९॥
translation: You should completely dispel this doubt of mine, Krishna. There is no one other than you who could dispel this doubt.
explanation: Arjuna's confidence in his teacher is now total, and stated as plain fact. The man who questioned the arithmetic in Chapter 4 has stopped looking for other sources.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
पार्थ नैवेह नामुत्र विनाशस्तस्य विद्यते।
नहि कल्याणकृत्कश्िचद्दुर्गतिं तात गच्छति ॥४०॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: Partha, there is no destruction for that one, either here or hereafter. For no one who does good, my friend, comes to a bad end.
explanation: The warmest line Krishna has spoken. Note tata, an affectionate word for a younger person, and the flat promise attached — effort in this direction is never simply wasted.

sanskrit:
प्राप्य पुण्यकृतां लोकानुषित्वा शाश्वतीः समाः।
शुचीनां श्रीमतां गेहे योगभ्रष्टोऽभिजायते ॥४१॥
translation: Attaining the worlds of the meritorious and dwelling there for countless years, the one fallen from yoga is born in the house of the pure and prosperous.
explanation: The answer to Arjuna's fear is continuity. Nothing is lost; the progress made becomes the starting conditions of another life, a strange and generous kind of bookkeeping.

sanskrit:
अथवा योगिनामेव कुले भवति धीमताम्।
एतद्धि दुर्लभतरं लोके जन्म यदीदृशम् ॥४२॥
translation: Or else he is born into a family of wise yogins. Such a birth as this is very hard to obtain in this world.
explanation: The second possibility is ranked above wealth, which is telling. Krishna treats being born among people who understand as the rarer and the better inheritance.

sanskrit:
तत्र तं बुद्धिसंयोगं लभते पौर्वदेहिकम्।
यतते च ततो भूयः संसिद्धौ कुरुनन्दन ॥४३॥
translation: There he regains the understanding acquired in his former body, and from there he strives once more toward perfection, Kurunandana.
explanation: The mechanism spelled out: the understanding is recovered, not rebuilt. Krishna describes spiritual work as the one investment that survives the loss of everything else.

sanskrit:
पूर्वाभ्यासेन तेनैव ह्रियते ह्यवशोऽपि सः।
जिज्ञासुरपि योगस्य शब्दब्रह्मातिवर्तते ॥४४॥
translation: By that very former practice he is carried onward, even against his will. Even one who merely wishes to know of yoga passes beyond the word of scripture.
explanation: Carried against his will is a fine reversal — momentum that usually drags people down here pulls upward instead. And mere curiosity is credited with real distance covered.

sanskrit:
प्रयत्नाद्यतमानस्तु योगी संशुद्धकिल्बिषः।
अनेकजन्मसंसिद्धस्ततो याति परां गतिम् ॥४५॥
translation: But the yogin who strives with effort, cleansed of faults and perfected through many births, then reaches the supreme goal.
explanation: Krishna's timescale is candid. Perfection is described as the work of many lifetimes, which reframes any single life's failure as an ordinary stage rather than a verdict.

sanskrit:
तपस्विभ्योऽधिको योगी ज्ञानिभ्योऽपि मतोऽधिकः।
कर्मिभ्यश्चाधिको योगी तस्माद्योगी भवार्जुन ॥४६॥
translation: The yogin is greater than ascetics, is considered greater even than those of knowledge, and greater than those who perform rites. Therefore be a yogin, Arjuna.
explanation: A ranking, then an instruction addressed to Arjuna by name. After forty-five verses of description, Krishna simply tells him which of these he ought to become.

sanskrit:
योगिनामपि सर्वेषां मद्गतेनान्तरात्मना।
श्रद्धावान्भजते यो मां स मे युक्ततमो मतः ॥४७॥
translation: And of all yogins, the one who worships me with faith, with the inner self absorbed in me — that one I consider the most deeply disciplined of all.
explanation: The final ranking narrows once more, and the criterion turns out to be neither technique nor endurance but faith and absorption. The chapter on discipline ends on devotion.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
मय्यासक्तमनाः पार्थ योगं युञ्जन्मदाश्रयः।
असंशयं समग्रं मां यथा ज्ञास्यसि तच्छृणु ॥१॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: With your mind attached to me, Partha, practising yoga and taking refuge in me, hear how you will know me completely and without doubt.
explanation: Krishna announces a change of subject. The first six chapters described what Arjuna should do; from here the subject becomes who Krishna is, and the manner of knowing changes with it.

sanskrit:
ज्ञानं तेऽहं सविज्ञानमिदं वक्ष्याम्यशेषतः।
यज्ज्ञात्वा नेह भूयोऽन्यज्ज्ञातव्यमवशिष्यते ॥२॥
translation: I shall declare to you in full this knowledge along with realization, knowing which nothing further remains to be known here.
explanation: Two words are paired throughout this chapter — jnana and vijnana, the understanding and the direct seeing of it. Krishna promises both, and not merely the first.

sanskrit:
मनुष्याणां सहस्रेषु कश्िचद्यतति सिद्धये।
यततामपि सिद्धानां कश्िचन्मां वेत्ति तत्त्वतः ॥३॥
translation: Among thousands of people, perhaps one strives for perfection. And among those who strive and succeed, perhaps one knows me in truth.
explanation: A sobering ratio, offered without apology. Krishna is not recruiting; he states the rarity plainly at the very opening of his most intimate teaching, which makes what follows feel given rather than sold.

sanskrit:
भूमिरापोऽनलो वायुः खं मनो बुद्धिरेव च।
अहङ्कार इतीयं मे भिन्ना प्रकृतिरष्टधा ॥४॥
translation: Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, understanding, and ego — this is my nature, divided eightfold.
explanation: The list runs from the grossest element to the subtlest sense of self without a break. Krishna does not separate matter from mind; both belong equally to his lower nature.

sanskrit:
अपरेयमितस्त्वन्यां प्रकृतिं विद्धि मे पराम्।
जीवभूतां महाबाहो ययेदं धार्यते जगत् ॥५॥
translation: This is the lower one. Know my other, higher nature, mighty-armed one — the very life by which this world is sustained.
explanation: The distinction that organizes the chapter. Everything nameable belongs to the lower nature; the higher is not another item on the list but what holds the whole list up.

sanskrit:
एतद्योनीनि भूतानि सर्वाणीत्युपधारय।
अहं कृत्स्नस्य जगतः प्रभवः प्रलयस्तथा ॥६॥
translation: Understand that all beings have their origin in these two. I am the source of the entire world, and its dissolution as well.
explanation: Krishna claims both ends of the process. Being the origin is the easier half; being the dissolution is what Arjuna, standing before a battlefield, most needs to hear.

sanskrit:
मत्तः परतरं नान्यत्किञ्चिदस्ति धनञ्जय।
मयि सर्वमिदं प्रोतं सूत्रे मणिगणा इव ॥७॥
translation: There is nothing at all higher than me, Dhananjaya. All this is strung upon me like rows of pearls on a thread.
explanation: The image is exact — the thread is invisible in the finished necklace, yet it is the only reason there is a necklace at all. Krishna describes presence as structure.

sanskrit:
रसोऽहमप्सु कौन्तेय प्रभास्मि शशिसूर्ययोः।
प्रणवः सर्ववेदेषु शब्दः खे पौरुषं नृषु ॥८॥
translation: I am the taste in water, Kaunteya, the radiance in the moon and the sun, the sacred syllable in all the Vedas, the sound in ether, and the manhood in men.
explanation: Krishna begins locating himself in the essential quality of ordinary things. Not the water but its taste — always the property that makes a thing recognizably itself.

sanskrit:
पुण्यो गन्धः पृथिव्यां च तेजश्चास्मि विभावसौ।
जीवनं सर्वभूतेषु तपश्चास्मि तपस्विषु ॥९॥
translation: I am the pure fragrance of the earth and the brilliance in fire, the life in all beings, and the austerity in ascetics.
explanation: The fragrance of earth after rain is the most sensory item in the list. Krishna keeps choosing qualities a person has actually noticed rather than abstractions to admire.

sanskrit:
बीजं मां सर्वभूतानां विद्धि पार्थ सनातनम्।
बुद्धिर्बुद्धिमतामस्मि तेजस्तेजस्विनामहम् ॥१०॥
translation: Know me, Partha, as the eternal seed of all beings. I am the intelligence of the intelligent and the splendour of the splendid.
explanation: A seed is small, hidden, and contains the whole plan. Krishna moves from qualities to origin, claiming to be what things grow out of rather than only what they display.

sanskrit:
बलं बलवतां चाहं कामरागविवर्जितम्।
धर्माविरुद्धो भूतेषु कामोऽस्मि भरतर्षभ ॥११॥
translation: I am the strength of the strong, free from desire and attachment. In beings I am desire that is not contrary to righteousness, best of the Bharatas.
explanation: A careful qualification. Krishna does not disown desire itself, only desire that breaks dharma — which leaves ordinary wanting inside the divine rather than outside it.

sanskrit:
ये चैव सात्त्विका भावा राजसास्तामसाश्च ये।
मत्त एवेति तान्विद्धि नत्वहं तेषु ते मयि ॥१२॥
translation: Know that all states of being — whether of purity, of passion, or of darkness — proceed from me. But I am not in them; they are in me.
explanation: The reversal in the last line is the crucial move. Containment runs one way only, which is how Krishna can be the source of darkness without being darkened by it.

sanskrit:
त्रिभिर्गुणमयैर्भावैरेभिः सर्वमिदं जगत्।
मोहितं नाभिजानाति मामेभ्यः परमव्ययम् ॥१३॥
translation: Deluded by these three states composed of the gunas, this whole world does not recognize me, who am beyond them and imperishable.
explanation: The gunas are described as a screen rather than a barrier. What blocks recognition is not distance but the fabric of ordinary experience, working exactly as it does.

sanskrit:
दैवी ह्येषा गुणमयी मम माया दुरत्यया।
मामेव ये प्रपद्यन्ते मायामेतां तरन्ति ते ॥१४॥
translation: This divine illusion of mine, made of the gunas, is hard to cross over. But those who take refuge in me alone cross beyond this illusion.
explanation: Krishna concedes maya is nearly impassable, then names the one crossing. Note that the method is refuge rather than effort — an admission that force will not work here.

sanskrit:
न मां दुष्कृतिनो मूढाः प्रपद्यन्ते नराधमाः।
माययापहृतज्ञाना आसुरं भावमाश्रिताः ॥१५॥
translation: The evildoers, the deluded, the lowest of people, do not take refuge in me. Their knowledge is carried off by illusion, and they cling to a demonic nature.
explanation: Even here the diagnosis is loss rather than malice — knowledge carried off, not refused. Krishna consistently describes wrongdoing as something that happened to a person's seeing.

sanskrit:
चतुर्विधा भजन्ते मां जनाः सुकृतिनोऽर्जुन।
आर्तो जिज्ञासुरर्थार्थी ज्ञानी च भरतर्षभ ॥१६॥
translation: Four kinds of virtuous people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the one who knows, best of the Bharatas.
explanation: All four are called virtuous, including the one who comes for money. Krishna refuses to disqualify anyone by motive, which is unusually generous for a devotional teaching.

sanskrit:
तेषां ज्ञानी नित्ययुक्त एकभक्ितर्विशिष्यते।
प्रियो हि ज्ञानिनोऽत्यर्थमहं स च मम प्रियः ॥१७॥
translation: Of these, the one who knows, ever disciplined and devoted to the one alone, excels. For I am exceedingly dear to that one, and that one is dear to me.
explanation: The ranking arrives, but the reason given is affection rather than merit. Krishna explains his preference by describing a mutual fondness — a strange basis for a hierarchy.

sanskrit:
उदाराः सर्व एवैते ज्ञानी त्वात्मैव मे मतम्।
आस्थितः स हि युक्तात्मा मामेवानुत्तमां गतिम् ॥१८॥
translation: All of these are noble, but the one who knows I consider to be my very self. For that one, disciplined, is established in me as the unsurpassed goal.
explanation: Krishna doubles back to protect the other three — all noble — before saying what he thinks of the fourth. The generosity and the ranking are allowed to stand together.

sanskrit:
बहूनां जन्मनामन्ते ज्ञानवान्मां प्रपद्यते।
वासुदेवः सर्वमिति स महात्मा सुदुर्लभः ॥१९॥
translation: At the end of many births, the one who knows takes refuge in me, understanding that Vasudeva is all. Such a great soul is very hard to find.
explanation: The insight is compressed into three words: vasudevah sarvam, Krishna is everything. And the timescale is honest — many births, and even then such a person is rare.

sanskrit:
कामैस्तैस्तैर्हृतज्ञानाः प्रपद्यन्तेऽन्यदेवताः।
तं तं नियममास्थाय प्रकृत्या नियताः स्वया ॥२०॥
translation: Those whose knowledge is carried away by various desires resort to other gods, adopting this or that observance, constrained by their own nature.
explanation: Krishna explains rival worship as a matter of temperament rather than treachery. People are described as constrained by their nature, which puts them beyond simple blame.

sanskrit:
यो यो यां यां तनुं भक्तः श्रद्धयार्चितुमिच्छति।
तस्य तस्याचलां श्रद्धां तामेव विदधाम्यहम् ॥२१॥
translation: Whatever form a devotee seeks to worship with faith, I make that very faith of theirs unwavering.
explanation: An extraordinary verse. Krishna does not merely tolerate worship directed elsewhere — he actively steadies it, which makes him a participant in every form of devotion.

sanskrit:
स तया श्रद्धया युक्तस्तस्याराधनमीहते।
लभते च ततः कामान्मयैव विहितान् हि तान् ॥२२॥
translation: Endowed with that faith, that person seeks the favour of that form, and obtains from it the desires that are in fact ordained by me alone.
explanation: The claim completes: even the answered prayer came from him. Krishna makes himself the silent supplier behind transactions in which he is never named, and never mentions it to the people receiving them.

sanskrit:
अन्तवत्तु फलं तेषां तद्भवत्यल्पमेधसाम्।
देवान्देवयजो यान्ति मद्भक्ता यान्ति मामपि ॥२३॥
translation: But finite is the fruit gained by those of small understanding. Worshippers of the gods go to the gods; my devotees come to me.
explanation: The only criticism offered is about scale, not legitimacy. The results are real and they are limited, and Krishna lets that stand as the whole of the objection.

sanskrit:
अव्यक्तं व्यक्ितमापन्नं मन्यन्ते मामबुद्धयः।
परं भावमजानन्तो ममाव्ययमनुत्तमम् ॥२४॥
translation: The unintelligent think of me, the unmanifest, as having come into manifestation, not knowing my higher nature, imperishable and unsurpassed.
explanation: A complaint about being underestimated by those who see only the visible Krishna — which is precisely what Arjuna was doing an hour ago on this same field.

sanskrit:
नाहं प्रकाशः सर्वस्य योगमायासमावृतः।
मूढोऽयं नाभिजानाति लोको मामजमव्ययम् ॥२५॥
translation: I am not revealed to everyone, veiled by my own power of illusion. This deluded world does not recognize me, the unborn and imperishable.
explanation: Krishna admits the concealment is his own doing. The hiddenness is not an accident or a failure of human attention but a deliberate feature of how he is present.

sanskrit:
वेदाहं समतीतानि वर्तमानानि चार्जुन।
भविष्याणि च भूतानि मां तु वेद न कश्चन ॥२६॥
translation: I know the beings that are past, that are present, and that are yet to come, Arjuna — but no one knows me.
explanation: The asymmetry is stated flatly and it stings a little. Krishna's knowledge is total and his own knowability is nil, which makes this the loneliest line in the chapter.

sanskrit:
इच्छाद्वेषसमुत्थेन द्वन्द्वमोहेन भारत।
सर्वभूतानि संमोहं सर्गे यान्ति परन्तप ॥२७॥
translation: By the delusion of the pairs of opposites arising from desire and aversion, Bharata, all beings fall into confusion at their very birth, scorcher of foes.
explanation: The confusion is dated to birth itself, before any wrongdoing. Krishna locates the problem upstream of choice, which is why he keeps prescribing refuge instead of resolve.

sanskrit:
येषां त्वन्तगतं पापं जनानां पुण्यकर्मणाम्।
ते द्वन्द्वमोहनिर्मुक्ता भजन्ते मां दृढव्रताः ॥२८॥
translation: But those people of virtuous deeds whose wrong has come to an end, freed from the delusion of the opposites, worship me with firm resolve.
explanation: The exit is described in the past tense — their wrong has already ended. Devotion is what becomes possible afterward, not the tool that did the clearing.

sanskrit:
जरामरणमोक्षाय मामाश्रित्य यतन्ति ये।
ते ब्रह्म तद्विदुः कृत्स्नमध्यात्मं कर्म चाखिलम् ॥२९॥
translation: Those who strive for release from old age and death by taking refuge in me know that Brahman entirely, the whole of the self, and the whole of action.
explanation: Krishna stacks up technical terms he has not yet defined. Arjuna's next question follows immediately, which suggests the density here is entirely deliberate — a way of prompting the request that opens the following chapter.

sanskrit:
साधिभूताधिदैवं मां साधियज्ञं च ये विदुः।
प्रयाणकालेऽपि च मां ते विदुर्युक्तचेतसः ॥३०॥
translation: Those who know me together with the material realm, the divine realm, and the realm of sacrifice, with disciplined minds, know me even at the hour of departure.
explanation: Three more terms, and then the phrase that matters — at the hour of departure. Krishna is steering toward death, which becomes the entire subject of the next chapter.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
किं तद्ब्रह्म किमध्यात्मं किं कर्म पुरुषोत्तम।
अधिभूतं च किं प्रोक्तमधिदैवं किमुच्यते ॥१॥
translation: Arjuna said: What is that Brahman? What is the self? What is action, best of persons? What is said to be the material realm, and what is called the divine realm?
explanation: Arjuna does the sensible thing and asks for definitions. Six technical terms were dropped on him in two verses, and he refuses to let a single one of them pass.

sanskrit:
अधियज्ञः कथं कोऽत्र देहेऽस्मिन्मधुसूदन।
प्रयाणकाले च कथं ज्ञेयोऽसि नियतात्मभिः ॥२॥
translation: Who is the lord of sacrifice here, and how does he dwell in this body, Madhusudana? And how are you to be known at the time of departure by those who are self-controlled?
explanation: The last question is the real one. Arjuna, surrounded by men about to die, wants to know what can be done in the final moment — and Krishna spends the chapter answering it.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
अक्षरं ब्रह्म परमं स्वभावोऽध्यात्ममुच्यते।
भूतभावोद्भवकरो विसर्गः कर्मसंज्ञितः ॥३॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: Brahman is the supreme imperishable. One's own essential nature is called the self. The creative force that brings beings into existence is named action.
explanation: Three definitions delivered without ornament. Note that karma is defined as the force producing beings, which ties the whole doctrine of action to birth itself.

sanskrit:
अधिभूतं क्षरो भावः पुरुषश्चाधिदैवतम्।
अधियज्ञोऽहमेवात्र देहे देहभृतां वर ॥४॥
translation: The material realm is perishable existence; the divine realm is the spirit. The lord of sacrifice is I myself, here in this body, best of the embodied.
explanation: The answers finish with Krishna placing himself inside Arjuna's own body. The abstractions collapse into something local, which is this chapter's method throughout: every cosmic term is eventually handed back at human scale.

sanskrit:
अन्तकाले च मामेव स्मरन्मुक्त्वा कलेवरम्।
यः प्रयाति स मद्भावं याति नास्त्यत्र संशयः ॥५॥
translation: And whoever, at the time of the end, remembers me alone and leaves the body, goes to my state of being. Of this there is no doubt.
explanation: The promise Arjuna asked for, given without conditions attached. On a field where thousands will die today, this is the most practical thing Krishna could possibly say.

sanskrit:
यं यं वापि स्मरन्भावं त्यजत्यन्ते कलेवरम्।
तं तमेवैति कौन्तेय सदा तद्भावभावितः ॥६॥
translation: Whatever state one remembers when finally leaving the body, Kaunteya, to that one goes, having always been absorbed in that state.
explanation: The general principle behind the promise, and the second half prevents any cheating. What comes to mind at the end is what the mind has been living in all along.

sanskrit:
तस्मात्सर्वेषु कालेषु मामनुस्मर युध्य च।
मय्यर्पितमनोबुद्धिर्मामेवैष्यस्यसंशयम् ॥७॥
translation: Therefore, at all times remember me and fight. With mind and understanding fixed on me, you will surely come to me.
explanation: The two imperatives sit side by side without tension — remember, and fight. Krishna's whole teaching compresses into his refusal to separate those two activities.

sanskrit:
अभ्यासयोगयुक्तेन चेतसा नान्यगामिना।
परमं पुरुषं दिव्यं याति पार्थानुचिन्तयन् ॥८॥
translation: With a mind disciplined by the practice of yoga and not straying to anything else, one reaches the supreme divine spirit, Partha, by constant contemplation.
explanation: Abhyasa, practice, is named as the mechanism. The extraordinary final moment is presented as the ordinary result of a long, unremarkable habit of attention, built up on days when nothing at all was happening.

sanskrit:
कविं पुराणमनुशासितार
मणोरणीयांसमनुस्मरेद्यः।
सर्वस्य धातारमचिन्त्यरूप
मादित्यवर्णं तमसः परस्तात् ॥९॥
translation: One who remembers the ancient seer, the ruler, subtler than the atom, the sustainer of all, of inconceivable form, sun-coloured, beyond all darkness...
explanation: A string of descriptions that keep undercutting each other — smaller than an atom, yet sustaining everything; inconceivable, yet the colour of the sun. The paradoxes are deliberate.

sanskrit:
प्रयाणकाले मनसाऽचलेन
भक्त्या युक्तो योगबलेन चैव।
भ्रुवोर्मध्ये प्राणमावेश्य सम्यक्
स तं परं पुरुषमुपैति दिव्यम् ॥१०॥
translation: ...at the time of departure, with an unmoving mind, endowed with devotion and the power of yoga, drawing the breath fully between the brows, reaches that supreme divine spirit.
explanation: The sentence lands on technique — the breath held at a precise point. Krishna gives the dying something physical to do, not merely a state of mind to achieve.

sanskrit:
यदक्षरं वेदविदो वदन्ति
विशन्ति यद्यतयो वीतरागाः।
यदिच्छन्तो ब्रह्मचर्यं चरन्ति
तत्ते पदं संग्रहेण प्रवक्ष्ये ॥११॥
translation: That state which the knowers of the Veda call imperishable, which the passionless ascetics enter, desiring which they practise continence — that path I shall declare to you in brief.
explanation: Krishna cites three separate authorities before speaking, then promises brevity. The build-up suggests he knows Arjuna is being handed something difficult to hold onto, and that a short statement will carry further than a long one.

sanskrit:
सर्वद्वाराणि संयम्य मनो हृदि निरुध्य च।
मूर्ध्न्याधायात्मनः प्राणमास्थितो योगधारणाम् ॥१२॥
translation: Restraining all the gates of the body, confining the mind in the heart, drawing one's breath up into the head, established in the concentration of yoga...
explanation: The gates are the senses from Chapter 5's nine-gated city. Krishna closes them one by one, moving inward and then upward, in a sequence meant to be actually followed.

sanskrit:
ओमित्येकाक्षरं ब्रह्म व्याहरन्मामनुस्मरन्।
यः प्रयाति त्यजन्देहं स याति परमां गतिम् ॥१३॥
translation: ...uttering the single syllable Om, which is Brahman, and remembering me, one who departs, leaving the body, reaches the highest goal.
explanation: A single syllable and a single memory. After all the preparation, the actual instruction turns out small enough to carry into the last second of a life.

sanskrit:
अनन्यचेताः सततं यो मां स्मरति नित्यशः।
तस्याहं सुलभः पार्थ नित्ययुक्तस्य योगिनः ॥१४॥
translation: For the yogin who is constantly disciplined and thinks of no other, remembering me always — for that one I am easy to reach, Partha.
explanation: Easy to reach is a startling phrase after the technical passage. Krishna quietly concedes the elaborate method is not the only door, and constancy is the real requirement.

sanskrit:
मामुपेत्य पुनर्जन्म दुःखालयमशाश्वतम्।
नाप्नुवन्ति महात्मानः संसिद्धिं परमां गताः ॥१५॥
translation: Having come to me, the great souls who have reached the highest perfection do not take birth again in this impermanent abode of sorrow.
explanation: The description of the world is bleak — an impermanent house of pain. Krishna rarely speaks this way, and it lands differently just before the cosmological verses.

sanskrit:
आब्रह्मभुवनाल्लोकाः पुनरावर्तिनोऽर्जुन।
मामुपेत्य तु कौन्तेय पुनर्जन्म न विद्यते ॥१६॥
translation: All worlds, up to the realm of Brahma, are subject to return, Arjuna. But on coming to me, Kaunteya, there is no rebirth.
explanation: Even the highest heaven is only a long stay. Krishna disqualifies the entire ladder of attainments, including its topmost rung, as still standing inside the cycle.

sanskrit:
सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः।
रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥१७॥
translation: Those who know that a day of Brahma lasts a thousand ages and a night lasts a thousand ages are the people who truly know day and night.
explanation: Krishna answers a question about a dying man's last breath by pulling back to cosmic time. The proportion is the point — a life is brief against a scale this vast.

sanskrit:
अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे।
रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ॥१८॥
translation: At the coming of day all manifest things arise from the unmanifest; at the coming of night they dissolve into that same thing called the unmanifest.
explanation: Creation is described as a rhythm rather than an event. Everything visible is on loan from a state it will return to, which makes individual endings far less exceptional.

sanskrit:
भूतग्रामः स एवायं भूत्वा भूत्वा प्रलीयते।
रात्र्यागमेऽवशः पार्थ प्रभवत्यहरागमे ॥१९॥
translation: This same multitude of beings, coming into being again and again, dissolves helplessly at the coming of night and comes forth at the coming of day, Partha.
explanation: The word avashah, helplessly, does the work here. Krishna is describing a vast process in which the beings involved have no say at all — exactly what Arjuna fears.

sanskrit:
परस्तस्मात्तु भावोऽन्योऽव्यक्तोऽव्यक्तात्सनातनः।
यः स सर्वेषु भूतेषु नश्यत्सु न विनश्यति ॥२०॥
translation: But beyond that unmanifest there is another unmanifest existence, eternal, which does not perish when all beings perish.
explanation: A second unmanifest, standing above the first. Krishna distinguishes the sleeping state of the cosmos from something that was never part of the cycle to begin with.

sanskrit:
अव्यक्तोऽक्षर इत्युक्तस्तमाहुः परमां गतिम्।
यं प्राप्य न निवर्तन्ते तद्धाम परमं मम ॥२१॥
translation: That unmanifest is called the imperishable, and is said to be the supreme goal. Those who reach it do not return. That is my supreme abode.
explanation: The claim lands quietly. Krishna identifies the philosophical absolute with his own dwelling, joining the impersonal ultimate to the person Arjuna is speaking with — two things the tradition had kept carefully apart.

sanskrit:
पुरुषः स परः पार्थ भक्त्या लभ्यस्त्वनन्यया।
यस्यान्तःस्थानि भूतानि येन सर्वमिदं ततम् ॥२२॥
translation: That supreme spirit, Partha, within whom all beings dwell and by whom all this is pervaded, is reached by undivided devotion.
explanation: After chapters of technique, the means is named as bhakti alone. Note ananya, undivided — the requirement is not intensity but the absence of anything competing.

sanskrit:
यत्र काले त्वनावृत्तिमावृत्तिं चैव योगिनः।
प्रयाता यान्ति तं कालं वक्ष्यामि भरतर्षभ ॥२३॥
translation: Now I shall tell you, best of the Bharatas, the times at which yogins depart and go to no return, and also to return.
explanation: Krishna announces a subject that will sound almost astrological. The chapter about the last moment now asks whether even the season of a death carries meaning.

sanskrit:
अग्निर्ज्योतिरहः शुक्लः षण्मासा उत्तरायणम्।
तत्र प्रयाता गच्छन्ति ब्रह्म ब्रह्मविदो जनाः ॥२४॥
translation: Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the sun's northern course — departing then, those who know Brahman go to Brahman.
explanation: A list of things that all share brightness. Whatever else the passage means, its imagery stays consistent: the upward route is described entirely in terms of light.

sanskrit:
धूमो रात्रिस्तथा कृष्णः षण्मासा दक्षिणायनम्।
तत्र चान्द्रमसं ज्योतिर्योगी प्राप्य निवर्तते ॥२५॥
translation: Smoke, night, the dark fortnight, the six months of the sun's southern course — the yogin attaining the moon's light by that route returns again.
explanation: The counterpart, built from obscurity and reflected light. The moon shines with borrowed brightness, which suits a destination described as temporary, and the whole route is named for things that fade rather than burn.

sanskrit:
शुक्लकृष्णे गती ह्येते जगतः शाश्वते मते।
एकया यात्यनावृत्तिमन्ययाऽऽवर्तते पुनः ॥२६॥
translation: These two paths, the bright and the dark, are held to be eternal for the world. By one a person goes to no return; by the other one returns again.
explanation: Krishna calls both paths eternal, which means the returning route is not a malfunction. The cycle has a permanent lane, and most of the traffic is on it.

sanskrit:
नैते सृती पार्थ जानन्योगी मुह्यति कश्चन।
तस्मात्सर्वेषु कालेषु योगयुक्तो भवार्जुन ॥२७॥
translation: Knowing these two paths, Partha, no yogin is deluded. Therefore at all times be established in yoga, Arjuna.
explanation: The instruction drawn from all the cosmology is disarmingly simple. Knowing the map does not change the route; it removes the confusion, and the practice stays the same.

sanskrit:
वेदेषु यज्ञेषु तपःसु चैव
दानेषु यत्पुण्यफलं प्रदिष्टम्।
अत्येति तत्सर्वमिदं विदित्वा
योगी परं स्थानमुपैति चाद्यम् ॥२८॥
translation: Knowing all this, the yogin transcends whatever fruits of merit are assigned to the Vedas, to sacrifices, to austerities, and to gifts — and reaches the supreme original abode.
explanation: The chapter ends by outbidding every conventional reward at once. Krishna does not deny the rites work; he says this knowledge steps past everything they can deliver.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
इदं तु ते गुह्यतमं प्रवक्ष्याम्यनसूयवे।
ज्ञानं विज्ञानसहितं यज्ज्ञात्वा मोक्ष्यसेऽशुभात् ॥१॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: To you, who do not carp, I shall declare this most secret knowledge together with realization, knowing which you will be freed from misfortune.
explanation: The qualification is not intelligence or lineage but the absence of a sneer. Krishna's condition for his deepest teaching is simply that Arjuna is not hunting for faults.

sanskrit:
राजविद्या राजगुह्यं पवित्रमिदमुत्तमम्।
प्रत्यक्षावगमं धर्म्यं सुसुखं कर्तुमव्ययम् ॥२॥
translation: This is the king of sciences, the king of secrets, supremely purifying, directly perceivable, in accord with righteousness, very easy to practise, and imperishable.
explanation: Seven claims, and two stand out — directly perceivable, and very easy. Krishna promises something verifiable in one's own experience and not difficult, which is rare here.

sanskrit:
अश्रद्दधानाः पुरुषा धर्मस्यास्य परन्तप।
अप्राप्य मां निवर्तन्ते मृत्युसंसारवर्त्मनि ॥३॥
translation: People who have no faith in this teaching, scorcher of foes, do not attain me and return to the path of death and rebirth.
explanation: The consequence of refusal is stated as continuation rather than punishment. Nothing is inflicted; one simply stays where one was, which is its own kind of answer.

sanskrit:
मया ततमिदं सर्वं जगदव्यक्तमूर्तिना।
मत्स्थानि सर्वभूतानि न चाहं तेष्ववस्थितः ॥४॥
translation: All this world is pervaded by me in my unmanifest form. All beings dwell in me, and I do not dwell in them.
explanation: The paradox that runs through the chapter. Krishna contains without being contained, and he will spend the next verses making this stranger rather than clearer.

sanskrit:
न च मत्स्थानि भूतानि पश्य मे योगमैश्वरम्।
भूतभृन्न च भूतस्थो ममात्मा भूतभावनः ॥५॥
translation: And yet beings do not dwell in me. Behold my divine power. Sustaining beings and yet not dwelling in them, my self causes beings to be.
explanation: Krishna contradicts the verse he has just spoken, then points at the contradiction and calls it his yoga. The logic is meant to fail; that failure is the demonstration.

sanskrit:
यथाऽऽकाशस्थितो नित्यं वायुः सर्वत्रगो महान्।
तथा सर्वाणि भूतानि मत्स्थानीत्युपधारय ॥६॥
translation: As the mighty wind, moving everywhere, always rests in space, so understand that all beings rest in me.
explanation: A resolving image after two verses of paradox. The wind is genuinely in space and space is entirely unaffected by it — containment without involvement, made ordinary.

sanskrit:
सर्वभूतानि कौन्तेय प्रकृतिं यान्ति मामिकाम्।
कल्पक्षये पुनस्तानि कल्पादौ विसृजाम्यहम् ॥७॥
translation: All beings, Kaunteya, return to my nature at the end of an age, and at the beginning of an age I send them forth again.
explanation: The cosmic rhythm from Chapter 8 restated in the first person. What was described there as a process is claimed here as an action, with someone actually doing it.

sanskrit:
प्रकृतिं स्वामवष्टभ्य विसृजामि पुनः पुनः।
भूतग्राममिमं कृत्स्नमवशं प्रकृतेर्वशात् ॥८॥
translation: Resting upon my own nature, I send forth again and again this whole multitude of beings, helpless under the sway of nature.
explanation: The helplessness of beings is stated bluntly beside Krishna's freedom. The contrast sets up the next verse, which asks why he is not implicated in what he does.

sanskrit:
न च मां तानि कर्माणि निबध्नन्ति धनञ्जय।
उदासीनवदासीनमसक्तं तेषु कर्मसु ॥९॥
translation: And these actions do not bind me, Dhananjaya. I remain seated as though indifferent, unattached to those actions.
explanation: As though indifferent is precisely hedged. Krishna does not claim indifference, only its appearance, which leaves room for everything he says later about love — and for the fondness already audible in this chapter.

sanskrit:
मयाऽध्यक्षेण प्रकृतिः सूयते सचराचरम्।
हेतुनाऽनेन कौन्तेय जगद्विपरिवर्तते ॥१०॥
translation: Under my supervision, nature gives birth to all that moves and does not move. For this reason, Kaunteya, the world revolves.
explanation: Krishna describes himself as overseer rather than craftsman. Nature does the producing; his role is presence, and that presence is given as the reason anything turns.

sanskrit:
अवजानन्ति मां मूढा मानुषीं तनुमाश्रितम्।
परं भावमजानन्तो मम भूतमहेश्वरम् ॥११॥
translation: Fools disregard me when I have taken a human form, not knowing my higher nature as the great Lord of all beings.
explanation: A verse with an edge to it. Krishna names the specific error of seeing the man in the chariot and concluding that is all there is — Arjuna's error, an hour ago.

sanskrit:
मोघाशा मोघकर्माणो मोघज्ञाना विचेतसः।
राक्षसीमासुरीं चैव प्रकृतिं मोहिनीं श्रिताः ॥१२॥
translation: Of vain hopes, vain actions, and vain knowledge, those senseless people are given over to a deluding nature, demonic and unrighteous.
explanation: Three kinds of futility in a row. Krishna's complaint is not that such people fail but that everything they achieve turns out to have been built on nothing.

sanskrit:
महात्मानस्तु मां पार्थ दैवीं प्रकृतिमाश्रिताः।
भजन्त्यनन्यमनसो ज्ञात्वा भूतादिमव्ययम् ॥१३॥
translation: But the great souls, Partha, who abide in a divine nature, worship me with an undistracted mind, knowing me as the imperishable source of beings.
explanation: The counterpart, and the distinguishing feature is again attention rather than achievement. An undistracted mind is all that separates these people from the last verse.

sanskrit:
सततं कीर्तयन्तो मां यतन्तश्च दृढव्रताः।
नमस्यन्तश्च मां भक्त्या नित्ययुक्ता उपासते ॥१४॥
translation: Always glorifying me, striving with firm resolve, bowing to me with devotion, ever disciplined, they worship me.
explanation: A description of ordinary devotional practice — praise, effort, bowing. Krishna keeps the great souls' behaviour recognizable, requiring nothing Arjuna could not do today, which is a deliberate contrast with the rarity claimed in Chapter 7.

sanskrit:
ज्ञानयज्ञेन चाप्यन्ये यजन्तो मामुपासते।
एकत्वेन पृथक्त्वेन बहुधा विश्वतोमुखम् ॥१५॥
translation: Others too, offering the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me as one, as many, and as facing in all directions in my universal form.
explanation: Three theologies named without ranking — the one, the many, and the omnipresent. Krishna accepts all three descriptions of himself as forms of the same worship.

sanskrit:
अहं क्रतुरहं यज्ञः स्वधाऽहमहमौषधम्।
मंत्रोऽहमहमेवाज्यमहमग्निरहं हुतम् ॥१६॥
translation: I am the rite, I am the sacrifice, I am the offering to the ancestors, I am the herb, I am the sacred chant, I am the clarified butter, I am the fire, and I am the oblation.
explanation: Krishna dismantles a ritual into its parts and claims every one of them. Nothing is left over to be the worshipper's own contribution — that is the quiet argument here.

sanskrit:
पिताऽहमस्य जगतो माता धाता पितामहः।
वेद्यं पवित्रमोंकार ऋक् साम यजुरेव च ॥१७॥
translation: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer, the grandfather, the object of knowledge, the purifier, the syllable Om, and the Rig, Sama, and Yajur Vedas.
explanation: The family terms come first and the scriptures second. Krishna reaches for kinship before authority, which sets the tone for all this chapter says later about love.

sanskrit:
गतिर्भर्ता प्रभुः साक्षी निवासः शरणं सुहृत्।
प्रभवः प्रलयः स्थानं निधानं बीजमव्ययम् ॥१८॥
translation: I am the goal, the supporter, the lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the origin, the dissolution, the foundation, the resting place, and the imperishable seed.
explanation: Twelve terms, and suhrit, friend, sits in the middle of them without any emphasis. Krishna slips the most intimate word into a list of cosmic functions.

sanskrit:
तपाम्यहमहं वर्षं निगृह्णाम्युत्सृजामि च।
अमृतं चैव मृत्युश्च सदसच्चाहमर्जुन ॥१९॥
translation: I give heat; I withhold the rain and send it forth. I am immortality and also death, Arjuna, both being and non-being.
explanation: The most unsettling verse of the list. Krishna claims death as directly as life, refusing the comfort of a god responsible only for the acceptable half of things.

sanskrit:
त्रैविद्या मां सोमपाः पूतपापा
यज्ञैरिष्ट्वा स्वर्गतिं प्रार्थयन्ते।
ते पुण्यमासाद्य सुरेन्द्रलोक
मश्नन्ति दिव्यान्दिवि देवभोगान् ॥२०॥
translation: Knowers of the three Vedas, who drink the soma and are purified of wrong, worship me with sacrifices and pray for the way to heaven. Reaching the holy world of Indra, they enjoy the divine pleasures of the gods.
explanation: Krishna describes conventional religion at its most successful and grants it everything it claims. The critique waits for the next verse, which makes it far more effective.

sanskrit:
ते तं भुक्त्वा स्वर्गलोकं विशालं
क्षीणे पुण्ये मर्त्यलोकं विशन्ति।
एव त्रयीधर्ममनुप्रपन्ना
गतागतं कामकामा लभन्ते ॥२१॥
translation: Having enjoyed that vast world of heaven, their merit exhausted, they enter the world of mortals. Thus, following the way of the three Vedas and desiring desires, they obtain the state of going and returning.
explanation: The critique arrives as arithmetic. Merit is a balance that can be spent, and heaven is described as an expensive stay that ends when the account finally empties.

sanskrit:
अनन्याश्चिन्तयन्तो मां ये जनाः पर्युपासते।
तेषां नित्याभियुक्तानां योगक्षेमं वहाम्यहम् ॥२२॥
translation: To those people who worship me alone, thinking of no other, ever disciplined, I bring what they lack and preserve what they have.
explanation: One of the most quoted promises in the Gita, and its terms are domestic. Yoga-kshema is the ordinary business of getting and keeping, and Krishna offers to take it over.

sanskrit:
येऽप्यन्यदेवता भक्ता यजन्ते श्रद्धयाऽन्विताः।
तेऽपि मामेव कौन्तेय यजन्त्यविधिपूर्वकम् ॥२३॥
translation: Even those who are devoted to other gods and worship them with faith worship me alone, Kaunteya, though not in the prescribed way.
explanation: A remarkably wide door. The only fault Krishna finds with worship aimed elsewhere is procedural, and he counts it as reaching him regardless of the address on it.

sanskrit:
अहं हि सर्वयज्ञानां भोक्ता च प्रभुरेव च।
न तु मामभिजानन्ति तत्त्वेनातश्च्यवन्ति ते ॥२४॥
translation: For I am the enjoyer and the lord of all sacrifices. But they do not know me in truth, and so they fall.
explanation: The gentleness has a limit, though the failure named is ignorance rather than offence. What such worshippers lose is not favour but accuracy — and accuracy turns out to matter.

sanskrit:
यान्ति देवव्रता देवान् पितृ़न्यान्ति पितृव्रताः।
भूतानि यान्ति भूतेज्या यान्ति मद्याजिनोऽपि माम् ॥२५॥
translation: Worshippers of the gods go to the gods; worshippers of the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who sacrifice to spirits go to the spirits; and those who sacrifice to me come to me.
explanation: A verse of perfect symmetry, with no threat anywhere in it. Krishna presents devotion as a matter of direction — everyone arrives exactly where they were already facing.

sanskrit:
पत्रं पुष्पं फलं तोयं यो मे भक्त्या प्रयच्छति।
तदहं भक्त्युपहृतमश्नामि प्रयतात्मनः ॥२६॥
