translation: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water — that offering of devotion I accept from the pure-hearted.
explanation: The most beloved verse in the chapter, and every item on the list is free. Krishna deliberately names four things that a person with nothing at all could still bring.

sanskrit:
यत्करोषि यदश्नासि यज्जुहोषि ददासि यत्।
यत्तपस्यसि कौन्तेय तत्कुरुष्व मदर्पणम् ॥२७॥
translation: Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer, whatever you give, whatever austerity you practise, Kaunteya — do that as an offering to me.
explanation: The practice generalizes past ritual into everything. Note that eating is on the list; Krishna is not adding a religious activity but recasting the ones already happening.

sanskrit:
शुभाशुभफलैरेवं मोक्ष्यसे कर्मबन्धनैः।
संन्यासयोगयुक्तात्मा विमुक्तो मामुपैष्यसि ॥२८॥
translation: Thus you will be freed from the bonds of action, from its good and evil fruits alike. With your self disciplined by the yoga of renunciation, liberated, you will come to me.
explanation: The chapter's method and its result stated together. Offering does not add merit to the ledger — it dissolves the ledger, which is why both kinds of fruit are named.

sanskrit:
समोऽहं सर्वभूतेषु न मे द्वेष्योऽस्ति न प्रियः।
ये भजन्ति तु मां भक्त्या मयि ते तेषु चाप्यहम् ॥२९॥
translation: I am the same toward all beings; there is none hateful or dear to me. But those who worship me with devotion are in me, and I am also in them.
explanation: The two halves seem to contradict and do not. Krishna's impartiality is constant; what devotion changes is proximity, and that is the devotee's doing rather than his.

sanskrit:
अपि चेत्सुदुराचारो भजते मामनन्यभाक्।
साधुरेव स मन्तव्यः सम्यग्व्यवसितो हि सः ॥३०॥
translation: Even if one of very bad conduct worships me with undivided devotion, that one should be regarded as good, for the resolve has been rightly made.
explanation: A door held open unusually wide. Krishna asks that such a person be considered good already, on the strength of the direction chosen rather than the record behind them.

sanskrit:
क्षिप्रं भवति धर्मात्मा शश्वच्छान्तिं निगच्छति।
कौन्तेय प्रतिजानीहि न मे भक्तः प्रणश्यति ॥३१॥
translation: Quickly that one becomes righteous and attains lasting peace. Kaunteya, know for certain that no devotee of mine is ever lost.
explanation: Krishna asks Arjuna to make the declaration himself — proclaim it. He gives away his own promise, letting the devotee be the one who states it aloud.

sanskrit:
मां हि पार्थ व्यपाश्रित्य येऽपि स्युः पापयोनयः।
स्त्रियो वैश्यास्तथा शूद्रास्तेऽपि यान्ति परां गतिम् ॥३२॥
translation: For taking refuge in me, Partha, even those of unfavourable birth, women, merchants, and labourers also reach the supreme goal.
explanation: A verse that steps past the social order of its own time. Whatever the categories meant then, the argument is that refuge outranks every single one of them.

sanskrit:
किं पुनर्ब्राह्मणाः पुण्या भक्ता राजर्षयस्तथा।
अनित्यमसुखं लोकमिमं प्राप्य भजस्व माम् ॥३३॥
translation: How much more, then, the pure brahmanas and the devoted royal sages. Having come into this impermanent and joyless world, worship me.
explanation: The reasoning runs downward from the previous verse, and the instruction is plain. Krishna's description of the world stays bleak, which is why he keeps pointing elsewhere.

sanskrit:
मन्मना भव मद्भक्तो मद्याजी मां नमस्कुरु।
मामेवैष्यसि युक्त्वैवमात्मानं मत्परायणः ॥३४॥
translation: Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, sacrifice to me, bow down to me. Having disciplined yourself thus, with me as your supreme goal, you will come to me.
explanation: Four short imperatives close the chapter, each one naming him. After all the cosmology, the practical residue is small enough to remember on a battlefield.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
भूय एव महाबाहो श्रृणु मे परमं वचः।
यत्तेऽहं प्रीयमाणाय वक्ष्यामि हितकाम्यया ॥१॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: Listen again, mighty-armed one, to my supreme word, which I shall speak to you — who are dear to me — out of a wish for your welfare.
explanation: Krishna gives his reason for continuing: Arjuna is delighted, and he wants to do him good. The teaching proceeds now from affection rather than from argument.

sanskrit:
न मे विदुः सुरगणाः प्रभवं न महर्षयः।
अहमादिर्हि देवानां महर्षीणां च सर्वशः ॥२॥
translation: Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin, for I am in every way the source of the gods and of the great seers.
explanation: A neat logical trap — nothing can witness its own beginning from outside. Krishna explains his unknowability structurally rather than by appealing to mystery, which makes the claim harder to argue with than an assertion.

sanskrit:
यो मामजमनादिं च वेत्ति लोकमहेश्वरम्।
असम्मूढः स मर्त्येषु सर्वपापैः प्रमुच्यते ॥३॥
translation: One who knows me as unborn and beginningless, as the great Lord of the worlds, is undeluded among mortals and is freed from all wrongs.
explanation: Three claims about Krishna, and the payoff is freedom from delusion first, from wrongdoing only after. The order suggests which he considers the deeper problem.

sanskrit:
बुद्धिर्ज्ञानमसंमोहः क्षमा सत्यं दमः शमः।
सुखं दुःखं भवोऽभावो भयं चाभयमेव च ॥४॥
translation: Understanding, knowledge, freedom from confusion, patience, truth, self-control, calm, pleasure, pain, coming into being and passing away, fear and fearlessness...
explanation: A list that refuses to sort itself into good and bad. Pain and fear sit beside truth and patience, all of them traced to a single origin without any apology.

sanskrit:
अहिंसा समता तुष्टिस्तपो दानं यशोऽयशः।
भवन्ति भावा भूतानां मत्त एव पृथग्विधाः ॥५॥
translation: ...non-violence, evenness, contentment, austerity, generosity, fame, and disgrace — the various states of beings arise from me alone.
explanation: Fame and disgrace end the list together, which is Krishna's usual move. Even the social outcomes Arjuna dreads are placed inside the same source as his virtues.

sanskrit:
महर्षयः सप्त पूर्वे चत्वारो मनवस्तथा।
मद्भावा मानसा जाता येषां लोक इमाः प्रजाः ॥६॥
translation: The seven great seers of old, and the four Manus as well, were born of my mind and share my nature. From them come these creatures in the world.
explanation: A genealogy that skips physical generation entirely. Krishna describes the founding figures as thoughts rather than offspring, which changes what descent means and quietly relocates ancestry from the body to the mind.

sanskrit:
एतां विभूतिं योगं च मम यो वेत्ति तत्त्वतः।
सोऽविकम्पेन योगेन युज्यते नात्र संशयः ॥७॥
translation: One who knows in truth this manifestation and this power of mine is united with unshakeable yoga. Of this there is no doubt.
explanation: Vibhuti and yoga — the display, and the power behind it. Krishna says grasping both together produces a steadiness that grasping either one alone would not.

sanskrit:
अहं सर्वस्य प्रभवो मत्तः सर्वं प्रवर्तते।
इति मत्वा भजन्ते मां बुधा भावसमन्विताः ॥८॥
translation: I am the origin of everything; from me everything proceeds. Knowing this, the wise, filled with feeling, worship me.
explanation: Filled with feeling is the phrase that matters. Krishna does not describe the wise as concluding something but as being moved — worship as response rather than decision.

sanskrit:
मच्चित्ता मद्गतप्राणा बोधयन्तः परस्परम्।
कथयन्तश्च मां नित्यं तुष्यन्ति च रमन्ति च ॥९॥
translation: With their thoughts on me, their lives given over to me, enlightening one another and constantly speaking of me, they are content and they rejoice.
explanation: The most sociable verse in the Gita. Devotion here is not solitary — people teaching each other and talking, with delight given as the whole of the result.

sanskrit:
तेषां सततयुक्तानां भजतां प्रीतिपूर्वकम्।
ददामि बुद्धियोगं तं येन मामुपयान्ति ते ॥१०॥
translation: To those who are constantly disciplined and worship me with love, I give that yoga of understanding by which they come to me.
explanation: The gift is the means itself. Krishna does not reward devotion with an outcome but with the faculty needed to continue, which makes the path quietly self-supplying.

sanskrit:
तेषामेवानुकम्पार्थमहमज्ञानजं तमः।
नाशयाम्यात्मभावस्थो ज्ञानदीपेन भास्वता ॥११॥
translation: Out of compassion for them alone, dwelling within their own being, I destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.
explanation: Note where he is standing while doing it — inside them. Krishna describes his help not as intervention from outside but as light from a position he already occupies.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
परं ब्रह्म परं धाम पवित्रं परमं भवान्।
पुरुषं शाश्वतं दिव्यमादिदेवमजं विभुम् ॥१२॥
translation: Arjuna said: You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the supreme purifier, the eternal divine spirit, the primal God, unborn and all-pervading.
explanation: Arjuna speaks at length for the first time since his despair, and all of it is praise. The man who could not lift his bow is now composing theology.

sanskrit:
आहुस्त्वामृषयः सर्वे देवर्षिर्नारदस्तथा।
असितो देवलो व्यासः स्वयं चैव ब्रवीषि मे ॥१३॥
translation: All the seers say this of you, and so do the divine sage Narada, Asita, Devala, and Vyasa — and you yourself tell me so.
explanation: Arjuna assembles his evidence like a careful student: four named authorities, and then the testimony of the person in front of him, listed last but decisive.

sanskrit:
सर्वमेतदृतं मन्ये यन्मां वदसि केशव।
न हि ते भगवन् व्यक्ितं विदुर्देवा न दानवाः ॥१४॥
translation: I hold all this to be true, what you tell me, Keshava. Neither the gods nor the demons know your manifestation, Blessed One.
explanation: The belief is stated as a choice — I hold it to be true. Arjuna commits before seeing anything, which makes the next chapter's vision a gift rather than a proof.

sanskrit:
स्वयमेवात्मनाऽत्मानं वेत्थ त्वं पुरुषोत्तम।
भूतभावन भूतेश देवदेव जगत्पते ॥१५॥
translation: You alone know yourself by yourself, supreme spirit, source of beings, Lord of beings, God of gods, Lord of the world.
explanation: Arjuna repeats back the logic of the second verse and draws the conclusion himself. The student has understood, which is exactly why he can now ask for more.

sanskrit:
वक्तुमर्हस्यशेषेण दिव्या ह्यात्मविभूतयः।
याभिर्विभूतिभिर्लोकानिमांस्त्वं व्याप्य तिष्ठसि ॥१६॥
translation: You should tell me completely of your divine manifestations, by which manifestations you pervade these worlds and abide within them.
explanation: The request that generates the rest of the chapter. Arjuna asks not for doctrine but for a list — where to look, which is a practical question from a practical man.

sanskrit:
कथं विद्यामहं योगिंस्त्वां सदा परिचिन्तयन्।
केषु केषु च भावेषु चिन्त्योऽसि भगवन्मया ॥१७॥
translation: How may I know you, yogin, by constantly meditating upon you? In what various states are you to be thought of by me, Blessed One?
explanation: The second question is the more useful one. Arjuna wants handles for his attention, admitting he cannot hold an abstraction in mind for very long at all.

sanskrit:
विस्तरेणात्मनो योगं विभूतिं च जनार्दन।
भूयः कथय तृप्तिर्हि श्रृण्वतो नास्ति मेऽमृतम् ॥१८॥
translation: Tell me again, and in detail, of your power and your manifestation, Janardana. I am not satisfied with hearing your nectar-like words.
explanation: A lovely admission of appetite. Arjuna has been given enough to be liberated and simply wants more, which is a different motive from the one he began the day with.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
हन्त ते कथयिष्यामि दिव्या ह्यात्मविभूतयः।
प्राधान्यतः कुरुश्रेष्ठ नास्त्यन्तो विस्तरस्य मे ॥१९॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: So be it — I shall tell you of my divine manifestations, but only the principal ones, best of the Kurus, for there is no end to my extent.
explanation: The catalogue that follows is announced as a selection. Krishna warns that the list will be incomplete before he begins it, which is a caution about lists generally.

sanskrit:
अहमात्मा गुडाकेश सर्वभूताशयस्थितः।
अहमादिश्च मध्यं च भूतानामन्त एव च ॥२०॥
translation: I am the self, Gudakesha, seated in the heart of all beings. I am the beginning, the middle, and the very end of beings.
explanation: The list opens where it should — not with anything grand but with the self in Arjuna's own chest. Everything that follows is further out than this.

sanskrit:
आदित्यानामहं विष्णुर्ज्योतिषां रविरंशुमान्।
मरीचिर्मरुतामस्मि नक्षत्राणामहं शशी ॥२१॥
translation: Among the Adityas I am Vishnu; among lights, the radiant sun. Among the Maruts I am Marichi; among the stars I am the moon.
explanation: The method becomes visible: Krishna names the best of each category. He is not claiming to be everything here but the peak of everything, which is easier to picture.

sanskrit:
वेदानां सामवेदोऽस्मि देवानामस्मि वासवः।
इन्द्रियाणां मनश्चास्मि भूतानामस्मि चेतना ॥२२॥
translation: Among the Vedas I am the Sama Veda; among the gods, Indra. Among the senses I am the mind, and in beings I am consciousness.
explanation: The Sama Veda is the one that is sung. Krishna's choices repeatedly favour the version of a thing that carries feeling over the version that carries information.

sanskrit:
रुद्राणां शङ्करश्चास्मि वित्तेशो यक्षरक्षसाम्।
वसूनां पावकश्चास्मि मेरुः शिखरिणामहम् ॥२३॥
translation: Among the Rudras I am Shankara; among the yakshas and rakshasas, the lord of wealth. Among the Vasus I am fire, and among mountains, Meru.
explanation: Even the fearsome categories get an entry. Krishna does not skip the yakshas and rakshasas, keeping the claim genuinely comprehensive rather than merely flattering — a catalogue of the admirable would have been a smaller thing.

sanskrit:
पुरोधसां च मुख्यं मां विद्धि पार्थ बृहस्पतिम्।
सेनानीनामहं स्कन्दः सरसामस्मि सागरः ॥२४॥
translation: Among household priests know me, Partha, to be the chief of them, Brihaspati. Among generals I am Skanda, and among waters, the ocean.
explanation: A general and a priest in the same breath, spoken to a man who must be one and reveres the other. The pairing is not accidental on this particular morning.

sanskrit:
महर्षीणां भृगुरहं गिरामस्म्येकमक्षरम्।
यज्ञानां जपयज्ञोऽस्मि स्थावराणां हिमालयः ॥२५॥
translation: Among the great seers I am Bhrigu; among words, the single syllable. Among sacrifices I am the sacrifice of quiet repetition, and among immovable things, the Himalaya.
explanation: Japa, murmured repetition, is named the highest sacrifice — the cheapest and least visible of all rites. Krishna keeps elevating what requires no apparatus at all.

sanskrit:
अश्वत्थः सर्ववृक्षाणां देवर्षीणां च नारदः।
गन्धर्वाणां चित्ररथः सिद्धानां कपिलो मुनिः ॥२६॥
translation: Among all trees I am the ashvattha; among the divine sages, Narada. Among the gandharvas I am Chitraratha, and among the perfected, the sage Kapila.
explanation: The ashvattha will return in Chapter 15 as an image of the whole world. Krishna plants it here quietly, inside a list, long before he makes anything of it.

sanskrit:
उच्चैःश्रवसमश्वानां विद्धि माममृतोद्भवम्।
ऐरावतं गजेन्द्राणां नराणां च नराधिपम् ॥२७॥
translation: Know me among horses to be Uchchaihshravas, born of nectar; among lordly elephants, Airavata; and among men, the king.
explanation: Three of the finest possessions a warrior could imagine. Krishna meets Arjuna's world on its own terms, naming things his listener would genuinely admire rather than the things a renunciate might have chosen.

sanskrit:
आयुधानामहं वज्रं धेनूनामस्मि कामधुक्।
प्रजनश्चास्मि कन्दर्पः सर्पाणामस्मि वासुकिः ॥२८॥
translation: Among weapons I am the thunderbolt; among cows, the wish-granting cow. I am the begetter, Kandarpa; and among serpents, Vasuki.
explanation: Kandarpa is desire itself, and Krishna claims it in its generative aspect — consistent with Chapter 7, where desire not opposed to dharma was named as his own.

sanskrit:
अनन्तश्चास्मि नागानां वरुणो यादसामहम्।
पितृ़णामर्यमा चास्मि यमः संयमतामहम् ॥२९॥
translation: Among the nagas I am Ananta; among water creatures, Varuna. Among the ancestors I am Aryaman, and among those who govern, Yama.
explanation: Yama is death, listed without a flinch among ordinary offices. Krishna's catalogues never quarantine the frightening entries into some separate section, which is consistent with a teaching that keeps claiming both halves of everything.

sanskrit:
प्रह्लादश्चास्मि दैत्यानां कालः कलयतामहम्।
मृगाणां च मृगेन्द्रोऽहं वैनतेयश्च पक्षिणाम् ॥३०॥
translation: Among the daityas I am Prahlada; among reckoners, time. Among beasts I am the lion, and among birds, the son of Vinata.
explanation: Prahlada was a demon who loved God against his own lineage. From the entire demonic host Krishna picks the one who defected — pointed, on a family battlefield.

sanskrit:
पवनः पवतामस्मि रामः शस्त्रभृतामहम्।
झषाणां मकरश्चास्मि स्रोतसामस्मि जाह्नवी ॥३१॥
translation: Among purifiers I am the wind; among bearers of weapons, Rama. Among fishes I am the crocodile, and among rivers, the Ganges.
explanation: The wind purifies simply by moving through. Krishna's examples of holiness are often things that clean by their nature rather than by any ritual intention.

sanskrit:
सर्गाणामादिरन्तश्च मध्यं चैवाहमर्जुन।
अध्यात्मविद्या विद्यानां वादः प्रवदतामहम् ॥३२॥
translation: Among creations I am the beginning, the end, and the middle as well, Arjuna. Among sciences I am the science of the self, and I am the argument of those who debate.
explanation: Being the argument itself, rather than the winner, is a curious claim. Krishna places himself in the reasoning instead of on either side of it — worth noting in a war.

sanskrit:
अक्षराणामकारोऽस्मि द्वन्द्वः सामासिकस्य च।
अहमेवाक्षयः कालो धाताऽहं विश्वतोमुखः ॥३३॥
translation: Among letters I am the letter A; among compounds, the pairing compound. I alone am inexhaustible time, and I am the ordainer facing in every direction.
explanation: The letter A is the sound a mouth makes when it simply opens. Krishna claims the simplest possible utterance, the one contained inside every other one.

sanskrit:
मृत्युः सर्वहरश्चाहमुद्भवश्च भविष्यताम्।
कीर्तिः श्रीर्वाक्च नारीणां स्मृतिर्मेधा धृतिः क्षमा ॥३४॥
translation: I am all-devouring death, and the origin of things yet to be. Among feminine qualities I am fame, prosperity, speech, memory, intelligence, firmness, and patience.
explanation: Death and origination in one line again. Then seven qualities, and the list is unusually tender — memory and patience placed among the powers of the universe.

sanskrit:
बृहत्साम तथा साम्नां गायत्री छन्दसामहम्।
मासानां मार्गशीर्षोऽहमृतूनां कुसुमाकरः ॥३५॥
translation: Among hymns I am the Brihat-saman; among metres, the Gayatri. Among months I am Margashirsha, and among seasons, the flowering spring.
explanation: Krishna picks the season everyone loves. There is no austerity anywhere in this verse, which is itself part of the point about where he can be found.

sanskrit:
द्यूतं छलयतामस्मि तेजस्तेजस्विनामहम्।
जयोऽस्मि व्यवसायोऽस्मि सत्त्वं सत्त्ववतामहम् ॥३६॥
translation: I am the gambling of cheats and the splendour of the splendid. I am victory, I am resolve, and I am the goodness of the good.
explanation: The most disquieting entry sits beside the most admirable. Krishna claims the dice game that cost the Pandavas everything — spoken to one of the men who lost it.

sanskrit:
वृष्णीनां वासुदेवोऽस्मि पाण्डवानां धनंजयः।
मुनीनामप्यहं व्यासः कवीनामुशना कविः ॥३७॥
translation: Among the Vrishnis I am Vasudeva; among the Pandavas, Dhananjaya. Among sages I am Vyasa, and among poets, the poet Ushanas.
explanation: Krishna names himself, and then names Arjuna, who is standing right there. The catalogue reaches into the chariot and includes the man who asked for it.

sanskrit:
दण्डो दमयतामस्मि नीतिरस्मि जिगीषताम्।
मौनं चैवास्मि गुह्यानां ज्ञानं ज्ञानवतामहम् ॥३८॥
translation: I am the rod of those who restrain and the statecraft of those who seek victory. Among secrets I am silence, and I am the knowledge of the knowing.
explanation: Silence as the best of secrets is a fine joke to place in the middle of a very long speech. Krishna knows exactly what he is doing at this point in the catalogue.

sanskrit:
यच्चापि सर्वभूतानां बीजं तदहमर्जुन।
न तदस्ति विना यत्स्यान्मया भूतं चराचरम् ॥३९॥
translation: And whatever is the seed of all beings, that am I, Arjuna. There is no being, moving or unmoving, that could exist without me.
explanation: The list is abandoned for a principle. Having named perhaps eighty things, Krishna concedes the method cannot work and simply states the point directly instead.

sanskrit:
नान्तोऽस्ति मम दिव्यानां विभूतीनां परंतप।
एष तूद्देशतः प्रोक्तो विभूतेर्विस्तरो मया ॥४०॥
translation: There is no end to my divine manifestations, scorcher of foes. What I have declared is only a brief indication of the extent of my power.
explanation: The warning from the nineteenth verse returns as a confession. Everything Arjuna just heard is labelled a sample, which prepares him for what he is about to see.

sanskrit:
यद्यद्विभूतिमत्सत्त्वं श्रीमदूर्जितमेव वा।
तत्तदेवावगच्छ त्वं मम तेजोंऽशसंभवम् ॥४१॥
translation: Whatever being is glorious, prosperous, or powerful — know that to have sprung from a fragment of my splendour.
explanation: A rule that replaces the entire catalogue. Arjuna is handed a method rather than a list, and can now generate the entries himself wherever he happens to look.

sanskrit:
अथवा बहुनैतेन किं ज्ञातेन तवार्जुन।
विष्टभ्याहमिदं कृत्स्नमेकांशेन स्थितो जगत् ॥४२॥
translation: But what is the use of knowing all this in detail, Arjuna? I support this entire world with a single fragment of myself, and remain.
explanation: The chapter ends by dismissing its own contents. One fragment holds everything Arjuna has heard about, and Krishna still stands outside it — a setup for what follows.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
मदनुग्रहाय परमं गुह्यमध्यात्मसंज्ञितम्।
यत्त्वयोक्तं वचस्तेन मोहोऽयं विगतो मम ॥१॥
translation: Arjuna said: Out of compassion for me you have spoken the supreme secret known as the highest self, and by these words my delusion has gone.
explanation: Arjuna reports the cure before asking for anything more. The problem he arrived with is solved — which makes everything that follows in this chapter a request, not a need.

sanskrit:
भवाप्ययौ हि भूतानां श्रुतौ विस्तरशो मया।
त्वत्तः कमलपत्राक्ष माहात्म्यमपि चाव्ययम् ॥२॥
translation: For I have heard from you in detail of the coming into being and the passing away of beings, lotus-eyed one, and also of your imperishable greatness.
explanation: Arjuna summarizes what he has been given, the way a good student checks his understanding. The compliment is affectionate, addressed to the face right beside him.

sanskrit:
एवमेतद्यथात्थ त्वमात्मानं परमेश्वर।
द्रष्टुमिच्छामि ते रूपमैश्वरं पुरुषोत्तम ॥३॥
translation: Even as you have declared yourself to be, supreme Lord, so it is. Yet I desire to see your divine form, best of persons.
explanation: The pivot of the chapter, and it is honest about itself. Arjuna believes completely and still wants to look — belief and sight turn out to be different appetites.

sanskrit:
मन्यसे यदि तच्छक्यं मया द्रष्टुमिति प्रभो।
योगेश्वर ततो मे त्वं दर्शयाऽत्मानमव्ययम् ॥४॥
translation: If you think it possible for me to see it, Lord, then, master of yoga, show me your imperishable self.
explanation: The request is carefully conditional. Arjuna leaves Krishna room to refuse and defers to his judgement about what a human being can actually withstand — a caution that turns out to have been well placed.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
पश्य मे पार्थ रूपाणि शतशोऽथ सहस्रशः।
नानाविधानि दिव्यानि नानावर्णाकृतीनि च ॥५॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: Behold my forms, Partha, by the hundreds and by the thousands — various, divine, of many colours and many shapes.
explanation: Consent is given at once, with no warning attached. Krishna's opening word is simply behold, and the plural forms arrive before anything else is explained.

sanskrit:
पश्यादित्यान्वसून्रुद्रानश्िवनौ मरुतस्तथा।
बहून्यदृष्टपूर्वाणि पश्याऽश्चर्याणि भारत ॥६॥
translation: Behold the Adityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Ashvins, and the Maruts. Behold many wonders never seen before, Bharata.
explanation: The vision begins with recognizable gods, the gentlest possible entry. Krishna shows Arjuna things he has names for before showing him things he does not.

sanskrit:
इहैकस्थं जगत्कृत्स्नं पश्याद्य सचराचरम्।
मम देहे गुडाकेश यच्चान्यद्द्रष्टुमिच्छसि ॥७॥
translation: See now, gathered together in one place in my body, the whole world, moving and unmoving, Gudakesha — and whatever else you wish to see.
explanation: The last clause is startlingly open-handed. Krishna offers not a fixed display but whatever Arjuna wants, making the vision partly a creation of the one looking.

sanskrit:
न तु मां शक्यसे द्रष्टुमनेनैव स्वचक्षुषा।
दिव्यं ददामि ते चक्षुः पश्य मे योगमैश्वरम् ॥८॥
translation: But you cannot see me with this eye of your own. I give you a divine eye. Behold my power as a master of yoga.
explanation: A necessary intervention. The problem is equipment, not distance, and Krishna solves it by altering the observer rather than by making himself any smaller, which tells us what kind of hiddenness has been at work.

sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच
एवमुक्त्वा ततो राजन्महायोगेश्वरो हरिः।
दर्शयामास पार्थाय परमं रूपमैश्वरम् ॥९॥
translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus, O King, the great master of yoga, Hari, showed Partha his supreme form as Lord.
explanation: Sanjaya's voice returns after ten chapters of silence. The reminder that this is being narrated to a blind king who can see none of it is quietly devastating.

sanskrit:
अनेकवक्त्रनयनमनेकाद्भुतदर्शनम्।
अनेकदिव्याभरणं दिव्यानेकोद्यतायुधम् ॥१०॥
translation: ...with many mouths and eyes, with many wondrous sights, with many divine ornaments, and with many divine weapons raised.
explanation: The description begins with multiplicity rather than magnitude. What overwhelms first is not size but number — too many of everything to take in at once.

sanskrit:
दिव्यमाल्याम्बरधरं दिव्यगन्धानुलेपनम्।
सर्वाश्चर्यमयं देवमनन्तं विश्वतोमुखम् ॥११॥
translation: ...wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine fragrances, made entirely of wonders, boundless, and facing in every direction.
explanation: Even scent is included, which makes the vision bodily rather than merely visual. And then the phrase that undoes it: facing every direction, so there is no front.

sanskrit:
दिवि सूर्यसहस्रस्य भवेद्युगपदुत्थिता।
यदि भाः सदृशी सा स्याद्भासस्तस्य महात्मनः ॥१२॥
translation: If the light of a thousand suns were to rise at once in the sky, that would perhaps resemble the splendour of that great being.
explanation: The most famous simile in the Gita, and note how carefully it is hedged — perhaps resemble. Sanjaya reaches for the largest comparison he has and admits it fails.

sanskrit:
तत्रैकस्थं जगत्कृत्स्नं प्रविभक्तमनेकधा।
अपश्यद्देवदेवस्य शरीरे पाण्डवस्तदा ॥१३॥
translation: There the son of Pandu saw the whole world, divided into many parts, gathered together in one place in the body of the God of gods.
explanation: The paradox Arjuna asked for is delivered exactly. Everything is separate and everything is in one place, and both remain true at the same moment.

sanskrit:
ततः स विस्मयाविष्टो हृष्टरोमा धनञ्जयः।
प्रणम्य शिरसा देवं कृताञ्जलिरभाषत ॥१४॥
translation: Then Dhananjaya, filled with amazement, his hair standing on end, bowed his head to the God and spoke with palms joined together.
explanation: The physical detail is precise — hair on end. Sanjaya reports the body's response before the mind's, which is how awe actually arrives in a person.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
पश्यामि देवांस्तव देव देहे
सर्वांस्तथा भूतविशेषसङ्घान्।
ब्रह्माणमीशं कमलासनस्थ
मृषींश्च सर्वानुरगांश्च दिव्यान् ॥१५॥
translation: Arjuna said: I see all the gods in your body, O God, and hosts of all kinds of beings — Brahma the Lord seated on his lotus, all the seers, and the divine serpents.
explanation: Arjuna narrates as he looks, and his first inventory is orderly. He is still trying to catalogue what he sees, which will not last very much longer.

sanskrit:
अनेकबाहूदरवक्त्रनेत्रं
पश्यामि त्वां सर्वतोऽनन्तरूपम्।
नान्तं न मध्यं न पुनस्तवादिं
पश्यामि विश्वेश्वर विश्वरूप ॥१६॥
translation: I see you everywhere, of boundless form, with many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes. I see no end, no middle, and no beginning in you, Lord of the universe.
explanation: The cataloguing breaks down here. Arjuna moves from listing what is present to reporting what is missing — the edges, without which nothing can be taken in.

sanskrit:
किरीटिनं गदिनं चक्रिणं च
तेजोराशिं सर्वतोदीप्तिमन्तम्।
पश्यामि त्वां दुर्निरीक्ष्यं समन्ता
द्दीप्तानलार्कद्युतिमप्रमेयम् ॥१७॥
translation: I see you with crown, mace, and discus, a mass of radiance shining everywhere, hard to look at, blazing all around like fire and sun, immeasurable.
explanation: The familiar emblems appear briefly, then dissolve into light. And then the honest admission: hard to look at. Arjuna is beginning to struggle with what he asked for.

sanskrit:
त्वमक्षरं परमं वेदितव्यं
त्वमस्य विश्वस्य परं निधानम्।
त्वमव्ययः शाश्वतधर्मगोप्ता
सनातनस्त्वं पुरुषो मतो मे ॥१८॥
translation: You are the supreme imperishable to be known; you are the ultimate resting place of this universe. You are the changeless guardian of eternal righteousness. I hold you to be the everlasting spirit.
explanation: A moment of composure in which Arjuna recites theology. It reads like someone steadying himself with familiar words while the ground shifts underneath him, and the steadiness will not survive the next few verses.

sanskrit:
अनादिमध्यान्तमनन्तवीर्य
मनन्तबाहुं शशिसूर्यनेत्रम्।
पश्यामि त्वां दीप्तहुताशवक्त्रम्
स्वतेजसा विश्वमिदं तपन्तम् ॥१९॥
translation: Without beginning, middle, or end, of infinite power and infinite arms, with the moon and the sun for eyes, I see you, your mouth a blazing fire, scorching this universe with your own radiance.
explanation: The sun and moon as eyes make the scale finally land. And the mouth appears for the first time as fire, which is where the vision begins to turn frightening.

sanskrit:
द्यावापृथिव्योरिदमन्तरं हि
व्याप्तं त्वयैकेन दिशश्च सर्वाः।
दृष्ट्वाऽद्भुतं रूपमुग्रं तवेदं
लोकत्रयं प्रव्यथितं महात्मन् ॥२०॥
translation: This space between heaven and earth, and all the directions, are pervaded by you alone. Seeing this wondrous and terrible form of yours, the three worlds tremble, great one.
explanation: Terrible enters the description here. Arjuna also notices he is not the only one afraid — the whole cosmos is reacting, which makes his own fear less private.

sanskrit:
अमी हि त्वां सुरसङ्घाः विशन्ति
केचिद्भीताः प्राञ्जलयो गृणन्ति।
स्वस्तीत्युक्त्वा महर्षिसिद्धसङ्घाः
स्तुवन्ति त्वां स्तुतिभिः पुष्कलाभिः ॥२१॥
translation: These hosts of gods enter into you; some, afraid, praise you with joined palms. Crying out may it be well, the throngs of great seers and perfected ones extol you with abundant hymns.
explanation: The gods are frightened too, and their prayer is a plea for safety. Even the beings Arjuna would have prayed to are visibly hoping this turns out well.

sanskrit:
रुद्रादित्या वसवो ये च साध्या
विश्वेऽश्िवनौ मरुतश्चोष्मपाश्च।
गन्धर्वयक्षासुरसिद्धसङ्घा
वीक्षन्ते त्वां विस्मिताश्चैव सर्वे ॥२२॥
translation: The Rudras, Adityas, Vasus, and Sadhyas, the All-gods, the two Ashvins, the Maruts, the ancestors, and the hosts of gandharvas, yakshas, demons, and perfected ones — all gaze at you in wonder.
explanation: A crowded verse in which every class of being is reduced to a spectator. The universe's entire population is doing exactly what Arjuna is doing: staring.

sanskrit:
रूपं महत्ते बहुवक्त्रनेत्रं
महाबाहो बहुबाहूरुपादम्।
बहूदरं बहुदंष्ट्राकरालं
दृष्ट्वा लोकाः प्रव्यथितास्तथाऽहम् ॥२३॥
translation: Seeing your great form with its many mouths and eyes, mighty-armed one, its many arms, thighs, and feet, its many bellies, terrible with many tusks — the worlds tremble, and so do I.
explanation: The list of parts has become grotesque rather than glorious. And Arjuna finally includes himself in the reaction: the worlds tremble, and so do I.

sanskrit:
नभःस्पृशं दीप्तमनेकवर्णं
व्यात्ताननं दीप्तविशालनेत्रम्।
दृष्ट्वा हि त्वां प्रव्यथितान्तरात्मा
धृतिं न विन्दामि शमं च विष्णो ॥२४॥
translation: Seeing you touching the sky, blazing with many colours, your mouths open, your great eyes shining, my inmost self trembles, and I find no steadiness and no peace, Vishnu.
explanation: The confession is total. Arjuna has lost the very steadiness Krishna spent six chapters teaching him, and he says so without any attempt at pretence.

sanskrit:
दंष्ट्राकरालानि च ते मुखानि
दृष्ट्वैव कालानलसन्निभानि।
दिशो न जाने न लभे च शर्म
प्रसीद देवेश जगन्निवास ॥२५॥
translation: Seeing your mouths terrible with tusks, like the fires of time, I do not know the directions and I find no refuge. Have mercy, Lord of gods, dwelling place of the world.
explanation: Losing the directions is a specific kind of terror — not knowing which way is which. And Arjuna asks for mercy, the first time he has begged for anything today.

sanskrit:
अमी च त्वां धृतराष्ट्रस्य पुत्राः
सर्वे सहैवावनिपालसङ्घैः।
भीष्मो द्रोणः सूतपुत्रस्तथाऽसौ
सहास्मदीयैरपि योधमुख्यैः ॥२६॥
translation: And these sons of Dhritarashtra, together with the hosts of kings, Bhishma, Drona, and the son of the charioteer, along with our own chief warriors as well...
explanation: The vision turns local and unbearable. Arjuna suddenly recognizes faces — including, in that final phrase, the men who are fighting on his own side.

sanskrit:
वक्त्राणि ते त्वरमाणा विशन्ति
दंष्ट्राकरालानि भयानकानि।
केचिद्विलग्ना दशनान्तरेषु
संदृश्यन्ते चूर्णितैरुत्तमाङ्गैः ॥२७॥
translation: ...rush headlong into your fearful mouths, terrible with tusks. Some are seen caught between your teeth, their heads crushed to powder.
explanation: The most graphic image in the Gita, and it answers Arjuna's morning. He asked whether he should kill these men; he is shown that they are already gone.

sanskrit:
यथा नदीनां बहवोऽम्बुवेगाः
समुद्रमेवाभिमुखाः द्रवन्ति।
तथा तवामी नरलोकवीरा
विशन्ति वक्त्राण्यभिविज्वलन्ति ॥२८॥
translation: As the many torrents of rivers race toward the ocean, so these heroes of the world of men enter your blazing mouths.
explanation: A strangely calm simile after the horror. Rivers do not choose the ocean; the comparison removes agency entirely, from the warriors and from Arjuna alike.

sanskrit:
यथा प्रदीप्तं ज्वलनं पतङ्गा
विशन्ति नाशाय समृद्धवेगाः।
तथैव नाशाय विशन्ति लोका
स्तवापि वक्त्राणि समृद्धवेगाः ॥२९॥
translation: As moths rush with headlong speed into a blazing fire to their destruction, so these worlds rush with headlong speed into your mouths to their destruction.
explanation: The second simile is crueller than the first. Moths are drawn toward what kills them, and the repeated headlong speed makes the whole thing look like eagerness.

sanskrit:
लेलिह्यसे ग्रसमानः समन्ता
ल्लोकान्समग्रान्वदनैर्ज्वलद्भिः।
तेजोभिरापूर्य जगत्समग्रं
भासस्तवोग्राः प्रतपन्ति विष्णो ॥३०॥
translation: You lick up and devour all the worlds on every side with your flaming mouths. Filling the whole world with radiance, your terrible rays scorch it, Vishnu.
explanation: The verb is the worst detail — licking. Something enormous and impersonal is described as tasting the world, which is more disturbing than mere destruction.

sanskrit:
आख्याहि मे को भवानुग्ररूपो
नमोऽस्तु ते देववर प्रसीद।
विज्ञातुमिच्छामि भवन्तमाद्यं
न हि प्रजानामि तव प्रवृत्तिम् ॥३१॥
translation: Tell me who you are, you of terrible form. Salutations to you, best of gods; have mercy. I wish to know you, the primal one, for I do not understand what you are doing.
explanation: Arjuna asks the question again from the beginning — who are you. Everything he understood in the first verse has been dislodged by what he has now seen.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो
लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः।
ऋतेऽपि त्वां न भविष्यन्ति सर्वे
येऽवस्थिताः प्रत्यनीकेषु योधाः ॥३२॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: I am time, grown mature, engaged here in destroying the worlds. Even without you, all these warriors arrayed in the opposing ranks shall cease to be.
explanation: The most famous line in the Gita, and the answer to everything Arjuna feared. He is not being asked to kill these men; he is told what has already been decided.

sanskrit:
तस्मात्त्वमुत्तिष्ठ यशो लभस्व
जित्वा शत्रून् भुङ्क्ष्व राज्यं समृद्धम्।
मयैवैते निहताः पूर्वमेव
निमित्तमात्रं भव सव्यसाचिन् ॥३३॥
translation: Therefore rise and win glory. Conquering your enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom. These have already been slain by me. Be merely the instrument, Savyasachin.
explanation: Merely the instrument — nimitta-matram. Krishna does not remove Arjuna's action, only his authorship of it, which is exactly what Chapter 3 was building toward.

sanskrit:
द्रोणं च भीष्मं च जयद्रथं च
कर्णं तथाऽन्यानपि योधवीरान्।
मया हतांस्त्वं जहि मा व्यथिष्ठा
युध्यस्व जेतासि रणे सपत्नान् ॥३४॥
translation: Drona, Bhishma, Jayadratha, Karna, and the other warrior heroes as well have already been slain by me. Kill them and do not waver. Fight; you shall conquer your rivals in battle.
explanation: The names are said aloud — his teacher, his grandsire. Krishna does not soften the list, answering Arjuna's first objection by naming the very men he could not face.

sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच
एतच्छ्रुत्वा वचनं केशवस्य
कृताञ्जलिर्वेपमानः किरीटी।
नमस्कृत्वा भूय एवाह कृष्णं
सगद्गदं भीतभीतः प्रणम्य ॥३५॥
translation: Sanjaya said: Hearing this speech of Keshava, the crowned one, trembling and with joined palms, bowed again and, terrified, spoke to Krishna in a faltering voice.
explanation: Sanjaya notes the voice breaking. After the grandest speech in the poem, the detail that lands is a frightened man unable to get his words out cleanly.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
स्थाने हृषीकेश तव प्रकीर्त्या
जगत् प्रहृष्यत्यनुरज्यते च।
रक्षांसि भीतानि दिशो द्रवन्ति
सर्वे नमस्यन्ति च सिद्धसङ्घाः ॥३६॥
translation: Arjuna said: It is right, Hrishikesha, that the world rejoices and delights in your glory. The demons flee in fear in all directions, and all the hosts of the perfected bow down.
explanation: Arjuna begins with the word sthane, it is fitting. His first move after terror is to say that the terror is appropriate — a remarkable act of composure.

sanskrit:
कस्माच्च ते न नमेरन्महात्मन्
गरीयसे ब्रह्मणोऽप्यादिकर्त्रे।
अनन्त देवेश जगन्निवास
त्वमक्षरं सदसत्तत्परं यत् ॥३७॥
translation: And why should they not bow to you, great one, greater even than Brahma, the original creator? Boundless Lord of gods, dwelling place of the world, you are the imperishable, being and non-being and what lies beyond.
explanation: Arjuna's praise now runs past the categories he has. He reaches for what lies beyond both because nothing in his vocabulary of being extends far enough.

sanskrit:
त्वमादिदेवः पुरुषः पुराण
स्त्वमस्य विश्वस्य परं निधानम्।
वेत्तासि वेद्यं च परं च धाम
त्वया ततं विश्वमनन्तरूप ॥३८॥
translation: You are the primal God, the ancient spirit; you are the supreme resting place of this universe. You are the knower and the known and the highest abode. By you the universe is pervaded, O being of endless form.
explanation: Knower and known at once, which quietly cancels the distance Arjuna has been feeling. If he is inside the pervaded universe, he was never actually outside it.

sanskrit:
वायुर्यमोऽग्निर्वरुणः शशाङ्कः
प्रजापतिस्त्वं प्रपितामहश्च।
नमो नमस्तेऽस्तु सहस्रकृत्वः
पुनश्च भूयोऽपि नमो नमस्ते ॥३९॥
translation: You are Vayu, Yama, Agni, Varuna, the moon, Prajapati, and the great-grandfather. Salutations to you a thousand times, and again and yet again, salutations to you.
explanation: Arjuna runs out of things to say and simply repeats his greeting. The verse enacts what awe does to language — it stops arguing and starts bowing instead.

sanskrit:
नमः पुरस्तादथ पृष्ठतस्ते
नमोऽस्तु ते सर्वत एव सर्व।
अनन्तवीर्यामितविक्रमस्त्वं
सर्वं समाप्नोषि ततोऽसि सर्वः ॥४०॥
translation: Salutations to you from in front and from behind, salutations to you from every side, O All. Of boundless valour and immeasurable might, you encompass everything, and so you are everything.
explanation: Bowing in every direction because there is no direction without him. The logic is simple and complete: he fills everything, and therefore he is everything.

sanskrit:
सखेति मत्वा प्रसभं यदुक्तं
हे कृष्ण हे यादव हे सखेति।
अजानता महिमानं तवेदं
मया प्रमादात्प्रणयेन वापि ॥४१॥
translation: Thinking of you as a friend, and not knowing this greatness of yours, I have rashly said: Krishna, Yadava, comrade — through carelessness, or through affection.
explanation: The chapter's most human moment. Arjuna apologizes for using nicknames, and the excuse he offers — or through affection — is the tenderest line in the poem.

sanskrit:
यच्चावहासार्थमसत्कृतोऽसि
विहारशय्यासनभोजनेषु।
एकोऽथवाप्यच्युत तत्समक्षं
तत्क्षामये त्वामहमप्रमेयम् ॥४२॥
translation: And for whatever disrespect I showed you in jest, at play, resting, sitting, or eating, alone or before others, unshaken one — for that I ask your pardon, immeasurable one.
explanation: A catalogue of ordinary intimacy: meals, naps, jokes. Arjuna is not confessing sins but remembering a friendship, and asking whether it was ever allowed — a stranger and sadder question than guilt.

sanskrit:
पितासि लोकस्य चराचरस्य
त्वमस्य पूज्यश्च गुरुर्गरीयान्।
न त्वत्समोऽस्त्यभ्यधिकः कुतोऽन्यो
लोकत्रयेऽप्यप्रतिमप्रभाव ॥४३॥
translation: You are the father of the world, of all that moves and does not move. You are its object of worship and its most venerable teacher. There is none equal to you — how could there be a greater, in all three worlds, O being of matchless power?
explanation: Arjuna reclassifies his charioteer as father and guru. The man giving him directions this morning is placed above everything Arjuna knows how to name, and that reclassification is what the whole vision was for.

sanskrit:
तस्मात्प्रणम्य प्रणिधाय कायं
प्रसादये त्वामहमीशमीड्यम्।
पितेव पुत्रस्य सखेव सख्युः
प्रियः प्रियायार्हसि देव सोढुम् ॥४४॥
translation: Therefore, bowing down and prostrating my body, I ask your grace, adorable Lord. As a father with a son, as a friend with a friend, as a lover with a beloved — bear with me, God.
explanation: Three relationships offered as models for forgiveness, and the last is boldest. Having just been terrified, Arjuna asks to be treated as someone who is loved.

sanskrit:
अदृष्टपूर्वं हृषितोऽस्मि दृष्ट्वा
भयेन च प्रव्यथितं मनो मे।
तदेव मे दर्शय देव रूपं
प्रसीद देवेश जगन्निवास ॥४५॥
translation: Having seen what was never seen before, I am delighted, and yet my mind trembles with fear. Show me that other form of yours, God; have mercy, Lord of gods, dwelling place of the world.
explanation: Both feelings reported honestly and side by side. Arjuna does not pretend the delight cancels the fear, and he asks for the vision to end regardless.

sanskrit:
किरीटिनं गदिनं चक्रहस्त
मिच्छामि त्वां द्रष्टुमहं तथैव।
तेनैव रूपेण चतुर्भुजेन
सहस्रबाहो भव विश्वमूर्ते ॥४६॥
translation: I wish to see you just as before, with your crown, your mace, and the discus in your hand. Assume that four-armed form, thousand-armed one, O universal form.
explanation: A specific request for a familiar shape. Arjuna asks not for the ordinary Krishna yet but for the traditional icon — one step down from infinity, and no further.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
मया प्रसन्नेन तवार्जुनेदं
रूपं परं दर्शितमात्मयोगात्।
तेजोमयं विश्वमनन्तमाद्यं
यन्मे त्वदन्येन न दृष्टपूर्वम् ॥४७॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: By my grace and through my own power, Arjuna, this supreme form has been shown to you — full of radiance, universal, endless, primal, which none but you has ever seen.
explanation: Krishna names it a favour, and adds that no one else has ever received it. The vision was not a proof offered to a doubter but a gift given to a friend.

sanskrit:
न वेदयज्ञाध्ययनैर्न दानै
र्न च क्रियाभिर्न तपोभिरुग्रैः।
एवंरूपः शक्य अहं नृलोके
द्रष्टुं त्वदन्येन कुरुप्रवीर ॥४८॥
translation: Not by the Vedas, nor by sacrifices or study, nor by gifts, nor by rites, nor by severe austerities can I be seen in this form in the world of men by any but you, hero of the Kurus.
explanation: Six standard paths listed, and all of them dismissed. Nothing Arjuna could have done would have earned this, which is precisely what makes it grace.

sanskrit:
मा ते व्यथा मा च विमूढभावो
दृष्ट्वा रूपं घोरमीदृङ्ममेदम्।
व्यपेतभीः प्रीतमनाः पुनस्त्वं
तदेव मे रूपमिदं प्रपश्य ॥४९॥
translation: Do not be afraid, and do not be bewildered at seeing this terrible form of mine. Free from fear and glad at heart, behold once more that other form of mine.
explanation: The comfort is immediate and unfussy. Krishna does not lecture Arjuna about his fear; he simply tells him it is over and then changes back.

sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच
इत्यर्जुनं वासुदेवस्तथोक्त्वा
स्वकं रूपं दर्शयामास भूयः।
आश्वासयामास च भीतमेनं
भूत्वा पुनः सौम्यवपुर्महात्मा ॥५०॥
translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vasudeva showed his own form again. The great one comforted the frightened Arjuna, becoming once more gentle in appearance.
explanation: Sanjaya's word for the returning form is saumya, gentle. The universe folds back into a man in a chariot, and the emphasis falls on how mild he looks.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
दृष्ट्वेदं मानुषं रूपं तवसौम्यं जनार्दन।
इदानीमस्मि संवृत्तः सचेताः प्रकृतिं गतः ॥५१॥
translation: Arjuna said: Seeing this human form of yours, so gentle, Janardana, I am now composed and restored to my own nature.
explanation: Arjuna reports his recovery in the plainest language he has used all day. He wanted the vision, he received it, and what steadies him is the ordinary face.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
सुदुर्दर्शमिदं रूपं दृष्टवानसि यन्मम।
देवा अप्यस्य रूपस्य नित्यं दर्शनकाङ्क्षिणः ॥५२॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: This form of mine which you have seen is very hard to see. Even the gods are constantly longing for a sight of this form.
explanation: A gentle reminder of what has just happened, offered after the fear has passed. Krishna waits until Arjuna is calm before telling him what he was given.

sanskrit:
नाहं वेदैर्न तपसा न दानेन न चेज्यया।
शक्य एवंविधो द्रष्टुं दृष्टवानसि मां यथा ॥५३॥
translation: Not by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by gifts, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in this way, as you have seen me.
explanation: The dismissal of the standard means is repeated almost word for word. The repetition is deliberate, since Krishna is about to name the one thing that does work.

sanskrit:
भक्त्या त्वनन्यया शक्यमहमेवंविधोऽर्जुन।
ज्ञातुं दृष्टुं च तत्त्वेन प्रवेष्टुं च परंतप ॥५४॥
translation: But by undivided devotion alone, Arjuna, can I be known and seen in this way, and truly entered into, scorcher of foes.
explanation: The answer to the whole chapter, and it is one word: bhakti. Three verbs follow it — known, seen, entered — with entering placed last, as the furthest thing.

sanskrit:
मत्कर्मकृन्मत्परमो मद्भक्तः सङ्गवर्जितः।
निर्वैरः सर्वभूतेषु यः स मामेति पाण्डव ॥५५॥
translation: One who does my work, holds me as supreme, is devoted to me, free from attachment and without enmity toward any being — that one comes to me, Pandava.
explanation: The final verse steps down from cosmic vision to conduct, ending on nirvairah, without enmity. After all that fire, the last requirement is bearing no one a grudge.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाचएवं सततयुक्ता ये भक्तास्त्वां पर्युपासते।
येचाप्यक्षरमव्यक्तं तेषां के योगवित्तमाः ॥१॥
translation: Arjuna said: Those devotees who are constantly disciplined and worship you, and those who worship the imperishable and unmanifest — which of them are better versed in yoga?
explanation: Arjuna asks the question the last five chapters made unavoidable. Krishna has praised both the personal and the impersonal, and Arjuna wants to know where to aim.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाचमय्यावेश्य मनो ये मां नित्ययुक्ता उपासते।
श्रद्धया परयोपेतास्ते मे युक्ततमा मताः ॥२॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: Those who fix their minds on me and worship me, ever disciplined and endowed with supreme faith — them I consider the most deeply disciplined.
explanation: Krishna answers immediately and without hedging. Given a direct choice between the two, he names the one that involves a relationship rather than an absolute.

sanskrit:
ये त्वक्षरमनिर्देश्यमव्यक्तं पर्युपासते।
सर्वत्रगमचिन्त्यं च कूटस्थमचलं ध्रुवम् ॥३॥
translation: But those who worship the imperishable, the indefinable, the unmanifest, the all-pervading, the unthinkable, the unchanging, the immovable, the constant...
explanation: Eight negations in a row, and the accumulation is the argument. Krishna describes the impersonal path by piling up everything that cannot be said about its object.

sanskrit:
संनियम्येन्द्रियग्रामं सर्वत्र समबुद्धयः।
ते प्राप्नुवन्ति मामेव सर्वभूतहिते रताः ॥४॥
translation: ...restraining the whole array of the senses, even-minded everywhere, delighting in the welfare of all beings — they too attain me.
explanation: The verdict is generous. That path does arrive, and Krishna adds that its travellers care for everyone — he will not let the abstract route seem cold or self-absorbed.

sanskrit:
क्लेशोऽधिकतरस्तेषामव्यक्तासक्तचेतसाम्।
अव्यक्ता हि गतिर्दुःखं देहवद्भिरवाप्यते ॥५॥
translation: The difficulty is greater for those whose minds are set on the unmanifest, for the unmanifest goal is reached with pain by those who are embodied.
explanation: The real objection, and it is practical rather than theological. Having a body makes formlessness hard to hold — a limitation of the equipment, not of the path.

sanskrit:
ये तु सर्वाणि कर्माणि मयि संन्यस्य मत्पराः।
अनन्येनैव योगेन मां ध्यायन्त उपासते ॥६॥
translation: But those who, renouncing all actions in me and regarding me as supreme, worship me, meditating on me with undivided yoga...
explanation: The alternative restated, and the crucial word is again ananya, undivided. Krishna asks for exclusivity of attention, a very different demand from intensity, and considerably easier for an ordinary person to attempt.

sanskrit:
तेषामहं समुद्धर्ता मृत्युसंसारसागरात्।
भवामि नचिरात्पार्थ मय्यावेशितचेतसाम् ॥७॥
translation: ...for them I become before long the deliverer from the ocean of death and rebirth, since their thoughts are absorbed in me.
explanation: Krishna casts himself as the one who does the lifting. On the other path the practitioner crosses; here someone reaches down, and that is the whole difference.

sanskrit:
मय्येव मन आधत्स्व मयि बुद्धिं निवेशय।
निवसिष्यसि मय्येव अत ऊर्ध्वं न संशयः ॥८॥
translation: Fix your mind on me alone; let your understanding rest in me. Thereafter you will dwell in me. Of this there is no doubt.
explanation: The instruction at its simplest, addressed to Arjuna directly. What follows is a descending series of alternatives for when this one proves to be too much.

sanskrit:
अथ चित्तं समाधातुं न शक्नोषि मयि स्थिरम्।
अभ्यासयोगेन ततो मामिच्छाप्तुं धनञ्जय ॥९॥
translation: If you are unable to fix your thought steadily upon me, then seek to reach me by the practice of yoga, Dhananjaya.
explanation: The first fallback. Krishna assumes the direct method will fail and offers repetition instead — practice as what you do when concentration is not available.

sanskrit:
अभ्यासेऽप्यसमर्थोऽसि मत्कर्मपरमो भव।
मदर्थमपि कर्माणि कुर्वन् सिद्धिमवाप्स्यसि ॥१०॥
translation: If you are incapable even of practice, be intent on working for me. Even performing actions for my sake, you will attain perfection.
explanation: The second fallback, and it asks nothing of the mind at all. Krishna moves the requirement from attention to activity, which anyone can manage on any day.

sanskrit:
अथैतदप्यशक्तोऽसि कर्तुं मद्योगमाश्रितः।
सर्वकर्मफलत्यागं ततः कुरु यतात्मवान् ॥११॥
translation: And if you are unable to do even this, then, taking refuge in my yoga, renounce the fruit of all action, with the self restrained.
explanation: The last rung, and it is Chapter 2's teaching offered as a minimum. Whatever else fails, one can still stop grasping at outcomes — nothing more is being required.

sanskrit:
श्रेयो हि ज्ञानमभ्यासाज्ज्ञानाद्ध्यानं विशिष्यते।
ध्यानात्कर्मफलत्यागस्त्यागाच्छान्तिरनन्तरम् ॥१२॥
translation: Knowledge is better than practice; meditation is better than knowledge; the renunciation of the fruit of action is better than meditation. Peace follows immediately upon renunciation.
explanation: The ladder is climbed back down in reverse, and the lowest rung turns out to be the highest. Krishna ranks the easiest option first because peace follows it at once.

sanskrit:
अद्वेष्टा सर्वभूतानां मैत्रः करुण एव च।
निर्ममो निरहङ्कारः समदुःखसुखः क्षमी ॥१३॥
translation: One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free of possessiveness and ego, the same in pain and pleasure, patient...
explanation: The famous portrait begins. Note the order — the first quality is an absence of hatred, which is what Arjuna most needed to hear on this particular field.

sanskrit:
सन्तुष्टः सततं योगी यतात्मा दृढनिश्चयः।
मय्यर्पितमनोबुद्धिर्यो मद्भक्तः स मे प्रियः ॥१४॥
translation: ...ever content, disciplined, self-restrained, of firm resolve, with mind and understanding given over to me — that devotee of mine is dear to me.
explanation: The refrain arrives for the first time: dear to me. Krishna is not listing entry requirements but describing people he is fond of, which is a far warmer thing.

sanskrit:
यस्मान्नोद्विजते लोको लोकान्नोद्विजते च यः।
हर्षामर्षभयोद्वेगैर्मुक्तो यः स च मे प्रियः ॥१५॥
translation: One from whom the world does not shrink and who does not shrink from the world, who is free of elation, impatience, fear, and agitation — that one is dear to me.
explanation: A two-way test of ease. Krishna asks not only that a person be undisturbed but that they be undisturbing, which rules out a certain kind of intimidating holiness.

sanskrit:
अनपेक्षः शुचिर्दक्ष उदासीनो गतव्यथः।
सर्वारम्भपरित्यागी यो मद्भक्तः स मे प्रियः ॥१६॥
translation: One who is free of expectation, pure, capable, impartial, untroubled, who has given up all undertakings — that devotee of mine is dear to me.
explanation: Daksha, capable, is a surprise in this company. Krishna wants competence alongside detachment; the person described is useful, not merely serene, and the list would be much weaker without that single word.

sanskrit:
यो न हृष्यति न द्वेष्टि न शोचति न काङ्क्षति।
शुभाशुभपरित्यागी भक्ितमान्यः स मे प्रियः ॥१७॥
translation: One who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has relinquished both good and bad fortune, and who is full of devotion — that one is dear to me.
explanation: Four movements of the heart, renounced in pairs. And again both halves of fortune go together, since Krishna never treats the pleasant one as safe to keep.

sanskrit:
समः शत्रौ च मित्रे च तथा मानापमानयोः।
शीतोष्णसुखदुःखेषु समः सङ्गविवर्जितः ॥१८॥
translation: The same toward enemy and friend, the same in honour and dishonour, the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, free from attachment...
explanation: Enemy and friend heads the list, and it is not an abstract example here. Arjuna is looking at both categories arranged in ranks about a bowshot away.

sanskrit:
तुल्यनिन्दास्तुतिर्मौनी सन्तुष्टो येनकेनचित्।
अनिकेतः स्थिरमतिर्भक्ितमान्मे प्रियो नरः ॥१९॥
translation: ...indifferent to blame and praise, silent, content with anything at all, having no fixed home, of steady mind and full of devotion — that person is dear to me.
explanation: Aniketa, without a home, is the starkest item. Yet it sits beside contentment with anything, suggesting the homelessness is inward rather than a call to wander.

sanskrit:
ये तु धर्म्यामृतमिदं यथोक्तं पर्युपासते।
श्रद्दधाना मत्परमा भक्तास्तेऽतीव मे प्रियाः ॥२०॥
translation: But those who honour this nectar of righteousness as it has been declared, full of faith, holding me as supreme — those devotees are exceedingly dear to me.
explanation: The chapter ends by raising its own refrain one degree: exceedingly dear. And the qualification is only faith, which puts the whole portrait within a beginner's reach.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
प्रकृतिं पुरुषं चैव क्षेत्रं क्षेत्रज्ञमेव च।
एतद्वेदितुमिच्छामि ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं च केशव ॥१॥
translation: Arjuna said: Nature and spirit, the field and the knower of the field, knowledge and the object of knowledge — these I wish to understand, Keshava.
explanation: Arjuna asks for six terms in a single breath. After the vision of Chapter 11 he has returned to being a student, and his questions have become notably precise.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाचइदं शरीरं कौन्तेय क्षेत्रमित्यभिधीयते।
एतद्यो वेत्ति तं प्राहुः क्षेत्रज्ञ इति तद्विदः ॥२॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: This body, Kaunteya, is called the field. One who knows it is called the knower of the field by those who know these things.
explanation: The definition is disarmingly concrete. Krishna begins the most abstract chapter in the Gita by pointing at Arjuna's own body and giving it a name.

sanskrit:
क्षेत्रज्ञं चापि मां विद्धि सर्वक्षेत्रेषु भारत।
क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञयोर्ज्ञानं यत्तज्ज्ञानं मतं मम ॥३॥
translation: Know me also as the knower of the field in all fields, Bharata. The knowledge of the field and of its knower — that I consider to be knowledge.
explanation: The claim that transforms the whole scheme. There is not one knower per body but one knower throughout, which makes every field the same field being watched.

sanskrit:
तत्क्षेत्रं यच्च यादृक् च यद्विकारि यतश्च यत्।
स च यो यत्प्रभावश्च तत्समासेन मे श्रृणु ॥४॥
translation: Hear from me in brief what that field is, what it is like, what its modifications are, from where it comes, and who that knower is and what his powers are.
explanation: A five-part agenda announced before the answer, which is how a careful teacher works. Krishna is organizing material he knows Arjuna is going to find difficult.

sanskrit:
ऋषिभिर्बहुधा गीतं छन्दोभिर्विविधैः पृथक्।
ब्रह्मसूत्रपदैश्चैव हेतुमद्भिर्विनिश्िचतैः ॥५॥
translation: This has been sung by the seers in many ways, in various distinct hymns, and also in the aphorisms about Brahman, well reasoned and conclusive.
explanation: Krishna cites his sources rather than claiming novelty. He has spoken as the ultimate authority for chapters, and here he defers to a tradition of inquiry.

sanskrit:
महाभूतान्यहङ्कारो बुद्धिरव्यक्तमेव च।
इन्द्रियाणि दशैकं च पञ्च चेन्द्रियगोचराः ॥६॥
translation: The great elements, the sense of ego, the understanding, the unmanifest, the ten senses and the one, and the five objects of the senses...
explanation: The inventory of the field begins, and the mind is counted as an organ alongside the ears and hands. Nothing interior is exempt from being listed as equipment.

sanskrit:
इच्छा द्वेषः सुखं दुःखं सङ्घातश्चेतनाधृतिः।
एतत्क्षेत्रं समासेन सविकारमुदाहृतम् ॥७॥
translation: ...desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, awareness, and firmness — this is the field, described in brief together with its modifications.
explanation: The startling inclusion is chetana, awareness. Even consciousness as it is experienced sits inside the field, on the observed side rather than the observing one.

sanskrit:
अमानित्वमदम्भित्वमहिंसा क्षान्तिरार्जवम्।
आचार्योपासनं शौचं स्थैर्यमात्मविनिग्रहः ॥८॥
translation: Humility, absence of pretence, non-violence, patience, uprightness, service of a teacher, purity, steadiness, self-restraint...
explanation: Krishna answers a metaphysical question with a list of virtues. Knowledge is defined here as a way of living, which is not what the question appeared to be asking.

sanskrit:
इन्द्रियार्थेषु वैराग्यमनहङ्कार एव च।
जन्ममृत्युजराव्याधिदुःखदोषानुदर्शनम् ॥९॥
translation: ...dispassion toward the objects of the senses, absence of ego, and keeping in view the pain and evil of birth, death, old age, and disease...
explanation: Anudarshanam, keeping in view, is precise. Not brooding on suffering but refusing to look away from it, which is a discipline rather than a mood.

sanskrit:
असक्ितरनभिष्वङ्गः पुत्रदारगृहादिषु।
नित्यं च समचित्तत्वमिष्टानिष्टोपपत्तिषु ॥१०॥
translation: ...non-attachment, absence of clinging to son, wife, home and the like, and constant evenness of mind toward what is wished for and what is not...
explanation: The specificity stings. Krishna names the household rather than speaking of attachment in general — and it is a household Arjuna is fighting today to secure.

sanskrit:
मयि चानन्ययोगेन भक्ितरव्यभिचारिणी।
विविक्तदेशसेवित्वमरतिर्जनसंसदि ॥११॥
translation: ...unswerving devotion to me with undivided yoga, resorting to solitary places, and taking no delight in crowds of people...
explanation: Devotion appears in the middle of a list of virtues rather than above it. And the preference for solitude is stated as a taste, not as a rule imposed from outside.

sanskrit:
अध्यात्मज्ञाननित्यत्वं तत्त्वज्ञानार्थदर्शनम्।
एतज्ज्ञानमिति प्रोक्तमज्ञानं यदतोन्यथा ॥१२॥
translation: ...constancy in knowledge of the self, and keeping in view the goal of the knowledge of truth — this is declared to be knowledge; whatever is contrary to it is ignorance.
explanation: The list closes with a definition by contrast. Twenty qualities have been named, and Krishna calls the whole cluster knowledge — a character, not a content.

sanskrit:
ज्ञेयं यत्तत्प्रवक्ष्यामि यज्ज्ञात्वाऽमृतमश्नुते।
अनादिमत्परं ब्रह्म न सत्तन्नासदुच्यते ॥१३॥
translation: I shall declare that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality. It is the beginningless supreme Brahman, said to be neither existent nor non-existent.
explanation: The last clause breaks the logic deliberately. Krishna refuses both categories, signalling that ordinary distinctions are about to stop working from here onward, and that the verses following will need to be read differently.

sanskrit:
सर्वतः पाणिपादं तत्सर्वतोऽक्षिशिरोमुखम्।
सर्वतः श्रुतिमल्लोके सर्वमावृत्य तिष्ठति ॥१४॥
translation: With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, with hearing everywhere, it stands enveloping all things in the world.
explanation: The vision of Chapter 11 restated as philosophy. What Arjuna saw and could not bear is here described calmly, in the third person, as a plain fact about reality.

sanskrit:
सर्वेन्द्रियगुणाभासं सर्वेन्द्रियविवर्जितम्।
असक्तं सर्वभृच्चैव निर्गुणं गुणभोक्तृ च ॥१५॥
translation: Shining with the qualities of all the senses, yet free of all the senses; unattached, yet supporting all; without qualities, yet the enjoyer of qualities.
explanation: Three contradictions in a row, each built the same way. Krishna is not being obscure — he is showing that any single statement about this needs its opposite.

sanskrit:
बहिरन्तश्च भूतानामचरं चरमेव च।
सूक्ष्मत्वात्तदविज्ञेयं दूरस्थं चान्तिके च तत् ॥१६॥
translation: It is outside and inside beings, unmoving and also moving. Because of its subtlety it cannot be known. It is far away, and also near.
explanation: Far away and also near is the pair that lands hardest. Distance turns out not to apply, which is why searching in any particular direction always misses.

sanskrit:
अविभक्तं च भूतेषु विभक्तमिव च स्थितम्।
भूतभर्तृ च तज्ज्ञेयं ग्रसिष्णु प्रभविष्णु च ॥१७॥
translation: Undivided, it yet stands as though divided among beings. It is to be known as the sustainer of beings, and as their devourer and their producer.
explanation: As though divided — iva. The appearance of separateness is granted without being conceded, which is this chapter's central move about individual persons, and the reason Arjuna's arithmetic of who kills whom fails.

sanskrit:
ज्योतिषामपि तज्ज्योतिस्तमसः परमुच्यते।
ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं ज्ञानगम्यं हृदि सर्वस्य विष्ठितम् ॥१८॥
translation: It is the light even of lights, and is said to be beyond darkness. It is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the goal of knowledge, seated in the hearts of all.
explanation: The abstraction is brought home in the final phrase. After being described as beyond everything, it is located in the chest of every person listening.

sanskrit:
इति क्षेत्रं तथा ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं चोक्तं समासतः।
मद्भक्त एतद्विज्ञाय मद्भावायोपपद्यते ॥१९॥
translation: Thus the field, knowledge, and the object of knowledge have been briefly described. My devotee, understanding this, becomes fit for my state of being.
explanation: Krishna closes the technical section by tying it back to devotion. Understanding produces fitness rather than achievement, which keeps it from becoming a prize and quietly prevents the chapter from rewarding cleverness.

sanskrit:
प्रकृतिं पुरुषं चैव विद्ध्यनादी उभावपि।
विकारांश्च गुणांश्चैव विद्धि प्रकृतिसंभवान् ॥२०॥
translation: Know that both nature and spirit are without beginning. Know also that the modifications and the qualities are born of nature.
explanation: Two beginningless principles, which means neither produced the other. Krishna sets up a real duality here, and what follows depends on keeping the two apart.

sanskrit:
कार्यकारणकर्तृत्वे हेतुः प्रकृतिरुच्यते।
पुरुषः सुखदुःखानां भोक्तृत्वे हेतुरुच्यते ॥२१॥
translation: Nature is said to be the cause in the production of cause and effect; spirit is said to be the cause in the experiencing of pleasure and pain.
explanation: A clean division of labour. Nature does everything that happens; the spirit does none of it and feels all of it, which is exactly the human predicament described.

sanskrit:
पुरुषः प्रकृतिस्थो हि भुङ्क्ते प्रकृतिजान्गुणान्।
कारणं गुणसङ्गोऽस्य सदसद्योनिजन्मसु ॥२२॥
translation: For the spirit, seated in nature, experiences the qualities born of nature. Attachment to these qualities is the cause of its birth in good and evil wombs.
explanation: The mechanism of rebirth in a single line, and the hinge is attachment. The spirit is not trapped by nature but by its interest in what nature is doing.

sanskrit:
उपद्रष्टाऽनुमन्ता च भर्ता भोक्ता महेश्वरः।
परमात्मेति चाप्युक्तो देहेऽस्मिन्पुरुषः परः ॥२३॥
translation: The supreme spirit in this body is also called the witness, the consenter, the supporter, the experiencer, the great Lord, and the highest self.
explanation: Six names, and the second is the strangest — the one who permits. Something in a person is watching and allowing, without ever once intervening.

sanskrit:
य एवं वेत्ति पुरुषं प्रकृतिं च गुणैःसह।
सर्वथा वर्तमानोऽपि न स भूयोऽभिजायते ॥२४॥
translation: One who thus knows the spirit and nature together with the qualities is not born again, in whatever way he may be living.
explanation: The escape clause returns from Chapter 6, and it is just as generous. Krishna keeps insisting that outward circumstances disqualify no one who has understood.

sanskrit:
ध्यानेनात्मनि पश्यन्ति केचिदात्मानमात्मना।
अन्ये सांख्येन योगेन कर्मयोगेन चापरे ॥२५॥
translation: Some perceive the self in the self by the self through meditation; others by the discipline of knowledge; and others by the discipline of action.
explanation: Three routes named without ranking, right after the most abstract passage in the poem. Krishna keeps reopening the door for temperaments unlike the one described.

sanskrit:
अन्ये त्वेवमजानन्तः श्रुत्वाऽन्येभ्य उपासते।
तेऽपि चातितरन्त्येव मृत्युं श्रुतिपरायणाः ॥२६॥
translation: But others, not knowing this, worship according to what they have heard from others. They too cross beyond death, devoted to what they have heard.
explanation: A fourth route, for those who simply trust what they were told. Krishna grants them the same result, a striking concession in a chapter about knowing.

sanskrit:
यावत्सञ्जायते किञ्चित्सत्त्वं स्थावरजङ्गमम्।
क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञसंयोगात्तद्विद्धि भरतर्षभ ॥२७॥
translation: Whatever being is born, moving or unmoving, know it to arise from the union of the field and the knower of the field, best of the Bharatas.
explanation: Birth is described as a joining rather than a creation. Nothing new appears; two beginningless things come into contact, and a life is what that contact looks like.

sanskrit:
समं सर्वेषु भूतेषु तिष्ठन्तं परमेश्वरम्।
विनश्यत्स्वविनश्यन्तं यः पश्यति स पश्यति ॥२८॥
translation: One who sees the supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings, not perishing when they perish, truly sees.
explanation: The verse that answers Arjuna's morning most directly. What he fears destroying is the perishing part, and Krishna tells him to look at what stands behind it.

sanskrit:
समं पश्यन्हि सर्वत्र समवस्थितमीश्वरम्।
न हिनस्त्यात्मनाऽऽत्मानं ततो याति परां गतिम् ॥२९॥
translation: For seeing the Lord established the same everywhere, one does not injure the self by the self, and thereby reaches the supreme goal.
explanation: The ethical consequence in an unexpected form. Harming another is described as self-injury, which makes non-violence a matter of accuracy rather than of restraint — one need not be forbidden, only able to see.

sanskrit:
प्रकृत्यैव च कर्माणि क्रियमाणानि सर्वशः।
यः पश्यति तथाऽऽत्मानमकर्तारं स पश्यति ॥३०॥
translation: One who sees that actions are performed in every way by nature alone, and that the self is not the doer, truly sees.
explanation: The refrain returns with a different object. Chapter 3 argued for this; here it is something to be seen rather than concluded, which is a considerably higher bar.

sanskrit:
यदा भूतपृथग्भावमेकस्थमनुपश्यति।
तत एव च विस्तारं ब्रह्म सम्पद्यते तदा ॥३१॥
translation: When one perceives the varied existence of beings as resting in one, and their expansion out from that alone, then one attains Brahman.
explanation: Both directions are required — gathering the many into one, and then watching the one spread back out. Neither half by itself counts as the full seeing.

sanskrit:
अनादित्वान्निर्गुणत्वात्परमात्मायमव्ययः।
शरीरस्थोऽपि कौन्तेय न करोति न लिप्यते ॥३२॥
translation: Being beginningless and without qualities, this imperishable supreme self, though dwelling in the body, Kaunteya, neither acts nor is tainted.
explanation: The resident metaphor from Chapter 5 returns. Dwelling in a place is not the same as being answerable for what happens there — that is the whole defence offered.

sanskrit:
यथा सर्वगतं सौक्ष्म्यादाकाशं नोपलिप्यते।
सर्वत्रावस्थितो देहे तथाऽऽत्मा नोपलिप्यते ॥३३॥
translation: As the all-pervading space is not tainted, because of its subtlety, so the self, present everywhere in the body, is not tainted.
explanation: Space is the perfect example because nothing has ever managed to stain it. Everything happens inside it, and it remains exactly what it was before.

sanskrit:
यथा प्रकाशयत्येकः कृत्स्नं लोकमिमं रविः।
क्षेत्रं क्षेत्री तथा कृत्स्नं प्रकाशयति भारत ॥३४॥
translation: As the one sun illumines this whole world, so the possessor of the field illumines the entire field, Bharata.
explanation: A single source lighting everything at once, and doing nothing else. The sun does not participate in what it reveals, which is precisely the point about the knower.

sanskrit:
क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञयोरेवमन्तरं ज्ञानचक्षुषा।
भूतप्रकृतिमोक्षं च ये विदुर्यान्ति ते परम् ॥३५॥
translation: Those who know, through the eye of knowledge, this distinction between the field and the knower of the field, and the liberation of beings from nature, go to the Supreme.
explanation: The chapter ends by naming its own method — an eye of knowledge, a faculty rather than a doctrine. What Krishna gave Arjuna in Chapter 11 has become a way of seeing.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाचपरं भूयः प्रवक्ष्यामि ज्ञानानां ज्ञानमुत्तमम्।
यज्ज्ञात्वा मुनयः सर्वे परां सिद्धिमितो गताः ॥१॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: I shall declare again the supreme knowledge, the best of all knowledge, by knowing which all the sages have gone from here to the highest perfection.
explanation: Krishna begins by citing results rather than credentials. The recommendation is that this teaching has already worked for people, which is a practical kind of authority.

sanskrit:
इदं ज्ञानमुपाश्रित्य मम साधर्म्यमागताः।
सर्गेऽपि नोपजायन्ते प्रलये न व्यथन्ति च ॥२॥
translation: Having resorted to this knowledge and attained likeness to my nature, they are not born at the time of creation and are not disturbed at the dissolution.
explanation: Not disturbed at the dissolution is a remarkable promise. The end of a universe is described as something a person could simply sit through, unbothered.

sanskrit:
मम योनिर्महद्ब्रह्म तस्मिन् गर्भं दधाम्यहम्।
संभवः सर्वभूतानां ततो भवति भारत ॥३॥
translation: My womb is the great Brahman; in it I place the seed. From that comes the birth of all beings, Bharata.
explanation: Krishna divides the act of creation into two roles and takes the smaller one. The vast material is called his womb, and he supplies only the seed.

sanskrit:
सर्वयोनिषु कौन्तेय मूर्तयः सम्भवन्ति याः।
तासां ब्रह्म महद्योनिरहं बीजप्रदः पिता ॥४॥
translation: Whatever forms are produced in all wombs, Kaunteya, the great Brahman is their womb, and I am the father who gives the seed.
explanation: The parental image extended to every birth without exception. Every creature has the same two parents, which quietly dissolves the family distinctions Arjuna is agonizing over.

sanskrit:
सत्त्वं रजस्तम इति गुणाः प्रकृतिसंभवाः।
निबध्नन्ति महाबाहो देहे देहिनमव्ययम् ॥५॥
translation: Purity, passion, and darkness — these qualities born of nature bind the imperishable embodied one in the body, mighty-armed one.
explanation: The subject of the chapter arrives, and note what all three of them do: they bind. Even sattva, the good one, is introduced as a form of restraint.

sanskrit:
तत्र सत्त्वं निर्मलत्वात्प्रकाशकमनामयम्।
सुखसङ्गेन बध्नाति ज्ञानसङ्गेन चानघ ॥६॥
translation: Among these, purity, being untainted, is illuminating and healthy. It binds by attachment to happiness and by attachment to knowledge, sinless one.
explanation: The most disquieting sentence in the chapter. Krishna says goodness binds too, and it binds by attachment to the two things that seem most worth having.

sanskrit:
रजो रागात्मकं विद्धि तृष्णासङ्गसमुद्भवम्।
तन्निबध्नाति कौन्तेय कर्मसङ्गेन देहिनम् ॥७॥
translation: Know passion to be of the nature of craving, arising from thirst and attachment. It binds the embodied one, Kaunteya, by attachment to action.
explanation: Trishna, thirst, is the diagnosis. Passion is described not as energy but as a lack — something in the person is dry, and activity is what it keeps reaching for.

sanskrit:
तमस्त्वज्ञानजं विद्धि मोहनं सर्वदेहिनाम्।
प्रमादालस्यनिद्राभिस्तन्निबध्नाति भारत ॥८॥
translation: Know darkness to be born of ignorance, deluding all embodied beings. It binds by heedlessness, laziness, and sleep, Bharata.
explanation: The three symptoms are unglamorous and familiar. Krishna describes the lowest quality not as wickedness but as fog — inattention, sluggishness, and too much sleep.

sanskrit:
सत्त्वं सुखे सञ्जयति रजः कर्मणि भारत।
ज्ञानमावृत्य तु तमः प्रमादे सञ्जयत्युत ॥९॥
translation: Purity attaches one to happiness, and passion to action, Bharata. But darkness, covering over knowledge, attaches one to heedlessness.
explanation: A summary in one line, and each quality is defined by what it makes a person want. The qualities are not states so much as directions of appetite.

sanskrit:
रजस्तमश्चाभिभूय सत्त्वं भवति भारत।
रजः सत्त्वं तमश्चैव तमः सत्त्वं रजस्तथा ॥१०॥
translation: Purity arises when passion and darkness are overcome, Bharata; passion when purity and darkness are overcome; and darkness when purity and passion are overcome.
explanation: The three are described as competing rather than coexisting. Whichever is currently winning is what a person experiences that day as their own personality, which makes character a weather report rather than a fixed fact.

sanskrit:
सर्वद्वारेषु देहेऽस्मिन्प्रकाश उपजायते।
ज्ञानं यदा तदा विद्याद्विवृद्धं सत्त्वमित्युत ॥११॥
translation: When the light of knowledge shines through all the gates of this body, then it should be known that purity has increased.
explanation: A practical test rather than a definition. Krishna gives Arjuna something observable — a general brightening at every sense door — by which to read his own state.

sanskrit:
लोभः प्रवृत्तिरारम्भः कर्मणामशमः स्पृहा।
रजस्येतानि जायन्ते विवृद्धे भरतर्षभ ॥१२॥
translation: Greed, activity, the undertaking of works, restlessness, and longing arise when passion has increased, best of the Bharatas.
explanation: The list is unflattering to the industrious. Undertaking things and being unable to rest are grouped with greed, as symptoms of one underlying condition, which is an uncomfortable diagnosis for anyone who works hard.

sanskrit:
अप्रकाशोऽप्रवृत्तिश्च प्रमादो मोह एव च।
तमस्येतानि जायन्ते विवृद्धे कुरुनन्दन ॥१३॥
translation: Absence of light, inertia, heedlessness, and delusion arise when darkness has increased, Kurunandana.
explanation: Four signs, and all of them are absences. Krishna characterizes tamas entirely by what is missing, which is exactly why it is so hard to notice from inside.

sanskrit:
यदा सत्त्वे प्रवृद्धे तु प्रलयं याति देहभृत्।
तदोत्तमविदां लोकानमलान्प्रतिपद्यते ॥१४॥
translation: If the embodied one meets dissolution when purity prevails, then he attains the spotless worlds of those who know the highest.
explanation: The chapter joins itself to Chapter 8's concern with the final moment. The quality dominant at death is described as determining where a person goes next.

sanskrit:
रजसि प्रलयं गत्वा कर्मसङ्गिषु जायते।
तथा प्रलीनस्तमसि मूढयोनिषु जायते ॥१५॥
translation: Meeting dissolution in passion, one is born among those attached to action. Likewise, dying in darkness, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.
explanation: The consequences are described as continuations rather than punishments. Each quality delivers a person into more of the same, which is its own kind of justice.

sanskrit:
कर्मणः सुकृतस्याहुः सात्त्विकं निर्मलं फलम्।
रजसस्तु फलं दुःखमज्ञानं तमसः फलम् ॥१६॥
translation: They say the fruit of good action is pure and spotless; but the fruit of passion is pain, and the fruit of darkness is ignorance.
explanation: Three outcomes, and the middle one is the most useful warning. Passion is not punished with failure but with pain, which arrives whether or not the effort succeeds.

sanskrit:
सत्त्वात्सञ्जायते ज्ञानं रजसो लोभ एव च।
प्रमादमोहौ तमसो भवतोऽज्ञानमेव च ॥१७॥
translation: From purity knowledge is born, and from passion greed. Heedlessness and delusion arise from darkness, and ignorance as well.
explanation: The qualities are shown producing offspring. Krishna keeps describing them as generative rather than static, which is why they cannot simply be waited out — each is busy manufacturing the conditions for its own continuation.

sanskrit:
ऊर्ध्वं गच्छन्ति सत्त्वस्था मध्ये तिष्ठन्ति राजसाः।
जघन्यगुणवृत्तिस्था अधो गच्छन्ति तामसाः ॥१८॥
translation: Those established in purity go upward; the passionate remain in the middle; and those of the lowest quality, abiding in its ways, go downward.
explanation: A vertical map drawn in one verse. And the passionate are placed exactly where most people live — in the middle, neither rising nor falling.

sanskrit:
नान्यं गुणेभ्यः कर्तारं यदा द्रष्टानुपश्यति।
गुणेभ्यश्च परं वेत्ति मद्भावं सोऽधिगच्छति ॥१९॥
translation: When the seer perceives no agent other than the qualities, and knows that which is beyond the qualities, he attains my state of being.
explanation: Two perceptions are required, not one. Seeing that the qualities do everything is only half; the other half is knowing that something stands outside them.

sanskrit:
गुणानेतानतीत्य त्रीन्देही देहसमुद्भवान्।
जन्ममृत्युजरादुःखैर्विमुक्तोऽमृतमश्नुते ॥२०॥
translation: Transcending these three qualities, which are the source of the body, the embodied one, freed from birth, death, old age, and sorrow, attains immortality.
explanation: The goal stated plainly at the chapter's midpoint. It prompts Arjuna's question, because describing a destination says nothing about how to recognize arrival, and he has learned by now to ask for signs.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाचकैर्लिंगैस्त्रीन्गुणानेतानतीतो भवति प्रभो।
किमाचारः कथं चैतांस्त्रीन्गुणानतिवर्तते ॥२१॥
translation: Arjuna said: By what signs is one known who has transcended these three qualities, Lord? How does he behave, and how does he pass beyond these three qualities?
