explanation: Arjuna asks the same shape of question he asked in Chapter 2 about the steady sage. He wants observable behaviour, not a definition — his consistent instinct.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाचप्रकाशं च प्रवृत्तिं च मोहमेव च पाण्डव।
न द्वेष्टि सम्प्रवृत्तानि न निवृत्तानि काङ्क्षति ॥२२॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: He does not hate illumination, activity, or delusion when they arise, Pandava, nor does he long for them when they cease.
explanation: The answer begins with what such a person does not do. Even delusion is not hated when it comes, which is a stranger requirement than it first appears.

sanskrit:
उदासीनवदासीनो गुणैर्यो न विचाल्यते।
गुणा वर्तन्त इत्येव योऽवतिष्ठति नेङ्गते ॥२३॥
translation: Seated as though indifferent, he is not disturbed by the qualities. Knowing that it is only the qualities that act, he remains firm and does not waver.
explanation: The same hedged phrase Krishna used of himself in Chapter 9 — as though indifferent. The transcendent person is described in exactly the language used for God.

sanskrit:
समदुःखसुखः स्वस्थः समलोष्टाश्मकाञ्चनः।
तुल्यप्रियाप्रियो धीरस्तुल्यनिन्दात्मसंस्तुतिः ॥२४॥
translation: The same in pain and pleasure, self-reliant, regarding a clod, a stone, and gold alike, the same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, steady, the same under blame and praise...
explanation: The portrait rhymes deliberately with Chapters 2 and 12. Krishna keeps returning to the same handful of tests, as though only a few things were worth checking.

sanskrit:
मानापमानयोस्तुल्यस्तुल्यो मित्रारिपक्षयोः।
सर्वारम्भपरित्यागी गुणातीतः स उच्यते ॥२५॥
translation: ...the same in honour and dishonour, the same toward the parties of friend and foe, renouncing all undertakings — he is said to have transcended the qualities.
explanation: Friend and foe again, and again on a battlefield where both parties are visible. Krishna will not let this ideal stay abstract while Arjuna stands between armies.

sanskrit:
मां च योऽव्यभिचारेण भक्ितयोगेन सेवते।
स गुणान्समतीत्यैतान् ब्रह्मभूयाय कल्पते ॥२६॥
translation: And one who serves me with unswerving devotion, passing beyond these qualities, becomes fit for becoming Brahman.
explanation: The method finally arrives, and it is not effort directed against the qualities. Devotion is offered as the way past a system that cannot be beaten from inside it.

sanskrit:
ब्रह्मणो हि प्रतिष्ठाऽहममृतस्याव्ययस्य च।
शाश्वतस्य च धर्मस्य सुखस्यैकान्तिकस्य च ॥२७॥
translation: For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and imperishable, of eternal righteousness, and of absolute happiness.
explanation: The chapter ends with a structural claim. Krishna places himself beneath the absolute rather than beside it, which is why devotion could carry someone past everything.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाचऊर्ध्वमूलमधःशाखमश्वत्थं प्राहुरव्ययम्।
छन्दांसि यस्य पर्णानि यस्तं वेद स वेदवित् ॥१॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: They speak of an imperishable ashvattha tree with its root above and its branches below, whose leaves are the sacred hymns. One who knows it knows the Veda.
explanation: An upside-down tree, rooted in what cannot be seen. The image says the visible world is the foliage of something growing downward into it, not upward out of it.

sanskrit:
अधश्चोर्ध्वं प्रसृतास्तस्य शाखा     गुणप्रवृद्धा विषयप्रवालाः।
अधश्च मूलान्यनुसन्ततानि     कर्मानुबन्धीनि मनुष्यलोके ॥२॥
translation: Its branches spread below and above, nourished by the qualities, with sense objects for twigs. And below, its roots stretch out, binding to action in the world of men.
explanation: The tree has a second root system growing downward into human activity. Every deed puts out another anchor, which is why the thing proves so hard to shift.

sanskrit:
न रूपमस्येह तथोपलभ्यते    नान्तो न चादिर्न च संप्रतिष्ठा।
अश्वत्थमेनं सुविरूढमूल    मसङ्गशस्त्रेण दृढेन छित्त्वा ॥३॥
translation: Its form is not perceived here in this way — neither its end, nor its beginning, nor its foundation. Having cut this firmly rooted ashvattha with the strong axe of non-attachment...
explanation: The tool is named precisely: asanga, non-attachment, and it is called an axe. Krishna does not ask for the tree to be understood but for it to be felled.

sanskrit:
ततः पदं तत्परिमार्गितव्य    यस्मिन्गता न निवर्तन्ति भूयः।
तमेव चाद्यं पुरुषं प्रपद्ये    यतः प्रवृत्तिः प्रसृता पुराणी ॥४॥
translation: ...one should then seek that place from which, having gone, none return again, thinking: I take refuge in that primal spirit from whom the ancient activity streamed forth.
explanation: Cutting is only the first act; the second is going somewhere. And Krishna supplies the words to think while going, which is unusually practical for this passage.

sanskrit:
निर्मानमोहा जितसङ्गदोषा    अध्यात्मनित्या विनिवृत्तकामाः।
द्वन्द्वैर्विमुक्ताः सुखदुःखसंज्ञै    र्गच्छन्त्यमूढाः पदमव्ययं तत् ॥५॥
translation: Free of pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever dwelling in the self, with desires turned away, released from the dualities known as pleasure and pain — the undeluded reach that imperishable place.
explanation: A short list of who arrives. The one surprise is that pleasure is named a duality to be released from, rather than the reward that waits at the destination.

sanskrit:
न तद्भासयते सूर्यो न शशाङ्को न पावकः।
यद्गत्वा न निवर्तन्ते तद्धाम परमं मम ॥६॥
translation: Neither the sun nor the moon nor fire illumines that place. Having gone there, they do not return. That is my supreme abode.
explanation: The three light sources of the ancient world, all declared unnecessary. What is being described is not a bright place but one with no need of being lit.

sanskrit:
ममैवांशो जीवलोके जीवभूतः सनातनः।
मनःषष्ठानीन्द्रियाणि प्रकृतिस्थानि कर्षति ॥७॥
translation: An eternal fragment of my own self, having become a living being in the world of the living, draws to itself the senses, of which the mind is the sixth, resting in nature.
explanation: The most intimate claim in the Gita. The individual person is not a creature made by God but a piece of him, currently gathering a body around itself.

sanskrit:
शरीरं यदवाप्नोति यच्चाप्युत्क्रामतीश्वरः।
गृहीत्वैतानि संयाति वायुर्गन्धानिवाशयात् ॥८॥
translation: When the lord of the body takes on a body, and when he departs from it, he goes taking these with him, as the wind carries scents away from their places.
explanation: The image is delicate and exact. Something invisible passes through and carries away what was there, leaving the flower behind — a gentle picture of dying.

sanskrit:
श्रोत्रं चक्षुः स्पर्शनं च रसनं घ्राणमेव च।
अधिष्ठाय मनश्चायं विषयानुपसेवते ॥९॥
translation: Presiding over hearing, sight, touch, taste, and smell, and over the mind as well, he experiences the objects of sense.
explanation: The senses are described as posts he presides over rather than parts he consists of. The distinction from Chapter 13 is restated here in the language of office.

sanskrit:
उत्क्रामन्तं स्थितं वापि भुञ्जानं वा गुणान्वितम्।
विमूढा नानुपश्यन्ति पश्यन्ति ज्ञानचक्षुषः ॥१०॥
translation: The deluded do not perceive him departing, or remaining, or experiencing while joined with the qualities. Those with the eye of knowledge perceive him.
explanation: Three moments named — leaving, staying, enjoying — and all of them missed. What is invisible is not hidden away somewhere but present in what is already happening.

sanskrit:
यतन्तो योगिनश्चैनं पश्यन्त्यात्मन्यवस्थितम्।
यतन्तोऽप्यकृतात्मानो नैनं पश्यन्त्यचेतसः ॥११॥
translation: The yogins who strive perceive him seated in the self. But those who have not perfected themselves, though striving, do not perceive him, being without discernment.
explanation: Both groups are striving, and only one succeeds. Krishna is candid that effort alone does not settle the matter, consistent with everything he says about grace.

sanskrit:
यदादित्यगतं तेजो जगद्भासयतेऽखिलम्।
यच्चन्द्रमसि यच्चाग्नौ तत्तेजो विद्धि मामकम् ॥१२॥
translation: The radiance that resides in the sun and illumines the whole world, and that which is in the moon and in fire — know that radiance to be mine.
explanation: Krishna gathers the three lights he dismissed earlier and claims them. What was unnecessary at the destination turns out to be his own, lent out to the journey.

sanskrit:
गामाविश्य च भूतानि धारयाम्यहमोजसा।
पुष्णामि चौषधीः सर्वाः सोमो भूत्वा रसात्मकः ॥१३॥
translation: And entering the earth, I support all beings with my energy. Becoming the sappy moon, I nourish all the plants.
explanation: The claim becomes agricultural. Krishna describes himself doing the slow, unglamorous work of holding up soil and swelling fruit — a long way from Chapter 11.

sanskrit:
अहं वैश्वानरो भूत्वा प्राणिनां देहमाश्रितः।
प्राणापानसमायुक्तः पचाम्यन्नं चतुर्विधम् ॥१४॥
translation: Becoming the digestive fire, I dwell in the bodies of living beings and, joined with the incoming and outgoing breaths, digest the four kinds of food.
explanation: The divine located in the stomach. After the vision of universal fire, Krishna's example of his own presence is the ordinary heat that breaks down a meal.

sanskrit:
सर्वस्य चाहं हृदि सन्निविष्टो    मत्तः स्मृतिर्ज्ञानमपोहनं च।
वेदैश्च सर्वैरहमेव वेद्यो    वेदान्तकृद्वेदविदेव चाहम् ॥१५॥
translation: And I am seated in the hearts of all. From me come memory, knowledge, and their loss. I alone am to be known by all the Vedas. I am the author of the Vedanta and the knower of the Veda.
explanation: The startling item is apohanam, forgetting. Krishna claims responsibility not only for what people know but for what quietly falls out of their minds, which makes forgetting something done rather than something failed.

sanskrit:
द्वाविमौ पुरुषौ लोके क्षरश्चाक्षर एव च।
क्षरः सर्वाणि भूतानि कूटस्थोऽक्षर उच्यते ॥१६॥
translation: There are these two spirits in the world, the perishable and the imperishable. The perishable is all beings; the unchanging is called the imperishable.
explanation: A clean two-part division offered as a summary of everything so far. It is set up carefully, because the next verse is about to add a third term to it.

sanskrit:
उत्तमः पुरुषस्त्वन्यः परमात्मेत्युदाहृतः।
यो लोकत्रयमाविश्य बिभर्त्यव्यय ईश्वरः ॥१७॥
translation: But the highest spirit is another, called the supreme self — the imperishable Lord who, entering the three worlds, sustains them.
explanation: The third term breaks the tidy pair. Krishna refuses to be identified with either the changing world or the changeless absolute, claiming a position above both.

sanskrit:
यस्मात्क्षरमतीतोऽहमक्षरादपि चोत्तमः।
अतोऽस्मि लोके वेदे च प्रथितः पुरुषोत्तमः ॥१८॥
translation: Since I transcend the perishable and am higher even than the imperishable, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the supreme spirit.
explanation: The title Purushottama is explained rather than asserted. Krishna derives his own name from the structure he has just laid out — a very deliberate piece of teaching.

sanskrit:
यो मामेवमसम्मूढो जानाति पुरुषोत्तमम्।
स सर्वविद्भजति मां सर्वभावेन भारत ॥१९॥
translation: One who, undeluded, knows me thus as the supreme spirit knows all, and worships me with his whole being, Bharata.
explanation: Worship with the whole being is the phrase that matters. Krishna asks not for the highest kind of devotion but for all of it, whatever kind a person happens to have.

sanskrit:
इति गुह्यतमं शास्त्रमिदमुक्तं मयाऽनघ।
एतद्बुद्ध्वा बुद्धिमान्स्यात्कृतकृत्यश्च भारत ॥२०॥
translation: Thus this most secret teaching has been declared by me, sinless one. Understanding this, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that is to be done, Bharata.
explanation: A short chapter ends with an unusually complete claim. Having done what was to be done is the closest the Gita comes to saying that the work is finished.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
अभयं सत्त्वसंशुद्धिः ज्ञानयोगव्यवस्थितिः।
दानं दमश्च यज्ञश्च स्वाध्यायस्तप आर्जवम् ॥१॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, generosity, self-control, sacrifice, study of scripture, austerity, uprightness...
explanation: The list opens with fearlessness, a pointed first word for a man who lost his nerve this morning. Everything else in the divine inventory follows on from it.

sanskrit:
अहिंसा सत्यमक्रोधस्त्यागः शान्तिरपैशुनम्।
दया भूतेष्वलोलुप्त्वं मार्दवं ह्रीरचापलम् ॥२॥
translation: ...non-violence, truth, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquillity, absence of slander, compassion toward beings, absence of greed, gentleness, modesty, absence of fickleness...
explanation: The virtues here are social rather than heroic. Not slandering people and being gentle with them sit among the highest qualities Krishna is able to name.

sanskrit:
तेजः क्षमा धृतिः शौचमद्रोहो नातिमानिता।
भवन्ति सम्पदं दैवीमभिजातस्य भारत ॥३॥
translation: ...vigour, patience, firmness, purity, freedom from malice, absence of excessive pride — these belong to one born to a divine destiny, Bharata.
explanation: The list ends with two absences and a curious pairing: tejas, vigour, set beside patience. Krishna's ideal is forceful and forbearing at the same time.

sanskrit:
दम्भो दर्पोऽभिमानश्च क्रोधः पारुष्यमेव च।
अज्ञानं चाभिजातस्य पार्थ सम्पदमासुरीम् ॥४॥
translation: Pretence, arrogance, self-importance, anger, harshness, and ignorance belong to one born to a demonic destiny, Partha.
explanation: Six items answer twenty-six, which is telling. The demonic inventory is short because it is repetitive — nearly all of it is some version of self-inflation.

sanskrit:
दैवी सम्पद्विमोक्षाय निबन्धायासुरी मता।
मा शुचः सम्पदं दैवीमभिजातोऽसि पाण्डव ॥५॥
translation: The divine destiny leads to liberation, the demonic to bondage. Do not grieve; you are born to a divine destiny, Pandava.
explanation: A moment of pure reassurance. Krishna interrupts his own analysis to tell Arjuna, who has spent the day doubting his own goodness, which category he belongs to.

sanskrit:
द्वौ भूतसर्गौ लोकेऽस्मिन् दैव आसुर एव च।
दैवो विस्तरशः प्रोक्त आसुरं पार्थ मे श्रृणु ॥६॥
translation: There are two kinds of created beings in this world, the divine and the demonic. The divine has been described at length; hear from me now of the demonic, Partha.
explanation: Krishna announces that the unpleasant half is coming. The chapter has spent five verses on virtue and will spend eighteen on its opposite, which is worth noticing.

sanskrit:
प्रवृत्तिं च निवृत्तिं च जना न विदुरासुराः।
न शौचं नापि चाचारो न सत्यं तेषु विद्यते ॥७॥
translation: Demonic people do not know what should be done or what should be refrained from. Neither purity nor good conduct nor truth is found in them.
explanation: The defining failure is not cruelty but a broken compass. Krishna begins the portrait with an inability to tell action from inaction — a problem of knowledge.

sanskrit:
असत्यमप्रतिष्ठं ते जगदाहुरनीश्वरम्।
अपरस्परसम्भूतं किमन्यत्कामहैतुकम् ॥८॥
translation: They say the world is without truth, without foundation, without a Lord; that it arose from mutual union, and that its cause is nothing but desire.
explanation: A philosophical position stated fairly before being rejected. Krishna's objection is not to the argument itself but to what living inside it does to a person.

sanskrit:
एतां दृष्टिमवष्टभ्य नष्टात्मानोऽल्पबुद्धयः।
प्रभवन्त्युग्रकर्माणः क्षयाय जगतोऽहिताः ॥९॥
translation: Holding to this view, these lost souls of small understanding come forth as enemies of the world, doing terrible deeds for its destruction.
explanation: The consequence traced from the premise. Krishna's claim is that a world held to be without meaning eventually gets treated as a world without limits.

sanskrit:
काममाश्रित्य दुष्पूरं दम्भमानमदान्विताः।
मोहाद्गृहीत्वासद्ग्राहान्प्रवर्तन्तेऽशुचिव्रताः ॥१०॥
translation: Clinging to insatiable desire, filled with pretence, pride, and arrogance, holding false views through delusion, they act with impure resolve.
explanation: Insatiable is the operative word again. Krishna keeps identifying the demonic not by what it wants but by the fact that getting it never once helps.

sanskrit:
चिन्तामपरिमेयां च प्रलयान्तामुपाश्रिताः।
कामोपभोगपरमा एतावदिति निश्िचताः ॥११॥
translation: Beset by immeasurable anxiety ending only in death, holding that the enjoyment of desires is the highest thing, convinced that this is all there is...
explanation: The most sympathetic verse in the passage. Krishna describes not villains enjoying themselves but people carrying unmeasurable worry until the day they die, which reads far closer to a diagnosis than a condemnation.

sanskrit:
आशापाशशतैर्बद्धाः कामक्रोधपरायणाः।
ईहन्ते कामभोगार्थमन्यायेनार्थसञ्चयान् ॥१२॥
translation: ...bound by a hundred nooses of hope, given over to desire and anger, they seek to accumulate wealth by unjust means for the enjoyment of desires.
explanation: A hundred nooses of hope is a devastating phrase. Hope is named as the binding agent, which turns the ordinary engine of ambition into a kind of trap.

sanskrit:
इदमद्य मया लब्धमिमं प्राप्स्ये मनोरथम्।
इदमस्तीदमपि मे भविष्यति पुनर्धनम् ॥१३॥
translation: They think: This I have gained today, and that longing I shall fulfil. This wealth is mine, and that too shall be mine hereafter.
explanation: Krishna switches into the first person and lets such a man speak for himself. The interior monologue is more damning than any description of him could be.

sanskrit:
असौ मया हतः शत्रुर्हनिष्ये चापरानपि।
ईश्वरोऽहमहं भोगी सिद्धोऽहं बलवान्सुखी ॥१४॥
translation: That enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay others too. I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful, and happy.
explanation: A boast about killing enemies, spoken on a battlefield to a man deciding whether to kill his. Krishna is holding up a mirror he expects Arjuna to recognize.

sanskrit:
आढ्योऽभिजनवानस्मि कोऽन्योऽस्ति सदृशो मया।
यक्ष्ये दास्यामि मोदिष्य इत्यज्ञानविमोहिताः ॥१५॥
translation: I am rich and of noble birth. Who else is equal to me? I shall sacrifice, I shall give, I shall rejoice — so they say, deluded by ignorance.
explanation: Even the religious acts have become boasts. Sacrifice and generosity appear in the monologue as further proofs of standing, which is exactly what ruins them.

sanskrit:
अनेकचित्तविभ्रान्ता मोहजालसमावृताः।
प्रसक्ताः कामभोगेषु पतन्ति नरकेऽशुचौ ॥१६॥
translation: Bewildered by many thoughts, caught in the net of delusion, addicted to the enjoyment of desires, they fall into a foul hell.
explanation: The monologue ends and the verdict lands. Note that the first symptom is being bewildered by many thoughts — the same many-branched mind from Chapter 2.

sanskrit:
आत्मसम्भाविताः स्तब्धा धनमानमदान्विताः।
यजन्ते नामयज्ञैस्ते दम्भेनाविधिपूर्वकम् ॥१७॥
translation: Self-important, stubborn, filled with the pride and arrogance of wealth, they perform sacrifices in name only, with pretence and contrary to the rules.
explanation: Sacrifice in name only is a precise charge. The forms are all correct and nothing whatever is being offered, which for Krishna makes it no sacrifice at all.

sanskrit:
अहङ्कारं बलं दर्पं कामं क्रोधं च संश्रिताः।
मामात्मपरदेहेषु प्रद्विषन्तोऽभ्यसूयकाः ॥१८॥
translation: Given over to egotism, force, insolence, desire, and anger, these malicious people hate me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others.
explanation: The strangest accusation in the chapter, and the deepest. Contempt for others is described as contempt for God, located inside the very people being despised.

sanskrit:
तानहं द्विषतः क्रूरान्संसारेषु नराधमान्।
क्षिपाम्यजस्रमशुभानासुरीष्वेव योनिषु ॥१९॥
translation: These hateful and cruel men, the lowest of humankind, I cast perpetually into demonic wombs in the cycles of rebirth.
explanation: The harshest verse Krishna speaks. It sits oddly beside Chapter 9's promise that no devotee is ever lost, and the two are best held together rather than reconciled.

sanskrit:
असुरीं योनिमापन्ना मूढा जन्मनि जन्मनि।
मामप्राप्यैव कौन्तेय ततो यान्त्यधमां गतिम् ॥२०॥
translation: Fallen into demonic wombs birth after birth, the deluded, never reaching me, Kaunteya, go from there to the lowest state.
explanation: The mechanism is self-reinforcing: each such birth makes the next likelier. What sounds like punishment is described as momentum with nothing to interrupt it, which is bleaker than a sentence that would eventually end.

sanskrit:
त्रिविधं नरकस्येदं द्वारं नाशनमात्मनः।
कामः क्रोधस्तथा लोभस्तस्मादेतत्त्रयं त्यजेत् ॥२१॥
translation: Threefold is this gate of hell, destroying the self — desire, anger, and greed. Therefore one should abandon these three.
explanation: The whole grim analysis compressed into three words. Krishna hands Arjuna something manageable after eighteen verses of description, which is a real mercy — and a reminder that the chapter had a practical purpose.

sanskrit:
एतैर्विमुक्तः कौन्तेय तमोद्वारैस्त्रिभिर्नरः।
आचरत्यात्मनः श्रेयस्ततो याति परां गतिम् ॥२२॥
translation: Released from these three gates of darkness, Kaunteya, a person works for the good of his own self and thereby reaches the supreme goal.
explanation: The exit is stated immediately after the entrance. Krishna never leaves a diagnosis without a remedy, and here the remedy is simply not walking through those doors.

sanskrit:
यः शास्त्रविधिमुत्सृज्य वर्तते कामकारतः।
न स सिद्धिमवाप्नोति न सुखं न परां गतिम् ॥२३॥
translation: One who abandons the injunctions of scripture and acts under the impulse of desire attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.
explanation: A rare appeal to external authority. After fifteen chapters on inner transformation, Krishna concedes that a person needs a standard outside their own wanting, since wanting is precisely the faculty under suspicion.

sanskrit:
तस्माच्छास्त्रं प्रमाणं ते कार्याकार्यव्यवस्थितौ।
ज्ञात्वा शास्त्रविधानोक्तं कर्म कर्तुमिहार्हसि ॥२४॥
translation: Therefore let scripture be your authority in determining what should and should not be done. Knowing what is declared by the rules of scripture, you should act here.
explanation: The chapter ends with a plain instruction, and it produces Arjuna's next question. The word shastra becomes the hinge on which the following chapter opens.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाचये शास्त्रविधिमुत्सृज्य यजन्ते श्रद्धयाऽन्विताः।
तेषां निष्ठा तु का कृष्ण सत्त्वमाहो रजस्तमः ॥१॥
translation: Arjuna said: Those who sacrifice with faith but set aside the injunctions of scripture — what is their condition, Krishna? Is it purity, passion, or darkness?
explanation: A precise follow-up to the last verse of Chapter 16. Arjuna has spotted the gap: what about sincere people whose practice does not match the rulebook?

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाचत्रिविधा भवति श्रद्धा देहिनां सा स्वभावजा।
सात्त्विकी राजसी चैव तामसी चेति तां श्रृणु ॥२॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: The faith of embodied beings is of three kinds, born of their own nature — pure, passionate, and dark. Hear now about it.
explanation: Krishna's answer relocates the question. Faith is not measured against scripture but sorted by the quality of the person holding it, which is a far better test.

sanskrit:
सत्त्वानुरूपा सर्वस्य श्रद्धा भवति भारत।
श्रद्धामयोऽयं पुरुषो यो यच्छ्रद्धः स एव सः ॥३॥
translation: The faith of each accords with his essential nature, Bharata. A person is made of faith. Whatever his faith is, that indeed is what he is.
explanation: One of the most quoted lines in the Gita, and among the most searching. Krishna makes faith constitutive — not something a person has but what they consist of.

sanskrit:
यजन्ते सात्त्विका देवान्यक्षरक्षांसि राजसाः।
प्रेतान्भूतगणांश्चान्ये यजन्ते तामसा जनाः ॥४॥
translation: Those of purity worship the gods; those of passion worship yakshas and rakshasas; and other people, those of darkness, worship ghosts and the hosts of spirits.
explanation: The taxonomy is applied to worship first. Krishna notices that what people find worth bowing to is a reliable report on what they themselves are made of.

sanskrit:
अशास्त्रविहितं घोरं तप्यन्ते ये तपो जनाः।
दम्भाहङ्कारसंयुक्ताः कामरागबलान्विताः ॥५॥
translation: Those who practise severe austerities not prescribed by scripture, full of pretence and egotism, driven by the force of desire and attachment...
explanation: The critique of extreme austerity begins, and note the motives named. What looks like renunciation is being driven by desire — the very thing it claims to defeat.

sanskrit:
कर्षयन्तः शरीरस्थं भूतग्राममचेतसः।
मां चैवान्तःशरीरस्थं तान्विद्ध्यासुरनिश्चयान् ॥६॥
translation: ...senselessly torturing the collection of elements in the body, and me who dwell within the body — know them to be of demonic resolve.
explanation: The argument against self-torture is theological. Krishna says he is in there too, which makes harsh asceticism an assault on the divine rather than an offering.

sanskrit:
आहारस्त्वपि सर्वस्य त्रिविधो भवति प्रियः।
यज्ञस्तपस्तथा दानं तेषां भेदमिमं श्रृणु ॥७॥
translation: The food that is dear to each is also of three kinds, and so are sacrifice, austerity, and giving. Hear now the distinction between them.
explanation: The threefold analysis is about to reach the dinner table. Krishna moves from cosmology to diet without changing register, which is characteristic of this chapter.

sanskrit:
आयुःसत्त्वबलारोग्यसुखप्रीतिविवर्धनाः।
रस्याः स्निग्धाः स्थिरा हृद्या आहाराः सात्त्विकप्रियाः ॥८॥
translation: Foods that increase life, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and cheer, and that are savoury, smooth, substantial, and agreeable, are dear to the pure.
explanation: The pure diet is not austere at all. Krishna's list is full of pleasure — tasty, rich, satisfying — which rules out any idea that goodness means eating joylessly.

sanskrit:
कट्वम्ललवणात्युष्णतीक्ष्णरूक्षविदाहिनः।
आहारा राजसस्येष्टा दुःखशोकामयप्रदाः ॥९॥
translation: Foods that are bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent, dry, and burning are liked by the passionate, and they produce pain, grief, and sickness.
explanation: The passionate palate wants intensity. Krishna's objection is consequential rather than moral: such food delivers exactly the agitation the person was already in, so the appetite keeps feeding the state that produced it.

sanskrit:
यातयामं गतरसं पूति पर्युषितं च यत्।
उच्छिष्टमपि चामेध्यं भोजनं तामसप्रियम् ॥१०॥
translation: Food that is stale, tasteless, putrid, left overnight, leftover, and unclean is dear to those in darkness.
explanation: The list is unpleasant and precise. What is being described is not poverty but indifference — someone who has stopped noticing what they put in their mouth.

sanskrit:
अफलाकाङ्क्षिभिर्यज्ञो विधिदृष्टो य इज्यते।
यष्टव्यमेवेति मनः समाधाय स सात्त्विकः ॥११॥
translation: That sacrifice is pure which is offered according to the rules by those who desire no fruit, with the mind concentrated on the thought that it simply must be offered.
explanation: The purest motive turns out to be almost tautological — it should be done, so it is done. No reason beyond the fittingness of the act itself is permitted.

sanskrit:
अभिसंधाय तु फलं दम्भार्थमपि चैव यत्।
इज्यते भरतश्रेष्ठ तं यज्ञं विद्धि राजसम् ॥१२॥
translation: But that sacrifice which is offered with an eye to its fruit, and for the sake of display, know to be passionate, best of the Bharatas.
explanation: Two motives named together: results, and being seen. Krishna treats the desire for an audience as the same category of error as the desire for a reward.

sanskrit:
विधिहीनमसृष्टान्नं मन्त्रहीनमदक्षिणम्।
श्रद्धाविरहितं यज्ञं तामसं परिचक्षते ॥१३॥
translation: The sacrifice that is contrary to the rules, in which no food is distributed, that is without sacred words, without gifts to the priests, and devoid of faith, is called dark.
explanation: Four procedural failures and one that matters far more. The absent food is the telling detail — a sacrifice that feeds nobody has missed the point of sacrifice.

sanskrit:
देवद्विजगुरुप्राज्ञपूजनं शौचमार्जवम्।
ब्रह्मचर्यमहिंसा च शारीरं तप उच्यते ॥१४॥
translation: Reverence for the gods, the twice-born, teachers, and the wise; purity, uprightness, continence, and non-violence — this is called austerity of the body.
explanation: Austerity is redefined before it is graded. Krishna's bodily tapas involves no suffering at all, only cleanliness, honesty, and treating people with respect, which removes self-punishment from the category entirely.

sanskrit:
अनुद्वेगकरं वाक्यं सत्यं प्रियहितं च यत्।
स्वाध्यायाभ्यसनं चैव वाङ्मयं तप उच्यते ॥१५॥
translation: Speech that causes no distress, that is true, agreeable, and beneficial, and the regular practice of study — this is called austerity of speech.
explanation: Four conditions on speech, and they are hard to satisfy together. True, kind, and useful at once is a much narrower gate than merely telling the truth.

sanskrit:
मनःप्रसादः सौम्यत्वं मौनमात्मविनिग्रहः।
भावसंशुद्धिरित्येतत्तपो मानसमुच्यते ॥१६॥
translation: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, and purity of being — this is called austerity of the mind.
explanation: Gentleness appears again — the same word Sanjaya used for Krishna's returning face in Chapter 11. Mental austerity is described as softening rather than hardening, which is the opposite of what the word usually suggests.

sanskrit:
श्रद्धया परया तप्तं तपस्तत्ित्रविधं नरैः।
अफलाकाङ्क्षिभिर्युक्तैः सात्त्विकं परिचक्षते ॥१७॥
translation: This threefold austerity, practised with the highest faith by disciplined people who desire no fruit, is called pure.
explanation: The three austerities are gathered and then qualified by motive. As always, the category is decided not by the act performed but by what was wanted from it.

sanskrit:
सत्कारमानपूजार्थं तपो दम्भेन चैव यत्।
क्रियते तदिह प्रोक्तं राजसं चलमध्रुवम् ॥१८॥
translation: That austerity which is performed for the sake of respect, honour, and reverence, and with pretence, is called passionate here — unsteady and impermanent.
explanation: The verdict includes a prediction. Austerity performed for admiration is not merely wrong but unstable, since it lasts only as long as someone is watching.

sanskrit:
मूढग्राहेणात्मनो यत्पीडया क्रियते तपः।
परस्योत्सादनार्थं वा तत्तामसमुदाहृतम् ॥१९॥
translation: That austerity which is performed with deluded notions, with self-torture, or for the purpose of destroying another, is declared to be dark.
explanation: Two very different failures in one verse. Hurting oneself and hurting someone else are placed in the same category, since both mistake damage for discipline.

sanskrit:
दातव्यमिति यद्दानं दीयतेऽनुपकारिणे।
देशे काले च पात्रे च तद्दानं सात्त्विकं स्मृतम् ॥२०॥
translation: That gift which is given because it ought to be given, to one who does no service in return, in the right place and time and to a worthy person, is held to be pure.
explanation: The condition that matters is the second: given to someone who cannot repay. Krishna quietly rules the entire economy of favours out of counting as generosity.

sanskrit:
यत्तु प्रत्युपकारार्थं फलमुद्दिश्य वा पुनः।
दीयते च परिक्लिष्टं तद्दानं राजसं स्मृतम् ॥२१॥
translation: But that which is given for the sake of a return, or with an eye to the fruit, or grudgingly, is held to be passionate.
explanation: Three ways to spoil a gift, and the last is the most familiar. Giving while resenting it is placed alongside giving in the expectation of being paid back.

sanskrit:
अदेशकाले यद्दानमपात्रेभ्यश्च दीयते।
असत्कृतमवज्ञातं तत्तामसमुदाहृतम् ॥२२॥
translation: That gift which is given at the wrong place and time, to unworthy persons, without respect, or with contempt, is declared to be dark.
explanation: Contempt is the decisive word. A gift given while despising the recipient is worse than no gift, since it delivers humiliation along with the goods.

sanskrit:
तत्सदिति निर्देशो ब्रह्मणस्त्रिविधः स्मृतः।
ब्राह्मणास्तेन वेदाश्च यज्ञाश्च विहिताः पुरा ॥२३॥
translation: Om Tat Sat — this is remembered as the threefold designation of Brahman. By that were ordained of old the brahmanas, the Vedas, and the sacrifices.
explanation: Three syllables introduced as the oldest formula there is. Krishna is about to use them to place every act discussed in this chapter under a single heading.

sanskrit:
तस्मादोमित्युदाहृत्य यज्ञदानतपःक्रियाः।
प्रवर्तन्ते विधानोक्ताः सततं ब्रह्मवादिनाम् ॥२४॥
translation: Therefore, with the utterance of Om, the acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity as laid down in the rules are always begun by those who speak of Brahman.
explanation: The first syllable governs beginnings. Krishna gives the chapter's whole list of activities a common opening word, dedicating them before they even start, so that the intention is settled before the act is.

sanskrit:
तदित्यनभिसन्धाय फलं यज्ञतपःक्रियाः।
दानक्रियाश्च विविधाः क्रियन्ते मोक्षकाङ्क्षि ॥२५॥
translation: With the word Tat, and without aiming at fruit, the various acts of sacrifice, austerity, and giving are performed by those who desire liberation.
explanation: Tat simply means that — a word pointing away from the speaker. Saying it while acting is a small linguistic act of handing the deed over to something else.

sanskrit:
सद्भावे साधुभावे च सदित्येतत्प्रयुज्यते।
प्रशस्ते कर्मणि तथा सच्छब्दः पार्थ युज्यते ॥२६॥
translation: The word Sat is used in the sense of reality and of goodness. And the word Sat is likewise applied to an auspicious act, Partha.
explanation: Sat means both what is real and what is good, and Krishna does not separate the two senses. Goodness is presented as a species of existing rather than a rule.

sanskrit:
यज्ञे तपसि दाने च स्थितिः सदिति चोच्यते।
कर्म चैव तदर्थीयं सदित्येवाभिधीयते ॥२७॥
translation: Steadfastness in sacrifice, in austerity, and in giving is also called Sat. And action for the sake of that is likewise called Sat.
explanation: Persistence gets its own designation. Krishna singles out staying with a practice as itself real and good, quite apart from whatever the practice accomplishes, which is a generous thing to say to a beginner.

sanskrit:
अश्रद्धया हुतं दत्तं तपस्तप्तं कृतं च यत्।
असदित्युच्यते पार्थ न च तत्प्रेत्य नो इह ॥२८॥
translation: Whatever is offered, given, or performed as austerity, and whatever is done without faith, is called Asat, Partha. It is nothing, here or hereafter.
explanation: The chapter closes where it opened, on faith. Everything correct can be present and the act still counts for nothing, which answers Arjuna's question completely.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच
संन्यासस्य महाबाहो तत्त्वमिच्छामि वेदितुम्।
त्यागस्य च हृषीकेश पृथक्केशिनिषूदन ॥१॥
translation: Arjuna said: I wish to know the truth about renunciation, mighty-armed one, and about relinquishment separately, Hrishikesha, slayer of Keshi.
explanation: Arjuna's final question returns to the confusion he raised in Chapter 5. Eighteen chapters on, he still wants these two words carefully told apart, and Krishna answers without any hint of impatience.

sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच
काम्यानां कर्मणां न्यासं संन्यासं कवयो विदुः।
सर्वकर्मफलत्यागं प्राहुस्त्यागं विचक्षणाः ॥२॥
translation: The Blessed Lord said: The sages understand renunciation to be the giving up of actions done from desire. The discerning call the abandonment of the fruit of all actions relinquishment.
explanation: A clean distinction at last. Renunciation drops certain actions; relinquishment keeps every action and drops only the appetite for what they produce, and it is the second that Krishna has been teaching throughout.

sanskrit:
त्याज्यं दोषवदित्येके कर्म प्राहुर्मनीषिणः।
यज्ञदानतपःकर्म न त्याज्यमिति चापरे ॥३॥
translation: Some thinkers say that action should be given up as an evil; others say that acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity should not be given up.
explanation: Krishna states the debate before entering it. He has strong views and still lays out the rival positions fairly, which has been his method throughout.

sanskrit:
निश्चयं श्रृणु मे तत्र त्यागे भरतसत्तम।
त्यागो हि पुरुषव्याघ्र त्रिविधः संप्रकीर्तितः ॥४॥
translation: Hear my conclusion in this matter of relinquishment, best of the Bharatas. Relinquishment, tiger among men, is declared to be of three kinds.
explanation: The threefold analysis of Chapter 17 is about to be applied one last time. Krishna adds no new material now; he is sorting what Arjuna already has.

sanskrit:
यज्ञदानतपःकर्म न त्याज्यं कार्यमेव तत्।
यज्ञो दानं तपश्चैव पावनानि मनीषिणाम् ॥५॥
translation: Acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity should not be given up, but should indeed be performed. Sacrifice, giving, and austerity are purifiers of the wise.
explanation: Krishna sides against the renouncers, and note the reason — these acts purify the one who performs them, so abandoning them costs the practitioner rather than anyone else, which reframes the whole debate.

sanskrit:
एतान्यपि तु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा फलानि च।
कर्तव्यानीति मे पार्थ निश्िचतं मतमुत्तमम् ॥६॥
translation: But even these actions should be performed while abandoning attachment and the fruits. This is my definite and highest view, Partha.
explanation: The qualification that saves the previous verse from being mere piety. Krishna endorses the acts and strips out the reason most people perform them, leaving the practice intact and its usual motive gone.

sanskrit:
नियतस्य तु संन्यासः कर्मणो नोपपद्यते।
मोहात्तस्य परित्यागस्तामसः परिकीर्तितः ॥७॥
translation: The renunciation of an obligatory action is not proper. Its abandonment through delusion is declared to be of the nature of darkness.
explanation: The first of three kinds, aimed squarely at Arjuna's morning. Walking off this field would have been tamas dressed up as conscience, and Krishna names it as such without softening the judgement.

sanskrit:
दुःखमित्येव यत्कर्म कायक्लेशभयात्त्यजेत्।
स कृत्वा राजसं त्यागं नैव त्यागफलं लभेत् ॥८॥
translation: One who abandons an action because it is painful, from fear of bodily trouble, performs a passionate relinquishment and does not obtain its fruit.
explanation: The second kind, and the diagnosis is unsparing. Quitting because something is hard is called passion rather than wisdom, and it earns nothing at all.

sanskrit:
कार्यमित्येव यत्कर्म नियतं क्रियतेऽर्जुन।
सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा फलं चैव स त्यागः सात्त्विको मतः ॥९॥
translation: But when an obligatory action is performed simply because it ought to be done, Arjuna, abandoning attachment and the fruit — that relinquishment is held to be pure.
explanation: The third kind, and it is the whole Gita in one sentence. The action stays, the duty stays, and only the private stake in the outcome is removed.

sanskrit:
न द्वेष्ट्यकुशलं कर्म कुशले नानुषज्जते।
त्यागी सत्त्वसमाविष्टो मेधावी छिन्नसंशयः ॥१०॥
translation: The relinquisher who is filled with purity, intelligent, and free of doubt does not hate disagreeable work nor cling to agreeable work.
explanation: A portrait rather than a rule. Such a person's relationship to their own work has gone flat — no dread on one side, no eagerness on the other.

sanskrit:
न हि देहभृता शक्यं त्यक्तुं कर्माण्यशेषतः।
यस्तु कर्मफलत्यागी स त्यागीत्यभिधीयते ॥११॥
translation: It is not possible for an embodied being to give up actions entirely. But one who abandons the fruit of action is called a relinquisher.
explanation: Krishna repeats Chapter 3's argument as a closing verdict. Total renunciation is neither virtuous nor wicked — it is unavailable, so the word must mean something else.

sanskrit:
अनिष्टमिष्टं मिश्रं च त्रिविधं कर्मणः फलम्।
भवत्यत्यागिनां प्रेत्य न तु संन्यासिनां क्वचित् ॥१२॥
translation: Unwished for, wished for, and mixed — action bears this threefold fruit after death for those who have not relinquished, but never for the renouncers.
explanation: The middle category is the honest one. Most consequences are mixed, which is exactly why chasing them is such an unreliable way to steer a life.

sanskrit:
पञ्चैतानि महाबाहो कारणानि निबोध मे।
सांख्ये कृतान्ते प्रोक्तानि सिद्धये सर्वकर्मणाम् ॥१३॥
translation: Learn from me, mighty-armed one, these five factors declared in the Sankhya teaching for the accomplishment of all actions.
explanation: Krishna is about to dismantle the idea of a single doer. The analysis is technical, and its purpose is to answer the guilt Arjuna has carried since Chapter 1.

sanskrit:
अधिष्ठानं तथा कर्ता करणं च पृथग्विधम्।
विविधाश्च पृथक्चेष्टा दैवं चैवात्र पञ्चमम् ॥१४॥
translation: The seat of action, the agent, the instruments of various kinds, the many different movements, and the divine as the fifth.
explanation: Five factors, and the last is left deliberately vague — the divine, or fate, or chance. Something not on anyone's list is always involved in what happens.

sanskrit:
शरीरवाङ्मनोभिर्यत्कर्म प्रारभते नरः।
न्याय्यं वा विपरीतं वा पञ्चैते तस्य हेतवः ॥१५॥
translation: Whatever action a person undertakes with body, speech, or mind, whether right or wrong, these five are its causes.
explanation: The scope is total: right actions and wrong ones alike. Krishna refuses to apply the analysis only where it would be comfortable to apply it.

sanskrit:
तत्रैवं सति कर्तारमात्मानं केवलं तु यः।
पश्यत्यकृतबुद्धित्वान्न स पश्यति दुर्मतिः ॥१६॥
translation: That being so, one who through an unrefined understanding sees the self alone as the agent does not see truly, being of poor judgement.
explanation: The conclusion drawn. Sole authorship is called a failure of perception rather than a moral fault, which changes what Arjuna's guilt is actually made of.

sanskrit:
यस्य नाहंकृतो भावो बुद्धिर्यस्य न लिप्यते।
हत्वापि स इमाँल्लोकान्न हन्ति न निबध्यते ॥१७॥
translation: One whose state of mind is not egoistic and whose understanding is not stained — even having slain these people, he does not slay and is not bound.
explanation: The most difficult verse in the Gita, and it should be felt as difficult. Krishna is not excusing killing but describing a state in which the killer is not the doer.

sanskrit:
ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं परिज्ञाता त्रिविधा कर्मचोदना।
करणं कर्म कर्तेति त्रिविधः कर्मसंग्रहः ॥१८॥
translation: Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower are the threefold impulse to action. The instrument, the action, and the agent are the threefold constituents of action.
explanation: A tidy piece of scaffolding. Krishna sets up six terms so that the verses following can sort the most important of them into the three qualities.

sanskrit:
ज्ञानं कर्म च कर्ता च त्रिधैव गुणभेदतः।
प्रोच्यते गुणसंख्याने यथावच्छृणु तान्यपि ॥१९॥
translation: Knowledge, action, and the agent are said in the theory of the qualities to be of three kinds according to the distinction of qualities. Hear about these as they are.
explanation: The final application of the threefold scheme. Krishna is grading the very faculties Arjuna would use to decide anything, which is a searching thing to do.

sanskrit:
सर्वभूतेषु येनैकं भावमव्ययमीक्षते।
अविभक्तं विभक्तेषु तज्ज्ञानं विद्धि सात्त्विकम् ॥२०॥
translation: That knowledge by which one sees a single imperishable being in all beings, undivided among the divided, know to be pure.
explanation: The best kind of knowing, and it is exactly what Krishna showed Arjuna in Chapter 11 and explained in Chapter 13. Everything has been building toward this.

sanskrit:
पृथक्त्वेन तु यज्ज्ञानं नानाभावान्पृथग्विधान्।
वेत्ति सर्वेषु भूतेषु तज्ज्ञानं विद्धि राजसम् ॥२१॥
translation: But that knowledge which, by reason of separateness, sees in all beings various entities of distinct kinds, know to be passionate.
explanation: Ordinary perception is classified as second-rate, not false. Seeing genuine differences is accurate as far as it goes, and it stops short of what matters.

sanskrit:
यत्तु कृत्स्नवदेकस्मिन्कार्ये सक्तमहैतुकम्।
अतत्त्वार्थवदल्पं च तत्तामसमुदाहृतम् ॥२२॥
translation: And that which clings to one single effect as though it were everything, without reason, without regard for the truth, and trivial, is declared to be dark.
explanation: A precise description of fanaticism. Krishna's mark of the worst knowledge is not error but disproportion — one thing treated as the whole of things.

sanskrit:
नियतं सङ्गरहितमरागद्वेषतः कृतम्।
अफलप्रेप्सुना कर्म यत्तत्सात्त्विकमुच्यते ॥२३॥
translation: That action which is prescribed, free from attachment, done without attraction or aversion by one who desires no fruit, is called pure.
explanation: The purest action is described entirely by what is absent from it. Nothing is added to the deed; four ordinary motives are simply not present when it is done.

sanskrit:
यत्तु कामेप्सुना कर्म साहङ्कारेण वा पुनः।
क्रियते बहुलायासं तद्राजसमुदाहृतम् ॥२४॥
translation: But that action which is done with great effort by one seeking desires, or done with egotism, is declared to be passionate.
explanation: Great effort is the giveaway. Krishna notices that desire-driven work is exhausting in a way the very same work done freely turns out not to be.

sanskrit:
अनुबन्धं क्षयं हिंसामनपेक्ष्य च पौरुषम्।
मोहादारभ्यते कर्म यत्तत्तामसमुच्यते ॥२५॥
translation: That action which is undertaken through delusion, without regard to consequences, loss, injury, or one's own capacity, is called dark.
explanation: Four things not looked at, and the last is quietly devastating. Not knowing one's own capacity is placed alongside not caring who gets hurt, as though self-ignorance were itself a form of recklessness.

sanskrit:
मुक्तसङ्गोऽनहंवादी धृत्युत्साहसमन्वितः।
सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योर्निर्विकारः कर्ता सात्त्विक उच्यते ॥२६॥
translation: The agent who is free from attachment, who does not speak of himself, who is full of firmness and enthusiasm, unchanged in success or failure, is called pure.
explanation: Utsaha, enthusiasm, is a surprising requirement. Krishna's ideal worker is not merely detached but keen, which rules out detachment as a form of coldness and makes the pure agent pleasant to work beside.

sanskrit:
रागी कर्मफलप्रेप्सुर्लुब्धो हिंसात्मकोऽशुचिः।
हर्षशोकान्वितः कर्ता राजसः परिकीर्तितः ॥२७॥
translation: The agent who is passionate, desiring the fruit of action, greedy, violent, impure, and moved by joy and sorrow, is declared to be passionate.
explanation: Joy and sorrow are listed as symptoms beside greed and violence. Being at the mercy of results is treated as the same condition, not a lesser one.

sanskrit:
अयुक्तः प्राकृतः स्तब्धः शठो नैष्कृतिकोऽलसः।
विषादी दीर्घसूत्री च कर्ता तामस उच्यते ॥२८॥
translation: The agent who is undisciplined, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, lazy, despondent, and procrastinating is called dark.
explanation: Eight failings, and the last is the most memorable. Krishna's word for a procrastinator is dirgha-sutri, someone forever drawing out the same long thread, which catches the particular exhaustion of unfinished work.

sanskrit:
बुद्धेर्भेदं धृतेश्चैव गुणतस्त्रिविधं श्रृणु।
प्रोच्यमानमशेषेण पृथक्त्वेन धनञ्जय ॥२९॥
translation: Hear now the threefold division of understanding and of firmness according to the qualities, declared fully and separately, Dhananjaya.
explanation: Two more faculties to be graded, and they are the ones a person decides with. Krishna is examining the instruments Arjuna will use the moment this ends.

sanskrit:
प्रवृत्तिं च निवृत्तिं च कार्याकार्ये भयाभये।
बन्धं मोक्षं च या वेत्ति बुद्धिः सा पार्थ सात्त्विकी ॥३०॥
translation: That understanding which knows action and withdrawal, what should and should not be done, fear and fearlessness, bondage and liberation, is pure, Partha.
explanation: Four pairs, and the first is Arjuna's exact dilemma. Pure understanding is defined as telling going forward from stepping back — which he could not do.

sanskrit:
यया धर्ममधर्मं च कार्यं चाकार्यमेव च।
अयथावत्प्रजानाति बुद्धिः सा पार्थ राजसी ॥३१॥
translation: That by which one wrongly understands righteousness and unrighteousness, and what should and should not be done, is passionate understanding, Partha.
explanation: The failure here is subtle: everything is being distinguished, just incorrectly. This is a person reasoning carefully and arriving somewhere wrong, which is far harder to correct than someone who is simply confused.

sanskrit:
अधर्मं धर्ममिति या मन्यते तमसाऽऽवृता।
सर्वार्थान्विपरीतांश्च बुद्धिः सा पार्थ तामसी ॥३२॥
translation: That understanding which, enveloped in darkness, holds unrighteousness to be righteousness and sees all things perversely, is dark, Partha.
explanation: The worst case is not confusion but confident inversion. Krishna describes a mind whose categories still work perfectly and have been swapped end for end.

sanskrit:
धृत्या यया धारयते मनःप्राणेन्द्रियक्रियाः।
योगेनाव्यभिचारिण्या धृतिः सा पार्थ सात्त्विकी ॥३३॥
translation: That firmness by which one holds together the activities of mind, breath, and senses through unwavering yoga is pure, Partha.
explanation: Firmness is defined as holding things together rather than pushing through. The image is coordination, not force, which is unusual for a word meaning resolve.

sanskrit:
यया तु धर्मकामार्थान् धृत्या धारयतेऽर्जुन।
प्रसङ्गेन फलाकाङ्क्षी धृतिः सा पार्थ राजसी ॥३४॥
translation: But that firmness by which one holds to duty, pleasure, and wealth with attachment and desire for results is passionate, Partha.
explanation: Notice that the things held onto are entirely respectable — duty, pleasure, wealth. What makes the grip passionate is the attachment, not the thing gripped.

sanskrit:
यया स्वप्नं भयं शोकं विषादं मदमेव च।
न विमुञ्चति दुर्मेधा धृतिः सा पार्थ तामसी ॥३५॥
translation: That firmness by which a dull-witted person does not give up sleep, fear, grief, despair, and arrogance is dark, Partha.
explanation: A brilliant redefinition. The same tenacity that could sustain a practice is here holding on to despair, which is exactly how despair manages to last so long.

sanskrit:
सुखं त्विदानीं त्रिविधं श्रृणु मे भरतर्षभ।
अभ्यासाद्रमते यत्र दुःखान्तं च निगच्छति ॥३६॥
translation: Now hear from me the threefold happiness, best of the Bharatas — that in which one comes to delight through practice, and reaches the end of sorrow.
explanation: Happiness is graded last, which suits a chapter of endings. And the pure kind requires practice, meaning it is learned rather than stumbled upon — an unusual claim to make about joy.

sanskrit:
यत्तदग्रे विषमिव परिणामेऽमृतोपमम्।
तत्सुखं सात्त्विकं प्रोक्तमात्मबुद्धिप्रसादजम् ॥३७॥
translation: That which at first is like poison but in the end like nectar — that happiness is declared pure, born of the serenity of one's own understanding.
explanation: The test is temporal. Krishna asks not how something feels now but how it will taste later, which is the only reliable way to tell the two kinds apart.

sanskrit:
विषयेन्द्रियसंयोगाद्यत्तदग्रेऽमृतोपमम्।
परिणामे विषमिव तत्सुखं राजसं स्मृतम् ॥३८॥
translation: That happiness which arises from the contact of the senses with their objects, at first like nectar but in the end like poison, is remembered as passionate.
explanation: The exact mirror of the previous verse, with the terms reversed. The two are identical except for the order in which the sweetness and the poison arrive.

sanskrit:
यदग्रे चानुबन्धे च सुखं मोहनमात्मनः।
निद्रालस्यप्रमादोत्थं तत्तामसमुदाहृतम् ॥३९॥
translation: That happiness which deludes the self both at the beginning and afterward, arising from sleep, indolence, and heedlessness, is declared to be dark.
explanation: The third kind never tastes good even at the start. Krishna describes a pleasure that is simply an absence of awareness, and it deludes at both ends.

sanskrit:
न तदस्ति पृथिव्यां वा दिवि देवेषु वा पुनः।
सत्त्वं प्रकृतिजैर्मुक्तं यदेभिः स्यात्ित्रभिर्गुणैः ॥४०॥
translation: There is no being on earth, or again among the gods in heaven, that is free from these three qualities born of nature.
explanation: A sweeping close to the whole analysis. Nothing anywhere escapes the scheme, which is why transcending it, rather than optimizing within it, is the goal.

sanskrit:
ब्राह्मणक्षत्रियविशां शूद्राणां च परंतप।
कर्माणि प्रविभक्तानि स्वभावप्रभवैर्गुणैः ॥४१॥
translation: The duties of brahmanas, kshatriyas, vaishyas, and shudras, scorcher of foes, are distributed according to the qualities born of their own nature.
explanation: Krishna returns to the fourfold order and grounds it, as in Chapter 4, in svabhava. The claim concerns temperament and its resulting work, not lineage.

sanskrit:
शमो दमस्तपः शौचं क्षान्तिरार्जवमेव च।
ज्ञानं विज्ञानमास्तिक्यं ब्रह्मकर्म स्वभावजम् ॥४२॥
translation: Calm, restraint, austerity, purity, patience, uprightness, knowledge, realization, and belief in what lies beyond are the natural work of a brahmana.
explanation: Nine qualities, and not one of them is a task. What is described is a disposition, which is what makes this a classification of natures rather than of jobs.

sanskrit:
शौर्यं तेजो धृतिर्दाक्ष्यं युद्धे चाप्यपलायनम्।
दानमीश्वरभावश्च क्षात्रं कर्म स्वभावजम् ॥४३॥
translation: Heroism, vigour, firmness, skill, not fleeing from battle, generosity, and a lordly bearing are the natural work of a kshatriya.
explanation: Arjuna's own description, delivered plainly. And there in the middle, unavoidable, sits the one item he has been unable to manage since the first chapter.

sanskrit:
कृषिगौरक्ष्यवाणिज्यं वैश्यकर्म स्वभावजम्।
परिचर्यात्मकं कर्म शूद्रस्यापि स्वभावजम् ॥४४॥
translation: Ploughing, protecting cattle, and trade are the natural work of a vaishya. Work consisting of service is likewise the natural work of a shudra.
explanation: The final two categories are described by activity rather than by quality. The verse is brief, and the framework it belongs to has been contested ever since.

sanskrit:
स्वे स्वे कर्मण्यभिरतः संसिद्धिं लभते नरः।
स्वकर्मनिरतः सिद्धिं यथा विन्दति तच्छृणु ॥४५॥
translation: Devoted to his own work, a person attains perfection. Hear now how one who is intent on his own work finds that perfection.
explanation: The point of the whole classification. Krishna is not ranking the four but saying that any of them, done wholly, arrives at exactly the same place.

sanskrit:
यतः प्रवृत्तिर्भूतानां येन सर्वमिदं ततम्।
स्वकर्मणा तमभ्यर्च्य सिद्धिं विन्दति मानवः ॥४६॥
translation: By worshipping with his own work the one from whom all beings arise and by whom all this is pervaded, a person attains perfection.
explanation: The mechanism given. An ordinary occupation becomes the act of worship itself, which quietly abolishes the distinction between working and praying, and makes the whole classification of duties beside the point.

sanskrit:
श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात्।
स्वभावनियतं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम् ॥४७॥
translation: Better one's own duty imperfectly performed than another's duty well performed. Performing the work dictated by one's own nature, one incurs no fault.
explanation: Chapter 3's hardest verse returns almost unchanged, now with a reason attached. Work that fits a person's nature does not stain them, even when done badly.

sanskrit:
सहजं कर्म कौन्तेय सदोषमपि न त्यजेत्।
सर्वारम्भा हि दोषेण धूमेनाग्निरिवावृताः ॥४८॥
translation: One should not abandon the work to which one is born, Kaunteya, even if it is faulty. For all undertakings are clouded by fault, as fire is clouded by smoke.
explanation: The image is exact and forgiving. Smoke does not mean the fire has failed; it means there is a fire. Krishna sets the standard at honest imperfection.

sanskrit:
असक्तबुद्धिः सर्वत्र जितात्मा विगतस्पृहः।
नैष्कर्म्यसिद्धिं परमां संन्यासेनाधिगच्छति ॥४९॥
translation: One whose understanding is unattached everywhere, whose self is conquered and desire departed, attains through renunciation the supreme perfection of freedom from action.
explanation: Freedom from action is reached through renunciation of the inner kind. The two words that confused Arjuna in the first verse have finally been reconciled.

sanskrit:
सिद्धिं प्राप्तो यथा ब्रह्म तथाप्नोति निबोध मे।
समासेनैव कौन्तेय निष्ठा ज्ञानस्य या परा ॥५०॥
translation: Learn from me in brief, Kaunteya, how one who has attained perfection also attains Brahman, that highest state of knowledge.
explanation: A summary is promised, and it runs over the next four verses. After the whole of his teaching, Krishna gathers everything into a single passage.

sanskrit:
बुद्ध्या विशुद्धया युक्तो धृत्याऽऽत्मानं नियम्य च।
शब्दादीन् विषयांस्त्यक्त्वा रागद्वेषौ व्युदस्य च ॥५१॥
translation: Endowed with a purified understanding, restraining the self with firmness, abandoning sound and the other objects of sense, and casting away attraction and aversion...
explanation: The summary begins with the intellect and moves outward to the senses. Krishna's order is deliberate — clarity first, then the letting go that clarity permits.

sanskrit:
विविक्तसेवी लघ्वाशी यतवाक्कायमानसः।
ध्यानयोगपरो नित्यं वैराग्यं समुपाश्रितः ॥५२॥
translation: ...dwelling in solitude, eating lightly, with speech, body, and mind controlled, ever devoted to the yoga of meditation, taking refuge in dispassion...
explanation: The practical middle of the summary, and everything in it is modest. Solitude, small meals, careful speech — nothing heroic, nothing beyond an ordinary person.

sanskrit:
अहङ्कारं बलं दर्पं कामं क्रोधं परिग्रहम्।
विमुच्य निर्ममः शान्तो ब्रह्मभूयाय कल्पते ॥५३॥
translation: ...having cast off egotism, force, arrogance, desire, anger, and possessiveness, unselfish and at peace, he is fit for becoming Brahman.
explanation: Six things put down, and the list nearly matches Chapter 16's demonic inventory. The summary of liberation is the exact reverse of the portrait of bondage.

sanskrit:
ब्रह्मभूतः प्रसन्नात्मा न शोचति न काङ्क्षति।
समः सर्वेषु भूतेषु मद्भक्तिं लभते पराम् ॥५४॥
translation: Having become Brahman, serene in self, he neither grieves nor desires. The same toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion to me.
explanation: The most surprising sequence in the Gita. Becoming Brahman is not the destination — it is the qualification for devotion, which Krishna places above it.

sanskrit:
भक्त्या मामभिजानाति यावान्यश्चास्मि तत्त्वतः।
ततो मां तत्त्वतो ज्ञात्वा विशते तदनन्तरम् ॥५५॥
translation: Through devotion he comes to know me in truth, what and who I am. Then, having known me in truth, he enters into me immediately.
explanation: Knowing, and then entering. Krishna orders these so that understanding is the doorway rather than the end, and the final verb is closer than knowledge.

sanskrit:
सर्वकर्माण्यपि सदा कुर्वाणो मद्व्यपाश्रयः।
मत्प्रसादादवाप्नोति शाश्वतं पदमव्ययम् ॥५६॥
translation: Though always performing all actions, one who takes refuge in me attains by my grace the eternal and imperishable abode.
explanation: The word is prasada, grace. After all the discipline described, Krishna attributes the final step to a gift — and to a person who never stopped working.

sanskrit:
चेतसा सर्वकर्माणि मयि संन्यस्य मत्परः।
बुद्धियोगमुपाश्रित्य मच्चित्तः सततं भव ॥५७॥
translation: Mentally renouncing all actions in me, holding me as supreme, resorting to the yoga of understanding, be constantly fixed in thought on me.
explanation: The instruction narrows to Arjuna alone and becomes imperative. Krishna has stopped describing anyone else, and the second person carries through to the end of the poem without returning to general statements.

sanskrit:
मच्चित्तः सर्वदुर्गाणि मत्प्रसादात्तरिष्यसि।
अथ चेत्त्वमहङ्कारान्न श्रोष्यसि विनङ्क्ष्यसि ॥५८॥
translation: Fixed in thought on me, you will pass over all difficulties by my grace. But if from egotism you will not listen, you shall perish.
explanation: The warning is sharp and personal. Krishna names the obstacle precisely — not doubt, not weakness, but the refusal that comes from simply being oneself.

sanskrit:
यदहङ्कारमाश्रित्य न योत्स्य इति मन्यसे।
मिथ्यैष व्यवसायस्ते प्रकृतिस्त्वां नियोक्ष्यति ॥५९॥
translation: If, taking refuge in egotism, you think: I shall not fight — vain is this resolve of yours. Nature will compel you.
explanation: Krishna quotes Arjuna's own words from Chapter 2 back at him. The entire conversation is framed by that sentence, which is now called simply mistaken.

sanskrit:
स्वभावजेन कौन्तेय निबद्धः स्वेन कर्मणा।
कर्तुं नेच्छसि यन्मोहात्करिष्यस्यवशोऽपि तत् ॥६०॥
translation: Bound by your own action born of your nature, Kaunteya, what you do not wish to do through delusion, you will do even against your will.
explanation: The most unsettling argument in the chapter. Krishna does not say Arjuna should fight but that he will, relocating the choice to how rather than whether.

sanskrit:
ईश्वरः सर्वभूतानां हृद्देशेऽर्जुन तिष्ठति।
भ्रामयन्सर्वभूतानि यन्त्रारूढानि मायया ॥६१॥
translation: The Lord dwells in the hearts of all beings, Arjuna, causing all beings to revolve by his power, as though they were mounted on a machine.
explanation: A startlingly mechanical image, and yantra means device or contrivance. The living world is something being turned, from a position inside each turner, which makes the Lord both the operator and the resident.

sanskrit:
तमेव शरणं गच्छ सर्वभावेन भारत।
तत्प्रसादात्परां शान्तिं स्थानं प्राप्स्यसि शाश्वतम् ॥६२॥
translation: Take refuge in him alone with your whole being, Bharata. By his grace you will attain supreme peace and the eternal abode.
explanation: The answer to the machine is not escape but refuge. And with your whole being asks for exactly the completeness Chapter 15 asked for, which is the only response the previous verse leaves available.

sanskrit:
इति ते ज्ञानमाख्यातं गुह्याद्गुह्यतरं मया।
विमृश्यैतदशेषेण यथेच्छसि तथा कुरु ॥६३॥
translation: Thus I have declared to you the knowledge that is more secret than all secrets. Reflect on it fully, and then do as you wish.
explanation: The most generous sentence in the poem. After seventeen chapters, Krishna hands the decision back without conditions — reflect, and then do as you like.

sanskrit:
सर्वगुह्यतमं भूयः श्रृणु मे परमं वचः।
इष्टोऽसि मे दृढमिति ततो वक्ष्यामि ते हितम् ॥६४॥
translation: Hear again my supreme word, the most secret of all. You are greatly beloved by me, and so I shall tell you what is good for you.
explanation: Having released Arjuna, Krishna immediately speaks once more, giving affection as his only reason. The teaching ends the way Chapter 10 began, with fondness rather than argument supplying the motive.

sanskrit:
मन्मना भव मद्भक्तो मद्याजी मां नमस्कुरु।
मामेवैष्यसि सत्यं ते प्रतिजाने प्रियोऽसि मे ॥६५॥
translation: Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, sacrifice to me, bow down to me. You shall come to me — truly I promise you, for you are dear to me.
explanation: The four imperatives from Chapter 9 return, now with a personal promise attached. Krishna gives his word, which he does nowhere else in the poem.

sanskrit:
सर्वधर्मान्परित्यज्य मामेकं शरणं व्रज।
अहं त्वा सर्वपापेभ्यो मोक्षयिष्यामि मा शुचः ॥६६॥
translation: Abandoning all duties, come to me alone for refuge. I shall free you from all wrongs. Do not grieve.
explanation: The Gita's final teaching, and its most debated line. After eighteen chapters insisting on duty, Krishna offers something above even that — and says do not grieve.

sanskrit:
इदं ते नातपस्काय नाभक्ताय कदाचन।
न चाशुश्रूषवे वाच्यं न च मां योऽभ्यसूयति ॥६७॥
translation: This is never to be spoken by you to one without austerity, nor to one without devotion, nor to one who does not wish to hear, nor to one who speaks ill of me.
explanation: A restriction placed on the teaching after it is complete. Three of the four disqualifications concern willingness rather than ability, which is telling — the barrier Krishna worries about is never intelligence.

sanskrit:
य इमं परमं गुह्यं मद्भक्तेष्वभिधास्यति।
भक्ितं मयि परां कृत्वा मामेवैष्यत्यसंशयः ॥६८॥
translation: One who, with supreme devotion to me, declares this highest secret among my devotees shall doubtless come to me.
explanation: Teaching is named as its own path. Krishna offers the same destination to whoever passes this on, which is how the conversation escapes the chariot.

sanskrit:
न च तस्मान्मनुष्येषु कश्िचन्मे प्रियकृत्तमः।
भविता न च मे तस्मादन्यः प्रियतरो भुवि ॥६९॥
translation: And there is no one among people who does more that is dear to me than he, nor shall there be another on earth dearer to me.
explanation: The highest praise in the Gita goes not to the sage or the warrior but to the person who explains it to someone else. Transmission is ranked above attainment.

sanskrit:
अध्येष्यते च य इमं धर्म्यं संवादमावयोः।
ज्ञानयज्ञेन तेनाहमिष्टः स्यामिति मे मतिः ॥७०॥
translation: And one who studies this righteous dialogue of ours — by him I would be worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge. This is my view.
explanation: Reading the text is itself called a sacrifice. Krishna extends the circle again, to anyone who merely takes the trouble to study what was said here.

sanskrit:
श्रद्धावाननसूयश्च श्रृणुयादपि यो नरः।
सोऽपि मुक्तः शुभाँल्लोकान्प्राप्नुयात्पुण्यकर्मणाम् ॥७१॥
translation: And the person who listens with faith and without carping shall also be freed, and shall attain the happy worlds of those of meritorious deeds.
explanation: The circle widens a final time to include mere listeners. Faith and the absence of a sneer are all that is asked — where Chapter 9 also began.

sanskrit:
कच्चिदेतच्छ्रुतं पार्थ त्वयैकाग्रेण चेतसा।
कच्चिदज्ञानसंमोहः प्रनष्टस्ते धनञ्जय ॥७२॥
translation: Has this been heard by you, Partha, with a concentrated mind? Has your delusion born of ignorance been destroyed, Dhananjaya?
explanation: Krishna ends by asking rather than declaring. After all the certainty, the teaching closes with a question about whether any of it actually worked, and he waits for Arjuna to answer.

sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाचनष्टो मोहः स्मृतिर्लब्धा त्वत्प्रसादान्मयाच्युत।
स्थितोऽस्मि गतसन्देहः करिष्ये वचनं तव ॥७३॥
translation: Arjuna said: My delusion is destroyed and I have gained recollection through your grace, Achyuta. I stand firm, my doubts gone. I shall do your word.
explanation: The answer the whole poem has been waiting for. Note smriti, recollection — Arjuna has not learned something new but remembered what he already was.

sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाचइत्यहं वासुदेवस्य पार्थस्य च महात्मनः।
संवादमिममश्रौषमद्भुतं रोमहर्षणम् ॥७४॥
translation: Sanjaya said: Thus I have heard this wondrous dialogue between Vasudeva and the great-souled Partha, causing my hair to stand on end.
explanation: Sanjaya returns, and his response is the same physical one Arjuna had in Chapter 11. The listener at the far end of the report has been changed too.

sanskrit:
व्यासप्रसादाच्छ्रुतवानेतद्गुह्यमहं परम्।
योगं योगेश्वरात्कृष्णात्साक्षात्कथयतः स्वयम् ॥७५॥
translation: By the grace of Vyasa I have heard this supreme secret, this yoga, from Krishna the master of yoga himself, declaring it in person.
explanation: A note of gratitude to his own teacher, and a reminder of the chain of transmission. Sanjaya heard it through a gift, exactly as Arjuna did.

sanskrit:
राजन्संस्मृत्य संस्मृत्य संवादमिममद्भुतम्।
केशवार्जुनयोः पुण्यं हृष्यामि च मुहुर्मुहुः ॥७६॥
translation: Remembering again and again this wondrous and holy dialogue between Keshava and Arjuna, I rejoice again and again, O King.
explanation: The verb doubles twice in a single line — remembering and remembering, rejoicing and rejoicing. Sanjaya's delight is in the recollection, not only the event.

sanskrit:
तच्च संस्मृत्य संस्मृत्य रूपमत्यद्भुतं हरेः।
विस्मयो मे महान् राजन् हृष्यामि च पुनः पुनः ॥७७॥
translation: And remembering again and again that most wondrous form of Hari, great is my astonishment, O King, and I rejoice again and again.
explanation: What Sanjaya cannot stop returning to is the vision, not the argument. The Gita's last witness is left holding an image rather than a conclusion.

sanskrit:
यत्र योगेश्वरः कृष्णो यत्र पार्थो धनुर्धरः।
तत्र श्रीर्विजयो भूतिर्ध्रुवा नीतिर्मतिर्मम ॥७८॥
translation: Wherever there is Krishna, the master of yoga, and wherever there is Partha the archer, there, I am convinced, are fortune, victory, prosperity, and sound conduct.
explanation: The poem ends with a teacher and a student named side by side, and with right conduct placed last. Everything rests on those two being in the same chariot.
